en: Preface: Now, as for the origin of this matter: writing is used to expound principles, and principles serve to verify the mind. When the mind is correct, affairs are carried out and all things are rectified;

when deportment is respectful, it necessarily moves things to respond. This is why the teaching of the Buddha must first emphasize the training in precepts (*śīla*). The training in precepts is the foundation for concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
The foremost of these. If one can indeed apply oneself with diligence to this, how could meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) fail to arise?

Throughout the world, those who preach the doctrines and those who preach Chan are as numerous as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds; yet when investigated, the single school of Vinaya is as swift in its efficacy as a shadow following a form or an echo responding to a sound.

Examining its essential purpose, it is nothing other than the desire for people to clarify the mind and realize their nature (*dharmatā*). If one can maintain this awareness in daily life, causing both body and mind—
When all things are gathered and condensed, how could the six perfections and myriad practices not be subsumed within the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom?
Amidst the dust and clamor of the mundane world, I have occasionally stilled my breath and severed external conditions to sit in quietude upon a single mat.

Therein, I have personally realized that within the inexhaustible treasury, all things manifest in perfect fusion, each clearly understood. Is it not truly so that a single hair can swallow the vast ocean, and a mustard seed can contain Mount Sumeru? Indeed, it is so.

The Vinaya Master Zhaoqing Yijie presented me with a single volume of his handwritten notes on the *Gandhakuṭī-vyākhyāna*. This coincided precisely with the season when the shadows of paulownia trees drip with dew and the osmanthus ripens and wafts its fragrance.

After reading it once with ritual purity, I recognized that he possessed a profound mastery of the Buddhist scriptures, specifically the five sections and three groups of precepts (*pañca-skandha-tri-śīla*).
He has enabled both monastics and laypeople alike to comprehend these texts; they shall surely uphold even half a verse in their practice.

Whether standing, sitting, or reclining, he practiced without interruption day and night. As he was about to behold the mani-jewel and Brahma-net light reflecting one another, it was truly not to fail the noble lineage of the Precious Flower.
He has provided detailed annotations on these strategic methods to graciously benefit later students; who could possibly abandon such a concise and clear model?

In the ninth month of the *wuyin* year of the Kangxi era, Yang Yongjian of Haining composed this preface for the "Fuguo Xuan" (The Studio of Not Transgressing) regarding the sentient beings of the *sāhasra-lokadhātu*.
Though their species differ in a thousand ways and the Buddhas who appear in the world preach the Dharma in ten thousand distinct manners, to speak of them in brief:
There are only the Sūtras, Vinaya, and Śāstras. The Sūtras elucidate meditative concentration (samādhi); the Vinaya elucidates ethical discipline (śīla); and the Śāstras elucidate wisdom (prajñā).

These three—discipline, concentration, and wisdom—are the guiding principles of the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) and the foundation of all practices. In the kingdom of Magadha, when discussing the ocean of Buddha-fields, they are called "Sūtras.
At the outskirts of Gayā City, [the Buddha] engaged in dialogues with various bodhisattvas concerning the various types of karmic retribution.
That which is called "discourse" (*sūtra*) refers to the causal conditions. That which is called "vinaya" refers to the initial formulation of the Bodhisattva Prātimokṣa beneath the Bodhi tree;
this is the Mahāyāna Tripiṭaka spoken by the Buddha. At Vārāṇasī, he taught the *sūtras* to the five bhikṣus;
at Rājagṛha, he taught the *vinaya* to Sudinna; and at the Monkey Pond in Vaiśālī, for [Vatsa]...

The son of the Elder (Śāriputra) expounded the Abhidharma; this is precisely the Small Vehicle Tripiṭaka spoken by the Buddha. Both Sūtra and Śāstra were transmitted through five [successive] masters, whereas the Vinaya was spoken solely by the Buddha.
From the time after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, even Mañjuśrī and Upāli did not dare to add or subtract a single word.

It is like the rites, music, and military expeditions, which must issue from the Son of Heaven; the feudal lords and great officers could not exercise independent authority over them. As for the Buddha...
After the [Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa, Mahākāśyapa led the various arhats to assemble the Tripiṭaka on Vulture Peak Mountain.
Mañjuśrī, Maitreya, and the various mahāsattvas led Ānanda to assemble the Mahāyāna. Therefore, Qingliang said: "The Avataṃsaka, Prajñāpāramitā, and others constitute the Mahāyāna Sūtra Piṭaka;
the Bodhisattva Precepts and the *Śīlasamvara-sūtra* constitute the Vinaya; and the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* [constitute the Abhidharma]."

The *Abhidharma* constitutes the treatises (*śāstra*). The four Āgamas of the Hīnayāna constitute the sūtras; the five divisions of the Vinaya constitute the precepts (*śīla*); and the *Mahāvibhāṣā* and other works constitute the treatises.

Worldly sentient beings receive and practice these three categories of Dharma. Those who contemplate the mind in accordance with the teachings are said to be practicing the training in higher mind (*adhicitta-śikṣā*).

Those who follow the Vinaya and maintain their physical conduct are said to be practicing the training in higher ethics (*adhiśīla-śikṣā*). Those who rely on the treatises to delight their speech are said to be practicing the training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*).

The training in higher wisdom (*adhiprajñā-śikṣā*)—thus the three untainted trainings (*anāsrava-śikṣā*) are established—and there is no fruit of either the Great or Small Vehicles that cannot be realized.
For this reason, during the Buddha’s lifetime, there were bhikṣus who upheld the Sūtras, bhikṣus who upheld the Vinaya, and bhikṣus who upheld the Mātṛkā.
After the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, there likewise arose the distinction between the three schools of Chan, Teaching (*jiao*), and Vinaya (*lü*). Eventually...

During the reign of Emperor Ming of the Han, [An] Shigao was dispatched to seek the Dharma, and [An] Sheng and [Kāśyapa] Mātanga transmitted the teachings. By the beginning of the Cao Wei dynasty, the monastic community had become very numerous;

however, they had not yet received the full precepts, relying instead on the mere shaving of their hair as a distinction from the common people. Later, Dharmakāla arrived, who recited the various Vinayas and established the *karmavācanā* for the conferral of full ordination (*upasampadā*), employing ten preceptors according to the standard.
This marked the beginning of the formal Vinaya tradition in China. During the Yao Qin, Kumārajīva translated the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.
He recited the Vinaya and the Brahmajāla Sūtra Precept Manual. Together with Zhu Fonian, Buddhayaśas translated the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya-piṭaka*.
During the Liu Song dynasty, the Kasmirian śramaṇa Buddhabhadra translated the *Mahīśāsaka-vinaya*. The Vinaya Master Sengyou of the Liang dynasty extensively propagated the *Vinaya* (Piṇī).
During the Tang dynasty, the Nanshan Vinaya Master Xuanchao composed the *Jieshu*, the *Jiemoshu*, and the *Shichao*, thereby propagating the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*.

Because of this, it shone brilliantly throughout the world; it was called the School of Practicing the Teachings to Prevent Error and Cease Evil. During the transition between the Jin, Wei, Chen, and Sui dynasties, this school flourished greatly.

During the Jiayu era of Emperor Renzong of the Song dynasty, Vinaya Master Kaixuan Yunkan composed the *Huizheng ji* (Record of Rectifying the Teachings), and Vinaya Master Lingzhi Zhaoyi authored the *Zichi ji* (Record of Supporting and Maintaining). From the Yuan and Ming dynasties onward, the Vinaya school was heard of no more. Fortunately, now...

On Mount Hua, he met the Venerable Master Yue Lao, from whom he diligently propagated the study of the precepts. He produced the *Zhizu Erchi* (The Two Codes of Restraint and Action), the *Hei Bai Fosu* (The Bi-monthly Retreat for Clergy and Laity), and the *Chuanjie Zhengfan* (The Authentic Model for Transmitting the Precepts).
He performed the *karmavācanā*, established the fixed period of the summer retreat, restored what was ruined, and promoted what had fallen into disuse.

His brilliance surpassed that of his predecessors and his legacy benefited those who followed; none could rival him in the great field of the Dharma. Great Master Yijie of Zhaokong Temple received his teachings most profoundly and widely proclaimed this wondrous [tradition].

Haizongyou has produced an annotated commentary on the essential points of the Vinaya, titled the *Xiangru ji* (Fragrant Milk Record). It harmonizes both doctrine and practice while elucidating both phenomena and principle;
it is truly a banner of light for this degenerate age and a blue lotus (*utpala*) within the Dharma-gate.
Formerly, our Master Kangzang circulated the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" as a separate work, and Master Gui of Xuancheng compiled it as the "Life-Buoy for the Ocean of Suffering. Now...

I have composed this "Record of the Incense and Milk" with the desire to lead all sentient beings of the Dharma-realm together into the nature-ocean of Vairocana, drawing from the milk of Avalokiteśvara’s hand of great compassion so that its fragrance may be distributed endlessly. Is the merit of such a worthy succession not more than a small contribution?
I have examined this source in detail to inform those who come to study; how would it be to create a strategy for their inspiration? At this time.

Now, the essential core of the *Vinaya* is the foundation for those with the mind of the Great Way to cultivate, realize, and benefit living beings.
If any person can read these words, give rise to this vow, and practice this conduct, they are identical to the *Perfect Enlightenment*, without duality or distinction.
Those who wish to deliver sentient beings and seek the Buddha-way must ensure their practice rests upon a single mind; then, naturally, the two benefits will be accomplished. Its...
If one's practices and vows are not yet complete, there will be no means by which to realize entry [into the path].

Out of compassion for this situation, my late Preceptor selected verses and mantras from the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (*Śīla-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* as well as from the Secret Mantra sections, compiling them into a single volume titled *The Essential Essentials of Daily Vinaya Practice*. His aim was to ensure that those who have newly resolved their minds [to attain enlightenment]...

Study and contemplate these teachings thoroughly; practice them morning and evening so that you may gradually realize the fruits of the Path and avoid wasting the offerings of the faithful in vain or letting your time pass in emptiness.
It is said that when the Great Sages deliver sentient beings, their merit lies solely in the precepts. From the sages of antiquity to those of later times, the principle remains one and the same.
I recall that in the past, my Upādhyāya admonished the assembly, saying: "The scripture used today is the wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle. It is the foundation for advancing on the Path;

its practice governs body and mind, and its principle returns to the Perfect and Sudden. You must not regard it as a mere ordinary verse or incantation. Know that its essential efficacy is supreme! How profound indeed!
You should practice and uphold it throughout your lives, never being negligent or lax. (Yu) — This was when he personally attended upon him.

In my later years, I have fortunately been spurred on by your exhortations. Like a draft horse, I press forward without being permitted even a moment’s rest. For twenty years, I have remained diligent and alert.

In the spring of the Jiazi year, while residing at Zhaokong Temple, I accepted the requests of the assembly to lecture; I provided word-by-word annotations and commentaries, which I entitled the *Xiangru ji* (Record of Fragrant Milk).
The Great Compassionate Hand of Avalokiteśvara nourishes all sentient beings with fragrant milk. I, for my part, am ashamed of my superficial learning; how could I dare to presume to receive this?
Yet, with the single-minded incense of a lowly fool, I offer it to repay the profound debt of gratitude for the Dharma-milk of the Venerable Master.
Fearing that as the days pass, the great rivers may run dry, I have taken an ancient mirror to reflect upon the present. [End of] Text.

It is not for its literary elegance; rather, its language draws upon the classical scriptures. If one can truly rely on this to guide one’s conduct, it will indeed be of great benefit to future students.

The four lines of the verse do not exceed two meanings. First, regarding the three categories of precepts (*tripuñja*), the first line subsumes the *saṃvara-śīla* (the morality of restraint).

The second phrase subsumes the precept of benefiting sentient beings; the third and fourth phrases subsume the precept of gathering virtuous dharmas. These two are categorized according to the Four Great Vows:

the first phrase is the vow to study the Dharma-gates; the second phrase is the vow to deliver sentient beings; and the third and fourth phrases comprise the two vows to sever afflictions and to attain Buddhahood.

These are to be correlated with the respective passages. All of these meanings are easy to contemplate; therefore, the first verse has been briefly explained, while the remainder have been left implicit and undeveloped.
I shall now clarify them first, so that the reader may understand them for themselves.
The intent of this annotated commentary is exclusively to elucidate the meaning of the present text;
therefore, regardless of whether they belong to the Sūtras or the Vinaya, all passages that correspond are cited here as aids for clarification.
This mantra belongs to the Secret Section (Guhyaka). It has not been translated since ancient times; following the example of past masters, I dare not attempt a forced interpretation.
If one can indeed recite it with devotion according to the ritual, one will ultimately be able to eliminate calamities and generate merit.

Those written on the top line belong exclusively to the Buddha’s own verses and mantras. Those marked with one space below the line and labeled as "compiled" (集) are the writings collected by the Master [the author].

Those marked with the character "explanation" (釋) are the words of the present author's commentary. If these distinctions were not clearly indicated, there would be a danger of confusing the original composition with the subsequent commentary.
The verses for the offering ritual were originally not included in the root text; however, since they are recited at the time of eating, how could crows fail to understand them?
Therefore, they have been appended here with a brief commentary, so that those who practice them will not encounter difficulties or doubts.

The characteristics of the precepts at the end of the verses are fully elucidated in the various schools. This brief commentary is provided for the convenience of beginners in their study and contemplation.

Now, prior to the title and the text, I shall also provide a preliminary exposition of these three thematic gates.
First: Regarding the causes and conditions for the arising of the Teaching, according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*:
Just as Sumeru, the King of Mountains, does not tremble without cause or condition, nor from minor causes and conditions, so too is it with the arising of the Vinaya Teaching;
it possesses many causes and conditions. First, to serve as a model for teachers and disciples; second, to serve as the foundation for conduct and rest; third, to extinguish [transgressions]...
1. Because of the various afflictions and karmic actions; 2. For the sake of generating all merit and wisdom; 3. For the sake of accomplishing the threefold aggregate of precepts (tri-śikṣā-saṃvara);
4. For the sake of propagating the four great vows; 5. For the sake of maintaining and upholding body and mind; 6. For the sake of benefiting oneself and others; 7.
For the sake of giving rise to the primary cause of enlightenment; 8. For the sake of perfecting the fruit of Buddhahood. Possessing these ten conditions.
This teaching was caused to arise.

Second, regarding the inclusion within the teachings of the *piṭakas* and *yānas*, three categories are opened therein. First, as for inclusion by *piṭaka*, there are three *piṭakas*: first, the three *piṭakas* of Sūtra, Vinaya, and Śāstra.

The Sūtras are the "teachings of transformation" (*hua-jiao*), which means opening, inducing, transforming, and guiding. The Vinaya is the "teaching of regulation" (*zhi-jiao*), which means restraining and limiting.
This is a treatise (*śāstra*). As for its discourse, it deduces and explains the meaning of the Sūtras and Vinaya.

The verses are from the "Chapter on Pure Conduct" (*Śīla-viśuddhi-parivarta*) of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and belong to the transformative teaching (*pariyatti*), being included within the Sūtra Piṭaka. This is determined by the sense of the questions and answers, as well as the establishment of the title.

The characteristics of the precepts following the verses belong to the *vinaya* (prescriptive teaching) and are subsumed within the *Vinaya Piṭaka*. However, because they lack questions, answers, or commentaries, they are not subsumed under the *śāstra* (treatises).
Second, outside of the first three of the four collections (*piṭakas*), there is added one *dhāraṇī* collection.
The various mantras following the verses are *dhāraṇīs*. While the sūtras and vinayas are subsumed under the exoteric teachings, the mantras are subsumed under the esoteric teachings. Third.

The two collections [of scriptures] consist of the Śrāvaka and the Bodhisattva. Since both aspire to benefit others rather than focusing solely on themselves, they are subsumed within the Bodhisattva collection and not the Śrāvaka.

Regarding the inclusion within the successive vehicles (*yāna*), there are two types of vehicles. First, the teachings of revelation clarify the five vehicles, namely: human, celestial, śrāvaka, pratyekabuddha, and... [bodhisattva].
"Awakening" refers to the Bodhisattva. This verse is Mañjuśrī’s response to Jñānaśrī;
it belongs to the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna and distinguishes itself from the previous four vehicles. Second, Esoteric Buddhism clarifies four vehicles, namely:
Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, Vaipulya, and Vajra. The *Ratnarāja-sūtra* states that all dhāraṇīs arise from the most supreme Vaipulya Mahāyāna.
These thirty-seven mantras flow forth from within the Vajrayāna; they are all subsumed under the latter two vehicles and do not belong to the former two types of vehicles.

Regarding the latter, the teachings that subsume them, there are two kinds of teaching: first, the twelve divisions of the teaching (*dvādaśāṅga-dharma-pravacana*). First, the Sūtra (*sūtra*), which is translated here as "契" (*qiè*) [the concordant].
1. Sūtra: This refers to the prose sections of the text. 2. Geya: This is translated as "repeated verse"; it refers to verses that restate the preceding prose.
3. Vyākaraṇa: This is translated as "prediction"; it refers to the proclamation of the attainment of the fruit of realization. 4. Gāthā: This is translated as "isolated verse."

Five: *Geya* (孤諷), which means "Verses"; these are verses recited in response to a discourse. Six: *Udāna* (優陀那), which means "Unprompted Utterance"; these are spoken spontaneously without being requested.
Seven: *Nidāna* (尼陀那), which means "Causes and Conditions"; these are spoken on account of a specific occasion. Eight: *Avadāna* (阿波陀那).
8. Avadāna (Piyū): This is translated as "Parable," meaning that understanding is attained by taking a metaphor. 9. Itivṛttaka:
This is translated as "Past Events," referring to deeds performed in former times. 10. Jātaka: This is translated as "Birth Stories," referring to the taking of birth in former times.
*Vaipulya*. This is translated as "Extensive" (*fangguǎng*), referring to a broad discourse that accords with principle. Eleven: *Adbhutadharma*.

This is translated as "Unprecedented Phenomena," referring to rare and marvelous spiritual powers. Twelve: *Upadeśa*. This is translated as "Exegesis" (*lùnyì*), consisting of successive questions and answers.
The present [text] is subsumed under three categories of the threefold teaching: *Itivṛttaka*, *Nidāna*, and *Vaipulya*. It is not...
The remaining nine schools [of the Lesser Vehicle].

Second: First, according to Huayan Master Xianshou’s *Five Teachings*, the Hinayana teachings speak only of the emptiness of the self (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). Even if they occasionally mention the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*), it is not clearly explained.
They establish the roots of defilement and purity based solely on the six consciousnesses and the three poisons, and thus do not exhaust the source of all phenomena.
Therefore, there are many disputes and debates. Second, the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna is also called the Partial Teaching (*bhinnadharmaparyāya*).
Within it, it is taught only that all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty; it does not yet exhaust the principles of the Mahāyāna Dharma, and is thus called "Initial.

It teaches only the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena, asserting that some do not attain Buddhahood, and is thus called "Partial. Third, the Final Teaching is also called the True Teaching (*bhūtadharmaparyāya*). It teaches the *tathāgatagarbha*. Following...
The ālayavijñāna is established through conditions; conditioned arising is non-arising; all things are thus.

Those of the two vehicles with fixed natures and icchantikas devoid of nature shall all attain Buddhahood. Only then is the ultimate teaching of the Mahāyāna fully exhausted; therefore, it is called the "Final."

It is called "Real" because it accords with the true principle. Fourth, the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao) does not speak of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) in general, but only discriminates the True Nature (*tathatā*).
It likewise lacks the distinctions of the eight consciousnesses; it reviles the teachings and exhorts detachment, disparages appearances and dissolves the mind.
Simply when not a single thought arises, one is named a Buddha. Because it does not rely on the gradual progression of stages and positions, it is called "Sudden. Fifth, the Perfect [Teaching]...
What is taught in the scriptures is exclusively the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Its nature-ocean is perfectly interfused; its dependent origination is unimpeded;

its characteristics are mutually identical and mutually inclusive; like Indra’s net, they are layered upon one another; and as principal and attendant elements, they are inexhaustible. Therefore, it is called "Perfect" (*yuan*).

Much of the verse-text of the *Avataṃsaka* belongs precisely to this Perfect Teaching. As a verse says: "Entering the profound Dharma-realm, the mind is without obstruction. And again: "Attaining the unimpeded eye."
"Beholding all Buddhas" refers to the complete meaning [of the ultimate]. Regarding the dharmas that are expounded, it also encompasses the previous three [categories].
A verse says: "Diligently seeking the Buddha-way, the mind never tires. It also says: "Fully endowed with and replete in all wholesome dharmas.

These refer to the categorized teachings (*vibhāga-śāsana*). A verse says: "Attaining the pure dharma-gate, forever free from defilement. It also says: "Accomplishing the Buddha-body and realizing the unconditioned."
The Dharma of Characteristics (*lakṣaṇadharma*) is the Initial Teaching (*ādikarmika-śāsana*). A verse states: "He establishes great assemblies of giving to demonstrate the principle of suchness.
It further states: "All attain the wondrous Dharma, which is ultimately pure. This is the Final Teaching (*niṣṭhā-śāsana*). A verse states: "The mind attains liberation and abides immovably."

It is further stated: "Entering the first stage and attaining the dharma of immovability" refers to the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*). This teaching possesses that which it universally penetrates while lacking that which it restricts.

Therefore, this Perfect Teaching (*yuan-jiao*) is broad in its expression, encompassing immeasurable vehicles of doctrine; yet it is profound in its expression, revealing only the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*).
By this standard, one should know that this section is subsumed within the Perfect-Sudden (*yuantun*) teaching.

Third, regarding the "doctrinal tenets" (*zongqiu*) that are expounded: what is taken as the primary principle of this specific school is called the "tenet" (*zong*); the ultimate destination to which the tenet leads is called the "purpose" (*qiu*).

First, there is the general [purpose], followed by the specific. Generally speaking, the tenet consists of following the Buddha’s precepts for one's own practice—ceasing evil and performing good—to purify the ground of the mind.

The Buddha-way for transforming others is identical to Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-avabodha*). Taking "one suchness without duality" as its goal, it opens five distinct pairs: First, the pair of Teaching and Meaning:
taking the characteristics of the Vinaya teachings as the primary principle, and causing one to awaken to the wondrous meaning of the verses and mantras as the goal.

Second, the pair of Practice and Vow: taking the arising of practice according to specific circumstances as the primary principle, and skillful aspiration as the goal. Third, the pair of Body... [text continues]

1. The correspondence between mind and body: taking the cultivation of vows through the body as its essence (*mūla*), and preventing the mind from being distracted as its goal (*prayojana*). 2. The correspondence between wisdom and compassion:
taking the movement of the mind through great wisdom as its essence, and benefiting sentient beings through great compassion as its goal. 3. The correspondence between cause and effect:

taking the perfection of compassion and wisdom as the cause as its essence, and the realization and attainment of the qualities of fruition as its goal. These five proceed from the former to the latter, developing progressively.
They arise through mutual dependence.
Fourth, a general explanation of the title, which is divided into two parts;
first, the explanation of the title "Dharma."
*The Essential Essentials for Daily Use in the Vinaya* [Commentary]: "The Essential Essentials for Daily Use in the Vinaya" is the general title of this collection.

In contrast to the verses and mantras—which possess the distinction between that which is regulated and that which effects transformation—the title serves as the expressive medium (*nengquan*). It derives its name from the *vinaya* (teachings on regulation) and belongs to the Vinaya Piṭaka.
The verses and mantras constitute that which is explained; they form the text based on the *vaipulya* (transformative) teachings and belong to the Sūtra Piṭaka.

Now, regarding the seven ways in which titles are established by the compilers of the sūtras, this work takes only the Dharma as its heading, just as among a person’s six sense organs, the eyes are primary; by opening those eyes, [one sees clearly].

Yet all the sense faculties manifest together. Upon seeing this title, one knows that there are such verses and dhāraṇīs. Furthermore, *vinaya* is the general name; "daily essential" is the specific name.
Its primary principle (*mūla*) is to cease evil and cultivate goodness; its purpose (*prayojana*) is to teach and transform sentient beings so they may enter the Buddha-way together.
It is called "ceasing" (*śīla/vinaya*) because it guards against all evils; it is called "exertion" (*pragraha*) because it encourages the cultivation of all virtues.
"Good. Therefore, it is called *karman* (action). *Vinaya* has the meaning of "stopping"; that which is evil should be stopped. It is essential for daily life. *Karman* has the meaning of "doing";
that which is good should be practiced. (The above is a brief explanation; the following is a detailed commentary. The Sanskrit term *vinaya*, in the language of China, means "skillful governance.
This refers to being able to govern all evils within oneself, and also being able to govern all evils among sentient beings. This [name] is derived from its functional capacity.
It is named [Vinaya]. It is also translated as "Discipline" (調伏, *dāmyati*), meaning to train and refine the three karmas (*trikarma*) and to subdue transgressions and faults.

"Training and refining" applies to both types of observance (*dharani*), while "subduing" specifically clarifies the cessation of evil. This name is derived from its functional application. The direct translation is "Law" (律, *vinaya*). "Law" refers to legal precepts;
it is named after the Dharma, meaning the adjudication of gravity and lightness, and the opening or closing, maintaining or violating of rules—what is not the Dharma.
Because it cannot be stabilized. For example, in a state, rewards, punishments, and proclamations must issue from the sovereign;
if the feudal lords usurp authority and the commoners lose their faith, then ruin will come before long. The Buddha-dharma is likewise: within the great trichiliocosm...
The Buddha is the Dharma King, and the Vinaya is his decree. Bodhisattvas and those of the Two Vehicles dare not add or subtract a single word.
If others were permitted to speak [of it], sentient beings would not revere it, and the Dharma would not endure for long. These two characters represent the explicit teaching.
As for daily practice: from dawn until dusk, and from dusk until dawn, throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, one employs this verse-mantra to bind body and mind.

This enables the beginner who has received the precepts to, amidst the five sensory objects and during the four modes of deportment—whether waking early, washing their feet, or encountering various circumstances—immediately give rise to great vows to remain detached from all [defilements].

To transcend faults and evils, one should uphold secret mantras to subdue the three karmas, universally causing all sentient beings to equally receive the benefits of the Dharma and together realize the path of enlightenment.

This is because the initial gateway to entering the Way takes the arousal of the bodhicitta as its primary focus; those who wish to ascend to the stages of the precepts must first establish this resolve.
Making the establishment of vows the priority: when the mind is aroused, sentient beings can be saved; when the vow is established, the Buddha-way can be accomplished.
For this reason, when first learning the precepts, one must recite these verses and mantras. If they are practiced daily, there will come a day of realization and entry [into the Way].
It is like a king fighting against an enemy: he must obtain a valiant general to lead the troops forward before victory can be achieved.

The victor prevails. It is the same for a person who has first resolved to attain enlightenment (*prathamacittotpādika*): wishing to wage war against the enemy thieves of birth and death (*saṃsāra*), one must first employ this verse-mantra.
Only by advancing with courage, governing body and mind, and diligently cultivating wholesome dharmas can one subdue the demonic armies of affliction (*kleśa*).
Thus, Master Huiyuan said: "The mind is the sovereign of the single body; it [governs] the myriad..."
The foundation of the Dharma is the mind-king. If the mind-king is upright, then the six thieves cannot invade; right mindfulness manifests before one, making it easy to enter the Way.
Today, I employ verses and mantras to rectify body and mind—what is called "transforming the familiar into the unfamiliar" and "transforming the unfamiliar into the familiar.
By applying the mind in this way, one's practice is renewed daily; therefore, it is called "daily use. These two characters signify actual practice.

The preceding [section] explains this. *Vinaya* refers to the teaching (*jiao*), while "daily practice" (*riyong*) refers to conduct (*xing*). If there is teaching without conduct, the teaching is established in vain;
if there is conduct without teaching, the conduct is erroneous. Only when teaching and conduct are mutually integrated do they begin to achieve their supreme utility.
Zen Master Wuzu Fayan said: "A monk (nàzǐ) guards the city of his mind and upholds the precepts; he contemplates them day and night and practices them morning and evening.
This is what that means. "Essential" (qièyào) refers to being intimate and concise, meaning it is not remote, diffuse, or redundant.
It means that these verses and mantras are close to one's body and mind, like a tool for cutting things; this is the Way.

Virtue is the essential task. Just as one must follow a path, those who study the precepts must, at every moment—whether dressing or eating, prostrating or meditating, or even when coming and going, walking, or attending to the calls of nature—restrain their faculties and consciousness so that not even a trace of negligence occurs.
This is likened to using a hook to subdue an elephant or a chain to control a monkey. Now...
Recite this verse-mantra while concentrating the mind on a single point, without interruption day or night; then there is nothing that cannot be accomplished.
However, one must not treat this verse-mantra lightly, regarding it as merely a matter of recitation.

One should know that it is, in fact, the great vow of the Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas to seek enlightenment above and transform beings below, as well as the secret and wondrous Dharma of the Buddhas' Mind-Seal.

If those who receive the precepts can truly give rise to a mind of compassion, possess authentic mindfulness, and—relying on phenomena to manifest the principle—make vows and practice accordingly, they are identical to ultimate awakening, without duality or distinction. These two words [refer to this].
"Urgent" (*qiè*) refers to the principle (*lǐ*): because it is most intimately connected with body and mind. "Essential" (*yào*) refers to the fruit (*guǒ*):
because it is the vital core of the path and its realization. Combining these four gates, they are collectively titled *The Daily Essentials of the Vinaya*.
In the "Chapter on Pure Conduct," Zhishou asks: "How does a bodhisattva attain faultless actions of body, speech, and mind? How does one attain perfection?"
[The question was: "Are the fulfillment of the *dāna-pāramitā* and the *śīla-pāramitā* not, in this context, the meaning of *vinaya*?

is this not, in this context, the meaning of daily practice (*jìnyòng*)? Furthermore, Zhishou asked: "How can one [attain] equality with all sentient beings..."
To be born [into this teaching] is to have it as one’s reliance, one’s refuge, one’s torch, and one’s guide—is this not the essential meaning within this context?

"The Bhikṣu Hongjietong of Baohua Mountain, Reading and Re-compiling.
[Commentary] Regarding the three points concerning the person: first is the place of residence, "Baohua," which is the name of a mountain. This mountain was opened by the Venerable Baozhi.
It is opened up. Because it manifests its name through the people [who dwell there], it is called "Treasure" (Bǎo). As for "Flower" (Huā), the mountain resembles the shape of a lotus flower.
The record states it is seventy li from Jinling and fifty li from Juong. It is surrounded by a multitude of peaks, their forms resembling hanging lotuses. The *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says:

Among the names of the Buddhas, there is one called Mount Hua Buddha. Empress Dowager Li once suddenly dreamed of a mountain entirely covered in lotuses;

As for not mentioning the sūtras and śāstras but mentioning the precepts (*śīla*): among the three trainings of the untainted (*anāsrava-śikṣā-traya*), there is certainly nothing that is not broad [in its scope].
However, because he specialized in propagating and benefiting others through the Vinaya school, it is said that he "propagated the precepts. "Bhikṣu" is a general designation for the Saṃgha;

Master Liangruo said: "The principle-body of self-nature is only realized through the study of the teachings; it is for this reason that one takes them up.
Now, residing at Mount Hua, he extensively expounds the Vinaya and transforms sentient beings, suddenly penetrating the source-ground of the mind.
According to the biography, the Master’s courtesy name was Jianyue. He was the son of the Xu family from Bailu County in Yunnan, with ancestral roots in Jurong, Jiangnan.
At the beginning of the Hongwu era, when Yunnan and Qianzhou were opened, he was enfeoffed as a General of Martial Valor for his military merit and became a hereditary Commander-in-Chief.

Consequently, his family resided in Bailu for generations. His father was Yinchang and his mother was Lady Wu; she conceived him after being moved by a miraculous sign. From birth, the Master was exceptionally perceptive and gifted.
As he grew older, he possessed a vast spirit and a liberated temperament. He was skilled in the art of painting, particularly excelling in portraits of the Great Being (Mahāsattva).
People vied to treasure him (at that time he was called the "Little Wu Daozi"). At the age of fourteen, his parents both passed away. His uncle had no son, so he raised the Master as his heir.
When he reached twenty-seven, he suddenly contemplated the impermanence of worldly phenomena and renounced his inherited title to depart.
At Chidang Cliff in Jianchuan Prefecture, he met an old monk at a hermitage; their conversation was deeply harmonious, and the monk transmitted the Avataṃsaka Sūtra to him.
Having gained insight while reading the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World-Honored One," he went to Mount Baohong to seek ordination from Dharma Master Liangru.
On the eve of this, the Master had dreamed of a man wearing a *kāṣāya* robe, whom a multitude of monks surrounded and knelt before as they requested his tonsure and initiation.
When he saw the Master at dawn, he rejoiced, considering him a person of renewed birth. He then conferred the prohibitive precepts upon him. [He heard that in the Jiangnan region there were] three...
Master Meilü admired him and, together with his friend Chengzhuo, took up their gourds and straw hats and traveled eastward. They underwent every kind of hardship and privation;
first they entered Mount Nanyue to visit Master Zhuan of Sanju, where he expounded the *Four Reliances Commentary* on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Subsequently, they ascended Mount Po’e and Mount Fengmao to pay homage at the various ancestral sites of practice, then proceeded to Mount Jiuhua and made a pilgrimage to Mount Wutai. Once again...
Crossing the Great River, he first met Master Mei at Haichao An, where he received full ordination, served as the *upādhyāya*, and took turns lecturing on the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*.
None of the fourfold assembly failed to praise him, yet the Master remained humble and unsatisfied; thus, within the Tripitaka...
He examined the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* in its extensive version as well as the vinaya texts of other schools; wherever he encountered obstructions, he prayed to the Buddha for resolution.
After sitting in silent meditation for some time, his doubts were suddenly dispelled like melting ice. Subsequently, he received the precepts from Master Meizǔ at Bào'ēn Monastery in Jīnlíng.
There were a thousand people seated before him as the Master presided over the altar to instruct them. Suddenly, he recalled a dream from the past:

he had arrived at a great temple, its golden and emerald surfaces shimmering with light, where bhikṣus gathered like clouds. Looking at himself, he saw that he had already assumed the appearance of a monk;

a Gautama, clad in crimson robes, sat upon a high throne, beckoning him upward to receive the scriptures and command him to preach. The assembly all knelt to listen, and he woke up with sweat pouring down his body. What he had seen now was exactly as it had been in that vision.
This coincided with his previous dream. Later, he followed Master Meizhu at Mount Hua, where he served as both instructor and administrator of the monastery.
He neglected sleep and forgot to eat, remaining diligent from beginning to end. Master Meizhu once said to the assembly, "For thirty years I have been a banner of the precepts;
had it not been for Jianyue, it would have been nearly broken. On the day of his passing, [Jianyue] took the purple [robe] of Princess Rongchang.

He entrusted him with the robes and the various Vinaya texts of the various schools. Upon succeeding to the seat, the Master exhorted the assembly by means of the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* (Ten Recitations), establishing these rules:
first, he would not ordain disciples; second, he would not accept offerings for the support of the elderly; third, he would not provide bedding or distribute alms registers;

fourth, he would not accumulate incense or ritual implements; fifth, he would not privately prepare fruit and food; sixth, he would not privately establish a kitchen or storehouse; seventh, he would not...

He avoided manual labor. Eighth, he did not engage in mourning or congratulatory visits. Ninth, he did not act as a proselytizer to solicit donations. Tenth, he did not permit silk garments or evening meals.

Those who violated these agreements were resolutely not permitted to remain. Thereafter, they received full ordination according to the Vinaya and entered the retreat period within established boundaries.
Those who saw or heard of this all said that the Nan-shan tradition had returned to life in a second generation. At the beginning of the dynasty, mountain bandits entered [the area].
The temple was being plundered. After the Master finished his midday meal, he enlightened the crowd with the principles of benefit and harm; they all bowed their heads and immediately fled.
The two Generals Ba and Ao, as well as Minister Chen, marveled at this and issued official documents to provide protection.
Thereupon, the Master personally practiced the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi*, serving as a model for the assembly. For ninety days and nights, he neither sat nor lay down. He remained thus.
The second time, he again followed the legacy of Jetavana and constructed a stone *śīla-maṇḍala* to the right of the Bronze Hall.

On the night the foundation was excavated, he perceived the manifestation of an auspicious omen by the Great Being (Mahāsattva), which was brilliantly radiant; the light from the altar and the hall intermingled, surging straight up toward the heavens.
When the Master opened the altar to recite the precepts, there were as few as five thousand participants and as many as fourteen thousand. He accepted special invitations as was his custom.

At Tianning in the province, Wutai in Zhenzhou, Bifeng and Zilin in Jinling, as well as Jile at Xuyang and his own mountain, Ciyun, and Tianlong—wherever he went, monks and laypeople, old and young alike, crowded the streets.
When he was about to pass away, he manifested a slight illness and instructed his disciples, saying: "Do not administer medicinal decoctions. After seven days...
The day arrived. At the appointed time, he sat upright and passed away. He was born on the third day of the third month in the *xin-chou* year of the Wanli era.
He entered *parinirvāṇa* on the twenty-second day of the first month in the *ji-wu* year of the Kangxi era.
His worldly age was seventy-nine; his years as a monk (*bhikṣu*) were forty-four; and his summer retreats (*varṣā*) numbered thirty-three. Seven days later, at the time of his cremation:
The fourfold assembly of disciples gathered from afar; their mournful cries resounded throughout the wilds. The Buddha’s voice shook the heavens.
Within the flaming light, some beheld the marks of the Buddha; within the purple smoke, lotus flowers appeared. After the fire was extinguished, his sacred relics were collected;
the five-colored śarīra obtained were beyond counting. Throughout his life, the Master sat upon the site of enlightenment eight times and opened the precepts.
There were over seventy ordination periods; he had more than sixty dharma heirs, and his disciples numbered in the tens of thousands. His writings include:

the *Zhizhi Huiji* (16 fascicles), the *Zuxiu Chushu* (15 fascicles), the *Chuanjie Zhengfan* (4 fascicles), the *Dacheng Xuanyi* (1 fascicle), the *Yaoshi Chanfa* (1 fascicle), the *Tidu Zhengfan* (1 fascicle), and the *Sengxing Guize* (1 fascicle). Three...

Various texts, including the *Gui wubajie zhengfan* (One fascicle), the *Jiaojie ni zhengfan* (One fascicle), the *Hei bai busa* (One fascicle), and the *Youming jie zhengfan* (One fascicle), were all circulated in the world.
His body was tall and large; he possessed a fleshly protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) upon his crown; his voice was like that of a great bell;
and his appearance resembled that of an ancient Buddha. There were those who came from Mount Nanyue (Jijuzhu Shan) who said, "The Master is [the incarnation of...]"

The Venerable Kāśyapa manifested a transformation body; at the dried-up spring of Maling, the waters overflowed of their own accord, and at Longmian, the three generations of grievous resentment were extinguished.
Through his solemn precepts, beings took refuge, and divine dragons protected the Dharma. Such various wonders and marvels are difficult to record in full.

May they serve as a goad for body and mind, ensuring that both precepts and vehicle are pursued with equal urgency, so that self and others may benefit together. What cause would not be perfected? What fruit would not be realized?

Part Five: A Separate Explanation of the Verses on Early Awakening.
[Commentary] "Early" refers to the dawn. When a person awakens from sleep, it is called "awakening. The first awakening at the end of the night is called "early.
If a person is in deep sleep, they are shrouded by afflictions (*kleśa*); the six consciousnesses return to their seeds, and no discrimination arises.
Even if lightning flashes, thunder roars, the wind blows, or stones strike, they cannot be awakened; this is termed "non-awakening. It is truly as has been said for a brief moment.
When the time [for practice] does not arrive, it is like being a dead person. The *Vinayamātṛkā-sūtra* states:
"At that time, because the bhikṣus were greedily attached to the pleasure of sleep, they abandoned their correct practice. The Vajrapāṇi thought to himself:
'The Tathāgata, through various ascetic practices over three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas, has finally attained Buddhahood. Yet now these bhikṣus are greedily attached to sleep...'"
Because they delight in sleep, they no longer practice the Path. How can this be so? Having heard this, the bhikṣus addressed the Buddha. The Buddha told the bhikṣus:

"Those who consume the faithful offerings of others should not be indolent. During the three periods of the night, one should spend two periods in meditation, recitation, and walking meditation, exerting oneself to advance on the Path to compensate for what was insufficient during the day. At midnight, when the body is weary, one may listen."
This refers to resting. Now, having awakened from sleep, it is called "awakening early.

According to the collective regulations of the Sūtras and Vinaya for ordained disciples, one should diligently apply oneself to the Buddha-way during the first and last watches of the night, rather than being greedy for sleep or succumbing to indolence and negligence.
Therefore, at the time of awakening, one should recite this verse.
Upon first awakening from sleep, one should wish that all sentient beings attain the awakening of omniscience and survey the ten directions.
[Commentary] "Sleep" is one of the five hindrances among the afflictions; it refers to the state where the mental consciousness becomes dull and heavy.
The five sensory faculties being shrouded in darkness is called "sleep" (*mian*); this refers to the time when the eyes are closed and the spirit is withdrawn as one lies down.
To awaken from sleep is called "waking" (*wu*). As the ancients said: "In sleep, the *hun* soul communes; in waking, the physical form opens.

What is now termed "beginning to wake" (*shiwu*) refers to the state between being about to awaken and not yet having awakened—prior to being deluded by sensory objects and before falling into the conceptual discrimination of consciousness. This is the passage of the True Eye.
When one squints, it is called "beginning to awaken," which refers to the initial state of waking. Furthermore, awakening is like the sun first rising, while sleep is like the sun sinking.
The spiritual root of humanity is born within heaven and earth and receives its mandate from the Way of Heaven;
therefore, when the heavenly sun sinks, the human eye also sleeps, and when the heavenly sun rises, the human eye also opens.
One day, one night, one movement, and one stillness follow the operation of the Way of Heaven.
If one acts in opposition to the Way of Heaven, then even under the clear blue sky and bright sun, it is as dark as the long night; thus, one cannot truly distinguish between sleep and awakening.
Only the Great Awakened World-Honored One, whether sleeping or awake, performs the Buddha-work. Therefore, at the very moment we first awaken, we should act in this manner.
Contemplation: When making this vow, one should consider that all sentient beings are obscured by ignorance, so that the light of wisdom does not manifest, as if dwelling in a long night.
I now awaken and illuminate them, causing all sentient beings to sever evil and cultivate goodness; therefore, it is said, "One should vow for all sentient beings.
Regarding "the awakening of all-knowledge": the term "wisdom" (*jñāna*) refers to the thorough illumination of the ten directions, while "equanimity" (*samaya*) refers to the three periods of time.

"Clarification" (*myō*) means awakening (*kakku*). Furthermore, it is said: when the mind has that which it knows, it is called wisdom (*chi*); when one brings forth and clarifies the great matter, it is called awakening (*kaku*).

[Commentary] The Sanskrit term *cīvara* is translated here as "clothing. In antiquity, people wore skins; it was the Yellow Emperor who first fashioned garments.

Those for the upper body were called *yi* (clothes), and those for the lower body were called *shang* (skirt). The *Baihutong* states: "As for *yi*, it means 'to conceal' (*yin*); as for *shang*, it means 'to shield' (*zhang*). Thus, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"Just like worldly clothing and skirts, they shield and cover the physical form; because they shield the form and conceal what is hidden, they are called 'clothing' (*yi*)."
The lower garment. Furthermore, "clothing" (yi) means reliance. All merits of the myriad virtues rely upon pure precepts as their foundation.
Thus, the *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states: "All disciples of the Buddha abide by relying on the precepts; from them, the myriad virtues grow and flourish.
If one can practice in reliance upon the precepts, one will immediately attain all supreme roots of goodness, and thus the ocean of suffering can be crossed. That...
The bank may be ascended.
If putting on the upper garment, one should wish that all sentient beings obtain supreme roots of goodness and reach the further shore of the Dharma.
[Commentary] "If" (*jue*) is a term used for formal determination; it refers to the moment of formally determining to don this garment. Upper garment (*shàngyī*).
In common parlance, these long robes are called *zhiduò*, *biǎnshān*, or *hǎiqīng*. A poem by Lü Dongbin says:

"Fluttering, they dance with wide sleeves, like birds coming from the East Sea. Another name is *daopáo* (Daoist robe), also called the *gōngjìng yī* (robe of reverence) or the *xiàngshàng yī* (upward-facing robe);
it is the most supreme garment for the person, signifying that one wears the most excellent attire.
One should give rise to the most supreme mind and give rise to the most supreme vow. One should know that this mind and this vow are themselves the most excellent roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*).
For all sentient beings have lost these roots of goodness and are submerged in the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*);
therefore, one should give rise to this vow so that their roots of goodness do not remain submerged, but rather cause them to reach the further shore of the Dharma and attain ultimate perfection.
These grounds—such as those of the Two Vehicles and the Three Vehicles—are all not called ultimate; only the Single Vehicle of the Buddha is termed the ultimate shore (*pāra*).
Furthermore, this shore is the place where sentient beings perform karma, undergo suffering, and transmigrate in the cycle of birth and death;
the other shore is the place of the Buddhas’ ultimate transcendence, purity, and peace.
When putting on the lower garment (*nivāsana*), one should wish that all sentient beings clothe themselves in all roots of goodness and be fully endowed with shame and remorse.
[Commentary] The Sanskrit term is *nivāsana*; in the language of Tang (Chinese), it means "skirt. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* calls it *nīpāśana*, and also *kuśulaka*.
It is one cubit in height and five cubits in width; this is the lower garment. It is also called *nirvāṇa-saṃgha*.
It is also called *śāṭaka*, translated as "inner garment" (*neiyi*). It is also referred to as a "short skirt" (*duanqun*), which is the lower robe.
As for "skirt" (*qun*), it means "a collection" (*qun*); this refers to the joining together of the panels of the skirt. The old term *nirvāṇasaṃghāṭī* is a corruption.

Since it lacks ties or loops, when one is about to wear it, one gathers the fabric into pleats and secures them with a corded belt. The *Vinayasamgraha* states: "That is, from the edge of the skirt..."
Fine cloth is folded into pleats and gathered together at the waist; its shape resembles the leaf of the *tāla* tree, characterized by being bunched at the top and spreading out below.
"Wearing" (*fu*) is synonymous with "wearing as an ornament" (*pei*). "All roots of goodness" (*zhū shàngēn zhě*) refers to the foundation of all virtues derived from the precepts.

Within the Vinaya, seven branches of virtuous precepts are clarified, namely the three of body and the four of speech; these constitute the virtuous precepts. Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies seven... [text fragment ends]
Wholesome dharmas: first, excellence in knowing the teachings, which refers to the twelve divisions of the scriptures; second, excellence in knowing the meaning, which refers to words and language;

third, excellence in knowing the proper time, which means practicing the six perfections at their appropriate times; fourth, excellence in knowing contentment, which concerns food, drink, clothing, and medicine.
Fifth, knowing one's own goodness: knowing that one inherently possesses the roots of goodness of faith and precepts. Sixth, knowing the goodness of the assembly:

[observing] their coming and going, sitting and rising, preaching the Dharma, and engaging in questions and answers. Seventh, knowing the goodness of the honorable and the base: such as those with faith being good and those without faith being not good, and so forth.
Shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*). These are two of the seven treasures of the Dharma, namely: faith, precepts, learning, relinquishment, wisdom, shame, and dread of blame.
Among these seven treasures, shame and dread of blame act as the guardians of the wealth. To feel shame within is *hrī*; to feel shame without is *apatrāpya*.
It is also said that not losing one's own integrity is *hrī*, and having no non-virtuous activity in the mind is *apatrāpya*. If one does not fall into inferior states...

Without a lower garment (*śīrṣaka*), the physical form would be exposed, and one would lack a sense of shame (*hrī*) and dread of blame (*apatrāpya*). Since there would be no one to provide protection, the wealth of merit and the Dharma would not be complete.
Now, when putting on the lower garment, wholesome dharmas manifest before one; one’s thoughts are free from depravity. This is the locus where shame and dread of blame are fully possessed.
This is the locus where shame and dread of blame are fully possessed; it is the locus of the pure source. It is for this reason that people...
Those who are deluded by the five desires and unable to attain purity do so solely because they lack a sense of shame and remorse (*hrī* and *apatrāpya*).

If one is fully endowed with shame and remorse, then the pure and wholesome dharmas will never be deficient. Therefore, it is said: "One who partakes of all roots of goodness is fully endowed with shame and remorse."
Adjusting their robes and fastening their belts, they should wish that all sentient beings restrain their roots of goodness so as not to let them be lost.
[Commentary: To fasten the belt with a corded sash, the various styles differ; the colors likewise vary, being yellow or red.
Without a belt, the lower garment cannot gather the body; without precepts, a person cannot subdue the mind. "Adjusting" (zhěng) [refers to this].
"Solemnity" (*yansu*) means to bind and restrain. It refers to the necessity of regulating the sense faculties; thus, one's external demeanor is solemn while the internal dharma restrains the mind.
When body and mind are solemnly restrained, the dharmas of all wholesome paths will naturally progress step by step, thereby accomplishing the function of the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*).
[Note on] "Descending to the Single Seat" (*xiàdān*). "Descending" (*xià*) means descending from awakening. "Single" (*dān*) refers to being solitary.

As for using a bed or couch as a "single seat" (*dān*), it means that one who receives the precepts should occupy a single couch alone; this is because they sit much more than they lie down. If [it is] in...
In the meditation hall, one follows the assembly in all matters.

When the group gathers, ring the finger-cymbal three times and silently recite this verse and mantra from the morning dawn until evening: "May all sentient beings protect themselves; if they should lose their lives beneath my feet..."
Form. May you be reborn in the Pure Land immediately. Oṃ vidi tvariṇi svāhā (recite three times; this is the mantra for rebirth as a celestial maiden).
[Commentary] "Yin" (寅) means it is not yet light; "dan" (旦) means it is already light, specifically referring to the moment when the first signs of dawn appear.
In Sanskrit, this is called *aruṇa*, or *loṇa*, or *sattva*; in the Chinese language, it is termed "the appearance of light.
It has various other names. The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya-ṭīkā* (*Míngliǎolùn*) states: "Because the eastern direction has already turned red. The *Tonghuì zhǐguī* states: "In this region, based on..."
Two *kṣaṇas* before sunrise is dawn; this is the appearance of light (*āloka-nimitta*). Its limit is defined by the ability to see the lines on the palm.
Within it, there are three kinds of colors: if the sun shines upon the Jambu trees, there is a black color;
if it shines upon the leaves of the trees, there is a blue color; and if it passes beyond the trees to shine upon the Jambudvīpa realm, there is a white color. Among these—

White is the primary color; this refers to the time of dawn. Furthermore, other schools clarify that it is the time when the earth is clearly perceived, meaning one sees the color of the ground with clarity.
As for "evening," it is the time when the golden bird falls to the west and the sun sets. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states:
"The five aggregates constitute day and night. When the sun reaches the boundary of Jambudvīpa, it is called sunset. This is...
"Evening. "All beings" (*sarvasattva*) is a term used as a general designation. They are called "sentient beings" (*sattva*) because they give rise to various phenomena;

that is, they receive their physical substance through the eight factors of subject and object—namely, earth, water, fire, wind, form, odor, taste, and touch. The *Puyao jing* (Lalitavistara Sūtra) states:
"The Tathāgata’s past mind was pure and free from attachment, and he did not afflict sentient beings. Wherever he traveled, his wheel-marked feet..."
It is not defiled; it is not damaged by insects or ants. Regarding "protecting oneself": this refers to all crawling and wriggling, minute insects, which possess the nature of spiritual awareness.
Thus, the Preface to the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "That which belongs to the category of blood and breath must have cognition;
whatever possesses cognition must share the same essence. Because we ordinary beings, with our physical forms, have not yet detached our minds from attachment...
While one’s practice has not yet reached the level of the sages, when about to perform an action, one should wish that those [beings] may protect their own lives.
Should they be mistakenly harmed in their physical forms, by the power of these verses and mantras, they shall immediately be reborn in the Pure Land and escape the cycle of saṃsāra.
As for the Pure Land, the world is so bright and pure that it is called "pure. This is...
That which purifies one’s dwelling is called a "land" (*kṣetra*); it is composed solely of goodness and lacks the four evil destinies. The *Fa-hua lun* states:

"The dwelling place of sentient beings free from afflictions is called a Pure Land. This is truly because the conduct of sentient beings—whether beautiful or foul—results in lands that are either defiled or sublime.
In the Sahā world, the five turbidities arise from the accumulation of evil, creating mounds and pits; whereas in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*), there are the seven treasures.
By practicing goodness, one flourishes in excellence. The *Samādhi Sūtra* states: "When ordinary people seek the Way and practice dhyāna, they must first sever discursive thought.
The reason people fail to attain the Way is simply that they sit amidst a profusion of impure thoughts; because of the defilements of the five turbidities, it is not called a Pure Land.
The Buddha ordained that those who cause injury by mistake are not punished for their crime, as they lacked intentional malice.
This is consistent with worldly laws. However, there are also cases where one causes injury through error and subsequently receives a retribution for that very injury.

As recorded in the *Chao-ye Qian-zai*: Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty had long held the Master Kētou in deep reverence and faith. At one time, he dispatched a messenger to summon him. Just then, the Emperor was playing go with someone;
wishing to kill off a portion of the board, he shouted, "Kill it! The messenger consequently executed the master. When the Emperor finished his game, he called out—
The messenger said, "The Master sent word that previously Your Majesty had ordered his execution. The Emperor asked, "What were the Master’s final words before his death?
The messenger replied, "The Master said, 'In a previous kalpa, when I was a śrāmaṇera, I used a spade to dig the earth and inadvertently severed a section of a melon vine.
The current Emperor is that very person. This retribution is indeed fitting. From this we may observe that even a mistaken killing still..."
To repay for errors—should one not be cautious?
To cite scriptural evidence, the *Vibhaṅga-guṇa-sūtra* states: "What is the first [practice] of mindfulness of the Buddha? The Buddha’s body is adamantine and free from any outflow.
When he walks, his feet remain four inches above the ground; the patterns of the thousand-spoked wheels appear as footprints upon the earth."
May all the insects on your feet be at peace for seven days. Should their lives come to an end, they shall all be reborn in the heavens.
Long ago, there was a wicked bhikṣu who was originally a non-Buddhist; he donned the robes of a monk only to slander the Buddha and follow in his footsteps, even killing flying insects along the way.

At the place where the Buddha had stepped, people said, "The Buddha has trampled it to death. Yet, although the insect died, upon encountering the place where the Buddha had stepped, it immediately regained life.
Such is the meaning of what is called "recollection of the Buddha" (buddhānusmṛti).
When walking, do not harm insects.

[Commentary] "Walking" refers to one of the four modes of deportment. "Not harming insects" means possessing a heart of benevolence and compassion and giving rise to the thought of protecting living beings.
Those with legs are called *chóng* (insects); those without legs are called *zhài*. This...
This follows from the preceding verse. That is to say, after striking the single finger-bell, when about to take a step, one should perform a visualization in the mind and recite this verse:
"When lifting my foot, may all sentient beings emerge from the ocean of birth and death and be endowed with all virtuous dharmas."
Oṃ dhiri dhiri svāhā (three times). [Note] "Lifting the foot" refers to deportment.
This means that a practitioner on the path, whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, must always regulate and collect their mind so that not even a single hair’s breadth of it leaks away.
Therefore, whenever one wishes to lift the foot, one must first lift the mind.

By upholding this verse-mantra, the mind will not wander outward and thoughts will not stir in vain. Wholesome dharmas will naturally be present, and the path of practice will spontaneously be accomplished.
Whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, one will always remain within this state; this is precisely to realize the principle of the Middle Way.
Thus, the great ocean of birth and death can be crossed, and the summit of the mountain of Nirvana can be ascended. [The great ocean of] birth and death...
"Vast" refers to being expansive. An ancient saying goes: "Not knowing where one comes from when born is called the greatness of birth;
not knowing where one goes when dying is called the greatness of death. Therefore, it is said to be as vast as the ocean. To emerge from such vastness is not difficult;
it simply requires possessing all wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*). These wholesome dharmas are precisely the practices and vows of a Bodhisattva. That is to say:
First, because his practice has fulfilled his vows, whenever the Bodhisattva lifts his foot, he immediately makes this vow for all sentient beings:
"May they emerge from the ocean of birth and death. If sentient beings were identical in their practice and vows to those of the Bodhisattva, where would there be birth and death?
It is precisely because their practice and vows differ that they falsely cling to worldly defilements and commit various unwholesome deeds; therefore—
Wandering in the sea of suffering, if one can turn back in a single thought and possess all wholesome dharmas, then the other shore is right here;
the flow of the sea of suffering is severed, the designation of "sentient beings" ceases, and even the Buddha does not exist—this is called ultimate goodness.
Why worry that wholesome dharmas will not be possessed?
**Exiting the Hall [Record]** "Exiting" (*chū*) is contrasted with "entering" (*nyū*); it refers to lifting one's feet and walking toward the outside. "Hall" (*dō*) means a temple hall;
specifically, it refers to the Zen meditation hall (*zendō*), which is the place where monks from the ten directions dwell their minds and cultivate the Way. Master P'ang said: "Ten..."
Now we gather together as one; each and every one studies non-action (*wuwei*). This is the place for selecting Buddhas; with an empty mind, one returns having passed the imperial examination.
This is what it means.
When departing from the dwelling, one should wish that all sentient beings deeply enter Buddha-wisdom and forever transcend the triple world.

[Commentary] "House" (*śālā*) means a dwelling. It is a dwelling for the purpose of resting; it also means to place [something]. It refers to a place where one can establish oneself and dwell securely.
It is also called a hall or a residence (*śālā*). Furthermore, a small hut is also called a house. To say "to enter deeply into the Buddha’s wisdom and forever transcend the triple world" means:
This, then, is to rely on phenomena to clarify principle; it means departing from the house of conditioned existence (*saṃskṛta*) and entering the wisdom of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
As for Buddha-wisdom, there is nothing equal to it in either the mundane or supramundane realms.

By means of the nature of cognition, it exhaustively penetrates the causal and karmic natures of sentient beings—whether good or evil—and knows every single detail of their origins and ends. (From the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*)
It is said: "The Tathāgata’s wisdom reaches everywhere; therefore it is called Buddha-wisdom. It is also termed spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*) and teacherless wisdom (*aśikṣita-jñāna*).

Furthermore, this Buddha-wisdom is inherently possessed by every person. It is only because of being shrouded by the dust of sensory objects that the distinction between the holy and the ordinary arises;
thus, one must penetrate deeply into it. Regarding the three realms, the *Huayan Kongmu* states: "First, the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Desire...
There are four kinds: namely, the desire for sensory objects (*kāma*), the desire for form (*rūpa*), the desire for attachment (*lobha*), and the desire for sexual intercourse (*maithuna*).

From the Avīci Hell below up to the sixth heaven, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin, men and women cohabit and are largely possessed by defiled desires; thus, it is called the *Kāmadhātu* (the Realm of Desire).
Second is the *Rūpadhātu* (the Realm of Form). "Form" refers to material substance. Having already departed from the foul and evil forms of the Realm of Desire, there still remains...
Pure matter exists from the Brahma heavens of the first dhyāna up to the Akaniṣṭha heaven; there are eighteen such heavens in total.
In all of them, there are no female forms and no defilement of desire; all beings are born by transformation, yet they still possess material substance.
Therefore, it is called the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). Third is the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), which means that there is only mind-consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*) and no material substance.
Beginning from the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*) and ending with the Sphere of Neither Perception nor Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), there are four heavens in total.

Therein exist only the four mental aggregates of feeling, perception, formations, and consciousness, and no physical form; therefore, it is called the Formless Realm. If one transcends the three realms, one attains the realization of *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* (Nirvana with remainder).

When one turns away from [the cycle], one cuts off birth-and-death through segmentation (*pariccheda-jarāmaraṇa*). If one eternally transcends the triple world and attains realization of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, then there is no birth-and-death through transformation (*pariṇāma-jarāmaraṇa*);
rather, the five stages of dwelling are exhausted, afflictions are forgotten, and one enters deeply into Buddha-wisdom. The combined commentary states:
"This verse is like a grand scroll of the profound mysteries of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra*, while simultaneously encompassing the entirety of the parables of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*."
Chapter. However, how could the Perfect Mirror of Vairocana have coming or going? And how could the narrow gate of the burning house be without entering and exiting?
Thus we know that where there is no fire, fire suddenly arises—this is the Great Burning House.

As for those of small wisdom, the Śrāvakas, who have already departed from this dwelling and briefly attained a state of play, this is the Small Burning House. They do not know what lies outside the house...

Fire! It is perhaps even more severe than that. Unless one penetrates deeply into the Buddha-wisdom, how could one swiftly depart from the burning house and immediately enter the cool and refreshing state?
[The following concerns] using the toilet.

[Commentary] To ascend from below is called *dēng* (climbing). To occupy a high position while looking down is called *cè* (toilet/privy). *Cè* refers to a latrine. According to the *Shuowen Jiezi*, it means "clear.
That which was anciently called a *qīng* (purification chamber) is so named because this most defiled place must be constantly maintained and repaired to keep it clean.
Furthermore, *cè* implies "mixture," as all people mingle and congregate upon it. The *Vinayaviniścaya-upāli-paripṛcchā* states: "One should..."
In the northeast corner of the monastery, one should establish a latrine. All four sides should be trimmed with thorny shrubs.

Separate facilities for both large and small needs must be constructed, each provided with a door-panel and secured with a side-bolt. The place for relieving oneself should be located in a screened area.
Whenever one intends to enter the latrine, one should remove one's upper garment and place it in a clean spot upwind.
When you have gathered [the necessary items] and feel the urge to defecate or urinate, you should go at once; do not wait until you are pressed by internal urgency and act in haste.

You must remove your shoes before entering. It is impermissible to enter the latrine wearing clean shoes. Upon arrival, you should snap your fingers three times. This has two purposes: first, to inform those inside.
2. One must not urge the person inside to come out, for fear that a defiled-demon might cause others to avoid it.
When mounting the trough, one should again snap the fingers three times and silently recite this verse-mantra:
When defecating or urinating, one should make this aspiration for all sentient beings: "May they cast off greed, anger, and ignorance;
may they eliminate all unwholesome dharmas. *Oṃ haṃ rudāya svāhā* (recite three times).
[Note] "Defecating or urinating" refers to the smooth discharge of impurities to bring the body lightness and ease. As the Sūtra says: "All..."
All sentient beings subsist by means of nutriment, for it benefits the sense faculties and nourishes the four great elements.

Once the flavors of food and drink have entered the intestines and stomach, that which is light and pure rises upward, while that which is heavy and turbid sinks downward; thus there is excrement and urine.
One can thus see that a single human body encompasses both the pure and the impure worlds. The pure world is precisely precept and meditative concentration.
The meritorious karma of wisdom concerns this defiled world, which consists of the unwholesome dharmas of greed, hatred, and delusion.

Greed, hatred, and delusion are termed the "three poisons" of affliction (*kleśa*). Now, by discarding impurity and turbidity, one counteracts these three poisons so that they are completely purified.
Since these three poisons are the cause for generating karma and committing transgressions, they are now guarded against through the precepts.
When the causes of the three poisons are thus empty, how can future karmic fruits remain? Therefore, an ancient worthy said:
"While dressing and eating, while defecating and urinating—when the mind is not distracted by other concerns, that is precisely excellent practice."
Why worry about not attaining liberation? If one can awaken to this source of purity and defilement, then one may realize that the great trichiliocosm does not exist outside the mind.
From this point on, when impurities are exhausted and the mind is pure, one no longer perceives the self as being distinct from the dharma-realm, nor the dharma-realm as being distinct from the self.
My body and the dharma-realm are neither one nor two; thus, the three poisons...
"Go away yourself; the unwholesome dharma will naturally be eliminated.
Regarding "approaching the water" [Record]: "Approaching" means drawing near. "Water" refers to that which purifies the body. The *Mūla-ekottara-karman* states:
The Blessed One’s teaching on impurity and defilement was intended to remove foul odors and enable one to dwell in peace and happiness.
The Buddha said: "There are three kinds of ultimate purification: first, purification of the body; second, purification of speech;
and third, purification of the mind. The Vinaya states: The Buddha told the bhikṣus, "You should know that this is the Dharma to be practiced; you must maintain it."
Monks, washing in this manner brings great benefit; it purifies the body and causes the devas to pay homage.
Therefore, you who take me as your teacher should all wash yourselves.
If you do not wash, you should not circumambulate stupas, prostrate to the Buddha, recite the sutras, pay homage to others, receive the homage of others, eat food, or sit among the Sangha.
One must not enter the assembly while on a bed or couch. Because the body is impure, this causes the devas to see one with displeasure;
consequently, the dhāraṇī practices one maintains will all lack efficacy. If one violates this rule, one incurs the offense of *duṣkṛta*.
Having finished defecating, one should recite this verse-mantra while facing the water.
When the task is completed and one approaches the water, one should make this aspiration: "May all sentient beings swiftly proceed within the supramundane Dharma."
Oṃ śrī-vāhe svāhā (three times).
[Note] "When the ritual is concluded" means when the major or minor rites have been completed and one proceeds to wash oneself in a secluded place.
"One should make this aspiration" refers to an aspiration that is not like worldly aspirations or worldly dharmas; it should be made for the sake of all sentient beings.
Regarding the aspiration for transcendence and the teaching of the supramundane Dharma, there exists a distinction of superiority and inferiority herein. Why is this?

In mundane dharmas, one merely deals with phenomena and appearances; whereas within the supramundane Dharma, principle is manifested through phenomena, profoundly penetrating the meaning of the Middle Way.
As for those who proceed swiftly, it is said that in the five turbidities and evil world, whatever is seen or heard is none other than [the manifestation of the ultimate].
Defilements and evil karma bind and fetter body and mind, causing one to sink into birth and death and transmigrate through the three realms as if confined within a prison.
Regarding the manner of undergoing punishment, even a prison has a limit to its duration, yet defilements truly have no end. Such are the grave harms of the three poisons;
therefore, they are likened to a foul latrine, where one must not remain for long, and thus one should depart from them with all haste.
While engaging in the defiled and turbid practices of the world, one should practice the supramundane dharma of purity as clarified in the Sūtras and Vinaya.
