For instance, when entering the latrine to perform cleansing, if one does not silently maintain the various dhāraṇīs, even if one were to wash with the waters of the seven Ganges Rivers, it would be of no avail.
It cannot be purified. Why? Because the seed is impure. Regarding "washing clean" [Record]:
"Washing" means to remove. That is to say, by removing the impurity, one achieves cleanliness; therefore, it is called "washing clean."
Washing away physical impurities, one should wish that all sentient beings be pure and supple, ultimately free from defilement.
Oṃ ha na mi li te svāhā (recite three times; wash with the last two fingers of the left hand).
[Commentary] "Washing away" has the meaning of purification, which is to say, the removal and abandonment. This refers to the impurities and turbidity inherent in this illusory body.
One must rely on pure water to properly eliminate [the defilement]; if one does not wash away the impure contact, it is improper to use the bedding and couches belonging to the Saṃgha.
The *Vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "If a bhikṣu receives food, until he has rinsed his mouth..."

This applies even until the completion of the small and large excretions; until one has used pure water to remove impurities, receiving prostrations, prostrating to others, bestowing the Dharma, or listening to the Dharma are all prohibited.
One must not sit upon beds or seats, nor consume food or drink. Those who violate this incur an offense.
Nevertheless, although one has washed and cleansed oneself, it is only by relying on the power of verses and mantras that body and mind can become pure, whereby one may attain harmony.
It is pliant. To say that it is ultimately stainless is to clarify the principle through the phenomenon;
that is, this body and mind are both entangled by the two obstacles of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognizable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Since the dual attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) have not been emptied, and from time immemorial have been shrouded by ignorance (*avidyā*), how could the true principle (*tattva*) ever be made manifest? This is why [it is now] ultimately...
Regarding the "stainless one": through the merit of upholding the precepts and by the power of meditative concentration and wisdom, one becomes ultimately pure and ultimately undefiled;
thus, it is known that the light of tranquil purity arises and afflictions are forever extinguished.
Washing the Hands [Commentary]: "Hand" is a general term for that which is possessed by the human body; it is a limb capable of grasping and holding objects.
If there were no palm, it could not be called a hand; if there were no fingers, it likewise could not be called a hand. Only when both palm and fingers are present can it be so designated.
They are named "hands. The two hands are the essence of the Great Yang (Taiyang). Their characters are *hun* and *yin*. The palm-patterns correspond to Heaven;
the fingers correspond to the Five Elements (*wuxing*). The first is called the thumb (*dazhi*); the second, the index finger (*shizhi*); the middle, the middle finger (*jiangzhi*);

the fourth, the ring finger (*wumingzhi*); the fifth, the little finger (*xiaozhi*); and the sixth, the extra finger (*zhizhi*). This means that once one has firmly grasped and held [the Way], it is no longer defiled.
Contact is unavoidable; therefore, one should wash.
When rinsing the hands with water, one should make this aspiration for all sentient beings: "May they obtain pure hands to receive and uphold the Buddha-dharma.
Oṃ Cukāraya Svāhā (three times).

[Commentary] Water has flexibility as its nature; to remove defilement and eliminate stains is its function. "Washing" (*guàn*) means cleansing. To cup water with the palms and wash for purification is called "washing the palms.
Now, as the hands are smeared with dust and grime, this pure water removes the filth from the palms; it symbolizes how the Dharma-water removes the impurities of the mind.
This is what is meant by "daily renewal," renewing again and again to purify one's virtue. May all sentient beings [attain this].
This refers to those who uphold the precepts; they cultivate the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) with the aspiration for their bodies and minds to be purified.
They receive and maintain the pure flavor of the Tathāgata’s Dharma, continuing the Buddha’s life of wisdom so that his transformation of beings remains uninterrupted.

As for what is called the "Buddha-Dharma," it is vast—comprising hundreds of thousands of samādhis, immeasurable dharma-gates, and even the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the scriptures. Yet, in its essence, it is one.
The four-line verse is entirely called the Buddha-dharma. When reciting the mantra following "Oṃ," wash once and then wash again;
from the second washing up to the seventh washing, the Buddha-dharma will naturally manifest before you.

Ultimately, my hand, the Buddha’s hand, and the hands of sentient beings are identical in purity and identical in receiving and upholding [the Dharma]. This is the truly pure hand of the Buddha-dharma that receives [it].
He upheld the Buddha-dharma.
To provide corroborating evidence: Śikṣānanda of Siṃhala was one who had attained the third fruit [of the śrāvaka path]. In the first year of the Linde era, he came to the capital.
During the Zongzhang era, when Emperor Gaozong was residing in seclusion within the inner palace, Kangzang was still a lay practitioner (*gṛhapati*). He requested to receive the Bodhisattva precepts.
The assembly addressed a foreign monk, saying, "This practitioner recites the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* and is also skilled in lecturing on the *Brahmajāla-sūtra*.

The foreign monk marveled and said, "If merely upholding the *Avataṃsaka* produces such unfathomable efficacy, how much more so if one understands its meaning! If a person recites the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*..."

The Chapter on Practice. Regarding the one hundred and forty vows, since they have already been attained by those who possess the full precepts of a bodhisattva, what need is there to confer them separately?

According to tradition from the Western Regions, if someone reads this sutra while rinsing their hands with water, even the insects and ants touched by that water which lose their lives will all be reborn in heaven;
how much more so for those who uphold and recite this sutra to teach and transform sentient beings! This...
The wise one who arrives later will surely bring vast benefit to all. [End of] Collection.
If it is merely a small urination, one becomes pure by washing the hands once with water; if it is a defecation, [the procedure is as follows].
After removing impurities, wash the hands. Use ash, clay, or soap pods (*sòjiào*) to wash according to the proper method. The *Xītáng zálù* states:
During the Yuányòu era, there was a monk from Shǔ named Dharma Master Zhìchāo who had been reciting the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* for thirty years.
He once encountered a youth of refined appearance who raised his hand in a formal salutation. Zhìchāo asked, "Where have you come from?"
Wu Tai said, "I have come from Wutai. Zichao asked, "How have you traveled so far? He replied, "It is because I wish to guide you regarding a certain matter.
Zichao said, "I wish to hear it. He continued, "While it is truly commendable that our master recites the sutras, there is a lapse in his practice when he goes to the toilet to wash clean.
When splashing water to rinse his hands, he does not habitually use ash and mud to wash them. As for the ash and mud used [for purification]..."

The Vinaya regulations prescribe seven washings; nowadays, however, there are only two or three. Because of this, even while touching [the body], one still commits offenses when prostrating to the Buddha or reciting sutras.
Having finished speaking, he was no longer seen. Chao felt ashamed and rectified his errors. Those who understood said, "This must have been a manifestation of Mañjuśrī to warn Chao.
Thus, one knows that washing the hands must necessarily be performed according to the Dharma. The *Caiguojing* (*Sūtra on Cause and Effect*) says:
If you touch the sutra with your hands, you shall receive the retribution of becoming a worm in a latrine.

Regarding "washing the face" (xiànmiàn): the area in front of the forehead is called the face; it is also the head and face. Generally, all things have a back and a face; furthermore, they are mutually oriented toward one another.
It serves as the face; it is the head of the single body. When one rises, it is the first thing seen by others. Since it is the first thing seen by others, it must first see the Buddha.
Therefore, one must perform daily morning purification so as to facilitate the performance of prostrations and the recitation of mantras.
Washing the face with water, one should make this aspiration: "May all sentient beings attain the gateway of the pure Dharma, forever free from defilement.
Oṃ. Laṃ. Svāhā. (Recite silently twenty-one times. [Note:
Regarding "washing the face with water," it refers to this illusory physical form, which is an impure substance from which the nine orifices constantly flow.
Regarding the exterior: the face is the location where impurities such as mucus and saliva constantly overflow.
Therefore, water is required to wash them away; for this reason, one washes the face every morning. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"Before having attained liberation oneself, first to liberate others—this is the resolve of a Bodhisattva. Thus, when a practitioner washes their face, they first generate this resolve.
This is the vow. As for the "Pure Dharma-gates," they manifest principle through phenomena.
By transforming the eighty-four thousand gates of affliction (*kleśa*) into eighty-four thousand pure dharma-gates, they are also the gates of *dhāraṇī*.

These gates encompass all dharmas and uphold immeasurable meanings; they are the gates traversed by those from the three stages of worthiness (*tri-kalyāṇaka*) up to the ten stages of sagehood (*daśārya-bhūmi*).
This is the gateway to liberation for all practitioners. If one can truly exhaust delusions to their end, the original face will be manifest without the need for polishing.
Once this aforementioned gateway has been spontaneously attained, it remains ultimately pure until the attainment of Buddhahood;
therefore, it is said that it is forever free from defilement.

**Drinking Water [Record]** "Drink" (yin) means to swallow. The Sanskrit term is *āpaḥ*, which here is translated as "water. "Water" (*shui*) signifies "to level" or "to standardize," for water serves to level all things.

The *Mingyi* (Explanations of Names and Meanings) states: "Nothing surpasses water in moistening the myriad things; in form it constitutes the four great elements, and in its vital energy it ranks foremost among the five."
Regarding the practice: the *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states that there are internal uses and external uses. Internal uses refer to things such as food and drink;
external uses refer to things such as pouring water, washing, bathing, and rinsing.
The aforementioned verse concerning washing the face and bathing refers to external uses, whereas this verse concerning swallowing and so forth refers to internal uses.
The Buddha observed a bowl of water and saw eighty-four thousand insects within it. He said: "If one does not maintain this mantra, it is as if eating the flesh of sentient beings.
Oṃ vaśīparāmaṇi svāhā (three times). [Commentary:
The living beings born in water are extremely minute; the human faculty of sight, being coarse and obstructed, cannot perceive them. Only the Buddha—
His five eyes were clear and pure; he saw through to even the most minute insects—beings that cannot be seen by the ordinary physical eye.
Having seen such creatures, out of compassion, he spoke this verse and mantra. The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-śāstra* states:
"With his purified divine eye, Śāriputra saw the insects in the air like the sands along a riverbank or like grains of millet in a vessel—immeasurable and boundless."

Having seen this, he fasted for two or three days. The Buddha commanded him to eat. Generally, when water containing insects is prohibited, it refers to what is visible to the naked eye or what is caught by a water-strainer;
it does not refer to what is seen by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). A bowl (*pātra*) is a vessel for receiving food.
Now, to clarify that a single bowl of water contains eighty-four thousand types of worms: it means that the human body possesses eighty-four thousand families of worms.
By using this bowl of water as an illustration, it is shown that if one maintains this mantra, it immediately becomes the water of the Dharma.
They are naturally kept at a distance, just as when a field is first plowed for the first fruit [of the harvest], where insects remain at least four inches away.

If one does not maintain this [protection], they would consume it entirely, turning it into blood and flesh. Therefore, whenever a monk who upholds the precepts drinks or uses water—even though he has filtered it through a strainer—he must still harbor doubts regarding residual impurities;
thus, he must rely on the power and efficacy of this verse-mantra, remaining silent [in its recitation].

Recite this three times; then those who drink or consume it shall be free from transgression. Therefore it is said: "If one does not maintain this mantra, it is as if one were eating the flesh of sentient beings."
The Five-Striped Robe [Commentary]: "Five" refers to the five strips. "Robe" (衣) means reliance; it signifies relying upon this to shield oneself from cold and heat.
This is the dharma-garment for transcending the world, not to be compared with worldly attire. One should protect it as one would one's own skin and revere it as one would a stupa.
The *Sarvāstivāda-vinaya-saṃgraha* states: "This robe is not possessed by any of the ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist practitioners; it exists only within the Buddha-dharma. [From the] *Ji*:
In Sanskrit, it is called *antaravāsaka*; here it is translated as "work-robe" (*zuowuyi*). It has five strips, with one long and one short. In all monasteries...
When performing manual labor or service, or when traveling to and fro on the road, one should wear this robe and recite this verse-mantra.
The *Jietan jing* (Sutra on the Ordination Platform) states: "The five strips symbolize the severance of greed; they purify the karma of the body."
Excellent is this robe of liberation, the supreme field of merit. I now receive it upon my head;
may I never be parted from it in life after life. Oṃ siddhya svāhā (three times).
[Note] This verse invokes the result through the cause, employing both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings so that the two benefits may equally be shared. The first two lines...
The name is given for the sake of designation. The following two lines constitute the aspiration.

The syllable *Oṃ* and what follows are secret mantras (*mantra*), which cannot be explained through conventional terminology. "Excellent" (*sādhu*) is a word of praise, extolling the supreme merit of this robe.
It is inconceivable. Because it brings great benefit, "removing stickiness" is called *jie* (liberation), and "removing bondage" is called *tuo* (release).
It is said that this robe is for liberation from stickiness and release from bondage; it is a garment free from defilement.

Just as fine garments in the world are mostly produced from the mouths of silkworms, so too do sentient beings in the mundane world touch upon subtle and smooth objects of craving, becoming stained by evil and failing to achieve wholesome liberation. Thus they emerge [from the cycle].

Having received full ordination at home, through the practice of the precepts, meditative concentration (samādhi) abides for a long time; through the practice of concentration, pure wisdom arises spontaneously.
Because these three trainings are thus refined and perfected, one attains liberation from each of the three poisons. This robe may serve as visible evidence of this.
It can generate wholesome dharmas and subdue afflictions; therefore, it is called the "garment of liberation.

As for its being "unsurpassed," this means that this robe possesses the power to transcend the world, surpassing all variegated brocades and the garments of kings and ministers, as well as those of the heavens and the earth, and even the ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist paths—none can excel this robe.
Therefore, it is called "unsurpassed. Regarding the "field of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*): this is a dual reference to both the Dharma and its metaphorical illustration.

The general meaning is that by borrowing the analogy of a field to explain the Dharma, it is said that the precepts constitute the field of merit for the human world; the donor (*dānapati*) plants the seeds of merit, while the monk, wearing the *kāṣāya*, manifests the appearance of the furrows of that field.

It is called the "Field of Merit. Just as a field in the world grows crops to nourish one's physical life, these robes of the Field of Merit can cause wisdom to grow within the śramaṇa and nurture the fivefold Dharma-body.

"One who now receives it upon their crown" refers to the person who puts it on; "to place it upon the head and wear it upon the body" indicates receiving and maintaining it in this manner, representing the height of reverence.
"Never to be parted from it in life after life" refers to this Dharma robe.
Not only shall I uphold [these robes] throughout this life until the end of my physical form, but even unto the end of the future eon, I vow never to abandon them.

Regarding the "Seven-Striped Robe" (Saptaka-cīvara): it refers to the robe consisting of seven strips. Furthermore, these three robes have numerous names and meanings; that is to say, they are capable of... [text continues].
Because it subdues all māras, it is called the Armor of Forbearance. Because it is not defiled by the mud of desire, it is named the Lotus Robe.
Because a dragon that possesses even a single thread of it cannot be devoured by the garuḍa, it is named the Dragon-Saving Garment.
Because one is liberated from the afflictions of birth and death through it, it is named the Liberation Robe. Sūtras and vinayas are both generally termed *kāṣāya*; this [term] means:
Dyed colors: such as the red, yellow, purple, green, and white found in the world, which all people love—this "love" is precisely craving.
When these are offered to us monastics and we receive them, we dye them according to the Dharma into the three types of colors: blue, black, and madder-brown.
By removing our own mind of attachment and destroying that beautiful color, it is called "dyed color" (*kasāya-varṇa*). It is also called "non-... [incomplete].
"Correct color" (*zhengse*) means not dwelling in form. To dwell in form is not correct color; it is also called "dyeing" (*ranse*), signifying that the mind is stained by phenomena.
Only when there is staining yet nothing is stained can it be called "staining. However, the staining of the Two Vehicles is not true staining;
one must have the mind stained by the Mahāyāna for it to be called true staining. True staining is the path of the Great Sage (*maharṣi*). It is able to...
Within the True Dharma, that which removes the fetters (*saṃyojana*) is called the "garment of ultimate quiescence.
In the Sanskrit language it is called *uttarāsaṅga*; in the vernacular it is called the "garment for entering the assembly. It consists of seven strips, with two long and one short.

Whenever attending a vegetarian feast, listening to lectures, reciting scriptures, practicing seated meditation, or performing prostrations to the Buddha, to a stūpa, or to the *upādhyāya* and senior monks, [one must wear this].
When assembling [the assembly], one should don this robe and recite this verse-mantra. The seven robes symbolize the severing of anger and the purification of verbal karma.
Excellent is this garment of liberation, the supreme field of merit; I now receive it upon my head, that I may wear it constantly in every lifetime.
Oṃ. Tūṣa tūṣa svāhā (three times). [Note: The Buddha ordained three robes.
Their use is restricted to specific occasions. Since they must be worn only at such times, one should always keep them close at hand.

"Do not allow it to be separated from you. The present change to the two characters "chang de" (always obtain) precisely clarifies that there are times for donning [this robe], so that they do not become intermingled.
Since those who don this robe wear the garment of liberation, may they always obtain and don it throughout every life and birth, thereby liberating themselves from afflictions.
*Saṃghāṭī* [Commentary]: "Great" (*dà*) means it is the principal among robes. Because it stands above the five and seven types of robes, it is called "great.
It is also named the "Patriarchal Robe" (*zúyī*), meaning that although this robe is made of coarse hemp cloth, it has been handed down from Buddha to Buddha and Patriarch to Patriarch.
The Patriarchs have transmitted this robe, the garment for manifesting the world and realizing the Way. The Tathāgatas of the three ages all donned this robe to achieve the fruit of the Way;

thus, the robe is named "Dharma. In the past, the World-Honored One transmitted the school of the markless reality-mark (lakṣaṇa-niḥsvabhāva) to Kāśyapa as the first patriarch of the Western Regions, using this very robe as a witness. It has been inherited and transmitted by means of this robe.
The lamp [of the Dharma]. Thus, the lineage of the Dharma has been transmitted down to the present day without ever becoming confused or disordered;

this is why it is so named. Therefore, this robe symbolizes the seal of faith in the transmission of the Dharma. It cannot be given to one who is deluded, nor can it be received by one who is deluded.

Only those who have realized the Buddha-Dharma may receive it; those who have not realized the Buddha-Dharma may not. Thus, the Fifth Patriarch entrusted it to Master Huineng, saying: "In the past..."
When Bodhidharma first came to the Eastern Land, people had not yet attained faith; therefore, he transmitted the robe to manifest that he had received the Dharma.
Because this principle exists, it is called the "Dharma-robe."
Citing evidence from the *Nanshan Gantong Zhuan* (Biographies of Spiritual Resonance from Mount Nanshan): A celestial being named Huang Qiong said to Master Xuan:

"When the Tathāgata was approaching his parinirvāṇa, he told Mañjuśrī: 'By your supernatural powers, go to the western jeweled pavilion within the main hall of the Jetavana and retrieve my pearl casket to show it to the great assembly.
When I first left the city, departing from my father the King’s palace, I arrived at [the pavilion]...'"
In that grove, my body became somewhat weary and I rested for a while. At that time, the tree deity manifested her form and said to me:
"As you now practice the Way, you will certainly attain a golden-colored body and become a Great Teacher of the Three Realms.
When Kāśyapa Buddha entered parinirvāṇa, he entrusted this jeweled casket and this silk saṃghāṭī robe to me, charging me to pass them on to you."
I said to the deity, "Your *kaṣāya* saṃghāṭī is not for my use. I have heard the words of the ancients: 'When Buddhas appear in the world, they do not wear silk.
As I now cultivate the Way, how could I harm living beings? You are surely a Māra who has come here to disturb me.
The tree deity replied, "You are a man of great wisdom; why do you speak such coarse words? The Buddhas are compassionate."
"One does not wear silk garments. This silk is produced through transformation; it is not obtained by harming living beings. You may now accept this.

He then opened the casket and saw a letter from Kāśyapa which said: "When I first attained the Way, the Great Brahmā King offered the warp and the Earth Goddess Sthāvarā offered the woof, together forming a single Dharma robe. This silk was produced through transformation; it is not spun from cocoons. For this reason...
For this reason, since I attained the Way, I have always worn this robe and have never let it be damaged. I now entrust it to Siddhārtha.
When you attain Buddhahood and turn the wheel of the Vinaya, you should wear it for me. I pray that you will receive and uphold it, and not allow it to be lost.
Furthermore, from the time I first attained the Way until my parinirvāṇa, I have worn only this coarse cotton saṃghāṭī.
[The Buddha said: "I possess a robe of fine linen and a set of three robes made of white wool. I have never worn garments made of silk or raw silk from silkworms.
Why do those wicked bhikṣus slander and defame me by saying that the *vinaya* permits their wearing?

When I first attained the Way, the Bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī held a golden-threaded *kāṣāya* in her hands and offered it to me. I did not dare to accept it, and instead instructed her to offer it to the Saṃgha."

"In the teachings of the Tripiṭaka, although I have heard that one may use silk and colored fabrics to make offerings to the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Saṅgha, these are fundamentally not the silk and cotton produced from the mouths of silkworms.
Within this Jambudvīpa of mine, as well as beyond the great continents, there are eighteen hundred great nations;
in all of them, there are silks and silks-cotton that are all produced from the mouths of women. Because of this...
Because they had taken the lives of many sentient beings, [the silk] was produced as a result of their meritorious karma; thus, it emerged from the mouths of women.
Question: How is this known? Answer: Whenever one desires to use silk to make clothing, one goes beneath a mulberry tree, and two transformed maidens emerge from that tree.
They appear like girls of eight years of age, and from their mouths they spit out silk. Such is the case for the people of that country.
It was merely a spinning wheel; it took silk from the mouth of the woman, transferred it onto the spinning wheel, and stopped once enough had been taken.

The transformed woman then vanished. When I permitted the wearing of silks and brocades, it was because this [silk] came from the thread of that woman and celestial brocades, and were not originally obtained by harming living beings to extract silk or cotton.
Therefore, this saṃghāṭī should be made of coarse cloth or hemp, and you must ensure it is finished.
"O Bhikṣus of the world, one must not seek fine or luxurious robes.
[The term] *saṃghāṭī* in the Sanskrit language is translated here as 'the robe of various fragments. There are nine grades of robes: superior, middling, and inferior.
The lowest-of-the-low grade has nine strips; the middle-of-the-low grade has eleven strips; and the highest-of-the-low grade has thirteen strips; all of these consist of two lengths."
One short [bow]. Fifteen [bows] for the middle-lower grade; seventeen for the middle-middle grade;
nineteen for the middle-upper grade—all consisting of three long and one short [bow]. Twenty-one for the lower-upper grade; twenty-three for the upper-middle grade;
twenty-five for the upper-upper grade—all consisting of four long and one short [bow]. The abundance of long [bows] and scarcity of short [bows] represent the holy.

Because it increases the ordinary and diminishes the mundane, whenever one enters a royal palace, ascends the seat to preach the Dharma, enters a village to beg for alms, or subdues non-Buddhists, one should wear this robe and recite these verses and mantras. This signifies the severing of delusion and the purification of mental karma.
Excellent is the robe of liberation, the garment of the unsurpassed field of merit. Upholding the command of the Tathāgata, may we extensively deliver all sentient beings.
Oṃ mahākāṣāyadhāriṇi svāhā (three times).
[Note] "Upholding the command of the Tathāgata" refers to the original vow of the Tathāgata to extensively deliver all sentient beings; now...

Having received the Tathāgata’s pure precepts, one should properly and reverently uphold the Tathāgata’s compassionate commands, practicing them to perpetuate the lineage of the Buddhas and, by means of these wholesome dharmas, to gather and transform sentient beings. The preceding two verses were intended solely for one's own benefit.

This verse is dedicated solely to the benefit of others; thus it says, "Extensively delivering all sentient beings," which means directly taking up and bearing the life-force of the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
Regarding the *Zenghui ji* (Record of Increasing Radiance), one asks: Why not increase by four and decrease by two? Why is there only three?

Answer: Three is an odd number, which belongs to the Yang (positive) principle. Yang is able to give birth to the myriad things. Now, the regulation of the three robes symbolizes the production of the myriad virtues;
this takes up the meaning of benefiting all beings. As with the aforementioned three robes, they were originally the dharma-robes of bhikṣus;

even śrāmaṇeras are not permitted to wear them, let alone those who have only recently resolved their minds toward enlightenment. If one now wishes to cause such persons to have prior knowledge [of these matters], they should read this verse.

Mantra. This is because one must first understand the excellence of the bodhisattva’s practices and vows. However, nowadays the Dharma is in its late autumn; those who possess the full vessel of the Way are rare.

Thus, when one first resolves to attain enlightenment, they receive the three ordination platforms all at once. Consequently, during the period of observing the precepts, there are few śrāmaṇeras who can maintain the practice for two months;
it is difficult even to find those who can keep the three robes, let alone wear the double-layered *saṃkakṣikā*. Therefore, one is first instructed to recite the verses.

Recite the mantra. When you are about to put them on, do so in order to maintain mindfulness of them. If one has not yet reached the required age, one must still wear the *maṇḍala-vastra* (inner robe).
The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The three robes are the insignia of the noble *śramaṇas*; they are not for laypeople.

The Master Ciyun’s *Bianhuo pian* (Chapter on Dispelling Delusions) says: "These three robes are definitively the garments of those who have left the home life; they are not to be worn by householders."
The *Śāriputra-paripṛcchā-sūtra* asks: "How is it that, within the instructions, you cause your disciples to bare their right shoulders?
Furthermore, in the *Nagara-upama-sūtra*, spoken for the sake of the people of Kāśyapa Village, it says:

"My disciples should properly don the *kāṣāya*, covering both shoulders and not exposing the flesh; they should keep the upper and lower parts level and even, manifesting the appearance of a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*)."
His gait was dignified and orderly. He further said, "Do not expose your chest. Regarding these two instructions, how should they be observed? The Buddha said:
When performing acts of worship, one should bared the right shoulder to facilitate the task; when serving as a field of merit, both shoulders should be covered to manifest the marks of a field.
How does one perform worship? It is like when seeing the Buddha: one should inquire after the well-being of one's teachers and elders.

At that time, one should act according to the specific circumstances: whether sweeping the bed, sweeping the floor, folding clothes, arranging mats and cushions properly, applying mud to the ground to form patterns, treading on the feet of those of higher status, sprinkling water, or moving things—during these various times of making offerings, how does one act when serving as a field of merit?
Whether invited by a king for a meal, entering a village to beg for food, practicing meditation, or reciting [scriptures].
The Sūtras state that when he walked beneath the trees, people saw him as dignified and worthy of admiration.
The Vinaya prescribes the three robes (*tricīvara*), concerning their names, substances, colors, and measurements, down to the minute details of their construction and so forth.

I pray that those who shoulder the burden of this Dharma-gate will examine these matters in detail and provide guidance to future students, so that this teaching does not perish. [Section on] Names and Meanings.

As stated above, the substance refers to ten kinds of cloth materials, which differ from grasses, tree bark, hair, wool, silk, brocade, and the like, because these latter items sought through wrong livelihood do not constitute [proper] robes.
Regarding color, there are three types: blue, black, and madder-brown; these are permitted because they are not among the five great superior colors.
It is allowed to cut them with a knife to form the robes of a śramaṇa, sewing them together with a "horse-tooth" or "bird-foot" stitch.

The strips must be aligned to the left and right and opened out; if they are not made thus, it is the same as wearing a seamless robe (*saṃkakṣikā*). It is not like the secular five-colored variegated patterns, nor like gauze, silk, and the like.

Regarding "measure," this refers to the length of the cubit (*hasta*); one should measure the body to make the garment. "Making" refers to sewing the strips and teeth according to the prescribed form.
If one increases or decreases them haphazardly, there will be fault in its use. If one does not rely on the Vinaya rules, one commits an offense by wearing it.
To defile [this teaching] with an evil mind incurs offenses according to the Vinaya. If one practices, one follows [the path]; if one dwells [in it], one dwells [in the fruit].

The instructions are exceedingly vast and extensive; their practice depends on the person. If one has faith, the attainment of Buddhahood may be expected; if one violates [them], the three miserable realms are difficult to avoid.
Collection. Regarding these three robes being called "fields of merit" (*puṇyakṣetra*), the *Zenghui ji* states:

"Just as a field of furrows holds water to grow fine seedlings that nourish the physical life, the field of the Dharma robe is moistened by the waters of the four benefits, increasing the seedlings of the three virtues to nourish the wisdom-life of the Dharma-body. The *Zangyi jing* states: "The *kāṣāya* has ten kinds."
Benefit. First is the preeminence of bodhi. [Commentary:
Bodhi—according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, this is explained as the name for the Buddha-way. "Preeminent" means foremost. It refers to those who seek to attain the Buddha-way.

First, one distinguishes the outward form and appearance: externally wearing the *kāṣāya* and internally restraining the mind. Once both body and mind are thus restrained, one gains entry to the gateway of the Path.
Thus we know that the *kāṣāya* is the foremost requisite for entering the Buddha-way.
Second, among the multitudes of humans and devas. [Commentary:

"Multitude" refers to the monastic community (*saṃgha*). "Place" means dwelling. Because the various devas are attached to pleasure, and those in the six realms of existence fluctuate between rising and sinking, they are unable to practice for unexcelled bodhi.
Therefore, the Vinaya states: "Having received the full precepts (*upasampadā*), one is superior to devas, humans, Māras, and Brahmās."
Among the assemblies of non-Buddhist Brahmins, the community of bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs is the most preeminent.
Thus it is known that those who wear the kāṣāya stand above all beings among gods and humans in every gathering.
Third, parents return the bow. [Commentary:

Parents are the root of one’s physical existence. When taking leave of them to enter the monastic life, one ought to have no further filial status toward them. "Return" means to respond; that is, to respond to their bow.
According to the Vinaya, upon seeing one's parents, one should merely offer greetings; yet, perhaps out of consideration for their past toil...
When one returns a bow out of gratitude for heavy labor or kindness, one's parents will surely say, "You wear the *kāṣāya*, you are a disciple of the Buddha," and they will respond with a bow.
This is the benefit of the *kāṣāya*. Without the dharma-robe upon one's body, it would not necessarily be so.
The *Lalitavistara Sūtra* (Puyao jing) states: King Śuddhodana addressed Udāyin: "Go to the Buddha's presence and convey my intent.
The Buddha previously made a vow that once he had attained the Way, he would return; you must rely upon these former words and come at the appointed time to meet him.
When Udāyin arrived, he fully proclaimed the King’s intention, and the Buddha immediately granted permission, saying he would go in seven days. At that time, Udāyin informed the King.
Upon receiving this news, the King was filled with joy. Together with his ministers, he went forty *li* outside the city to welcome the World-Honored One.
The Buddha, accompanied by Vajrapāṇi, Brahmā, Śakra, the Four Heavenly Kings, and the assembly of bhikṣus, emitted a great radiance and arrived traveling through the air.
As they drew near the King, the monarch, along with his subjects, queens, and court ladies, beheld him and prostrated themselves in worship. The Buddha—
He manifested various supernatural transformations, appearing and disappearing in all directions, intending to prevent sentient beings from engaging in slanderous acts.
After the King had prostrated, the Buddha descended to the ground and inquired after his father, the King, asking whether he suffered little illness or distress and was living with ease and vigor.
Having completed these greetings, the King and the Buddha, along with the entire great assembly, returned to the kingdom, where they preached the Dharma to benefit and transform sentient beings.

Those who attained the Way were numerous; this was as if parents were returning the prostrations. The Buddha showed that he would not accept them. The Buddha then returned to inquire after their welfare and preached the Dharma to transform and benefit them.
Monastics of future generations should reflect upon this accordingly.
Fourth is the Lion’s Relinquishment of the Body.
[Commentary] In the Sanskrit language, *saṃghāta* means "lion" in this language. The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states: "In the past, there was a Pratyekabuddha."
In the mountain forests, he brought blessings and salvation to sentient beings; even the birds and beasts followed him.
At that time, there was a lion named Firm Vow (*Dṛḍhapratijñā*), whose fur was golden in color; it ate fruits and chewed grass, never harming living creatures.
There was a hunter who had shaved off his beard and hair and wore a *kāṣāya* robe, yet he carried a bow and arrows hidden within. Seeing the lion approaching, he thought to himself: "I can..."
He killed it to take its skin, intending to present it to the king so that he might escape his poverty. He then struck it with a poisoned arrow, wounding it.
As the lion was about to kill him, it saw that he wore the *kāṣāya* robe and thought to itself: "One who wears the *kāṣāya* will surely attain liberation.
This *kāṣāya* is the distinguishing mark of the sages of the three periods. If I were to harm him, I would be giving rise to an evil mind toward [the Dharma]."
These are the worthies and sages of the three periods. Having reflected thus, he ceased his harmful intent and died; it was because of his reverence for the *kāṣāya* that he relinquished his body.
Fifth is the dragon who donned [the robe] and escaped calamity.
[Commentary] The Sanskrit term *nāga* is translated here as "dragon" (*long*). It is the sovereign among scaled creatures. It can become large or small, long or short.
It ascends to heaven at the spring equinox and enters the earth at the autumn equinox; this is its natural order. The *Nāgarāja Sūtra* states:
The Dragon King addressed the Buddha, saying, "In this ocean, there are countless species of dragons, whom the Garuḍa kings constantly come to devour."
"We are terrified day and night; we seek the Buddha’s protection so that we may attain peace and security.

At that time, the World-Honored One immediately removed the black robe he was wearing and gave it to the Dragon King, saying, "Take this robe and distribute it among all the dragons, ensuring it reaches everyone.
Even those who receive but a single thread shall not be harmed by the Garuḍa King."
One is able to commit transgressions.
Sixth, the king respects and has faith [in them].
[Commentary: The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The Venerable Daṇḍaka took official timber in secret; his offense was such that it could not be relinquished. [This refers to] the *kumbha* [offense].

King Śrīṣeṇa had faith and reverence for the Triple Gem. When he saw Dhaniya wearing the saṃghāṭī robe, although he was taking timber from the royal domain, the king felt relieved and did not question him.
Seventh, sentient beings pay homage.

[Commentary] A sutra states: "Among the six realms and four modes of birth, there are none who, upon seeing one wearing the *kāṣāya*, do not pay respect and prostrate, regarding them as the supreme field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*).
Therefore, the Vinaya says: When a bhikṣu washed his old *kāṣāya*, a lake deity took the wash-water and sprinkled it over its own body.
Later, when a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*) brought a new cloth to wash, the lake deity refused, saying, "Do not defile my water. This is clearly visible [in the records].
The Kāṣāya. One should respect it in this manner.
Eighth, the rākṣasas show reverence.
[Commentary] Formerly, there was a mountain-dwelling monk who stayed overnight in a deep cave. He used his robe to screen himself from the front. A strange person came there.
Its form was utterly terrifying. It extended its arms inward to probe, yet it feared touching the *kāṣāya* robe; obstructed from entering, it was thus unable to escape.
Such various manifestations are difficult to describe in full detail.
Ninth, protection and assistance by devas and nāgas.
[Commentary] The Vinaya states: "Wherever the *kāṣāya* robe is present, all devas, nāgas, and benevolent deities shall provide protection."
Tenth, one attains the Buddha-way.
[Commentary] The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: The Buddha told Ānanda, "The Buddhas of the past wore such robes as these and attained the Buddha-way;
the Buddhas of the future shall likewise wear such robes as these and attain the Buddha-way, just as I do now."
[One] uses a blade to cut [the cloth] and fashions it into the robes of a śramaṇa, so that one will not be plundered by enemies or thieves;

this is the garment of liberation, the robe of the field of merit. If there are sentient beings who give rise to a single evil thought toward the Buddhas of the three periods of time, pratyekabuddhas, arhats, or those who wear dyed robes, they shall incur immeasurable sin. Why is this? Because [it is the robe of] the ruined color...
The robe is the emblem of the noble ones. If one can resolve to give rise to a mind of reverence for those who wear the dyed robes, they shall obtain immeasurable merit.
It was through the utmost sincerity of my faith and veneration that I attained the Way of the Buddha.
Citing evidence: The *Xuanlao lishi ganying yinyuan* (Causes and Conditions of Master Xuan’s Spiritual Resonance) states:
At that time, a ministerial son of one of the Four Heavenly Kings addressed Master Xuan, saying: "When the Tathāgata was approaching his parinirvāṇa, he told Mañjuśrī and the great assembly:
'When I first entered the mountains to study the Way, I traded a priceless precious robe to obtain a deer-skin garment, which I wore. Then a tree spirit manifested its form.'"
Holding his saṃghāṭī robe in his hand, he said to me: "As you now cultivate the path, you will certainly attain perfect enlightenment.
At the time of the parinirvāṇa of the past Buddha Kāśyapa, he entrusted this cloth saṃghāṭī to me, commanding me to preserve and maintain it well."
"I shall wait for a virtuous person to appear in the world so that I may entrust it to them. When I wished to receive it, the earth shook violently.
The tree deity said, 'I shall now open the garment for you to reveal the marks of a field of merit. Having seen these marks, I immediately entered the Vajra-samādhi;
the earth shook again. The tree deity spoke once more: 'You are still but a worldly person; you have not yet..."
"You should wear this Dharma robe; you should place it upon the crown of your head and venerate it with reverence. As you seek the Buddha-way, you shall not be disturbed by Māra.
I, relying on the tree deity, shall carry it upon my head. Even during my six years of ascetic practice, the great earth shook."
His body was already emaciated, yet his robe remained upon his head; he did not dare to cast it off despite his exhaustion. When Brahmā saw this, he gave rise to great compassion and pity.
Taking my *kāṣāya* robe, he ascended to the Brahma Heaven, whereupon the earth shook violently once more and the sun and moon lost their radiance.
The Earth Goddess Sthāvarā addressed Brahmā, saying, "You should take this robe and return it to its place upon [the Buddha's] head. Brahmā followed these instructions. Great...
The earth became peaceful; the sun and moon returned to their brilliance. The Prince asked the Brahma King, "Do you know my intention regarding the saṃghāṭī robe upon the crown of my head?

He replied, "I do not know. [The Prince said: "This is for the sake of future wicked bhikṣus and bhikṣuṇīs who will show no respect for my dharma-robes of liberation, who will not maintain the three robes, and who likewise will not uphold the precepts."
The Dharma perishes quickly; therefore, the robe remains upon the crown of the head.

Furthermore, the *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: When the Buddha made his vow before the Buddha Ratnagarbha, he prayed that when he attained Buddhahood, his *kāṣāya* would possess five kinds of merit.
First, those who enter my Dharma and commit grave offenses or hold wrong views—within their mindfulness... [text continues].
1. Those who revere it with a heart of respect will certainly receive a prediction of enlightenment within the Three Vehicles. 2.
Devas, nāgas, ghosts, and others who can show even a small measure of respect toward this *kāṣāya* shall immediately attain non-retrogression from the Three Vehicles. 3.

If any ghosts, spirits, or humans obtain even four inches of the *kāṣāya*, they will have their food and drink sufficiently provided. 4. When sentient beings are in mutual conflict, if they bring the *kāṣāya* to mind, [they shall be reconciled].
He immediately gave rise to a mind of loving-kindness. Fifth, if one upholds even a small portion of this [teaching], honoring and respecting it, one will always surpass others.
[Commentary] These five kinds of merit are precisely the ten types of benefits mentioned previously, as well as the meaning produced by the second verse.
First, this corresponds to the previous meaning of "the foremost of Bodhi. Second, this corresponds to the parents bowing in return and sentient beings performing prostrations.
1. Devas and nāgas provide protection and blessings; this is the meaning of attaining the path of Buddhahood. 2. This is the meaning of the second verse concerning subsequent rebirth. 3.
This is the meaning of the lion’s self-sacrifice and the king’s faith and respect. Thus, the *Yingluo jing* (Ākāśagarbha Sūtra) states:

"If the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas, engage in strife, one should contemplate this kāṣāya and give rise to a mind of compassion. 4. This is the meaning of the multitude of humans and devas, and nāgas wearing [it].
To be exempt from calamity is the meaning of *rākṣasa* (the respectful one). Reflect on this in sequence, and it will become naturally clear.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "For the sons of Śākya, the observance of the prohibitive precepts is their nature; shaving the head and donning dyed robes is their mark."

In the *Caturvargika-vinaya-piṭaka*, the Buddha told the bhikṣus: "Wherever you dwell, you must always be accompanied by the three robes (*tricīvara*), just as a bird’s two wings are constantly with its body. You have abandoned your original clans and lineages to go forth out of faith;
you should act in this manner. Wherever you go, let the Dharma-robes follow you; they must not be left overnight. — *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* (Sengqi lü).
In the Vinaya, the Buddha said: "A bhikṣu’s three robes and one alms bowl must always accompany him. One who violates this incurs an offense upon crossing the boundary.
One should revere the three robes as if they were a stūpa. In the *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya*, the Buddha said: "Guard the three robes as you would your own skin;
guard the alms bowl as you would your own eyes. Wherever you go, be accompanied by your robes and bowl, without any lingering attachment."
Like a flying bird: if one enters a village or a layperson’s dwelling without carrying these three robes, one commits an offense (*pañcavargīya-vinaya*).
One must guard the three robes as carefully as one's own thin skin; they must always remain with the body, like the feathers of a bird that follow it whether it flies or walks.
In the *Brahmajāla-bodhisattva-śīla-sūtra* of the Mahāyāna, the Buddha said: "If a disciple of the Buddha, at the two times..."

The dhūta practitioner, during winter and summer, while practicing seated meditation and observing the summer retreat, constantly uses tooth-sticks, cleansing powder, the three robes, a water flask and alms bowl,
a sitting mat, a mendicant’s staff, an incense burner, a water filter, a hand towel, a knife,
a fire-starter, tweezers, a rope bed, and the Sūtras, Vinaya, images of the Buddha, and images of Bodhisattvas; this is so when the Bodhisattva practices the dhūtas or travels abroad.
At that time, whether traveling a hundred li or a thousand li, these eighteen items must always accompany one's person; to be without them constitutes an offense.
Indeed, the three robes and the single alms bowl were personally held by each Buddha and transmitted from patriarch to patriarch; they are to be observed equally by all seven classes of disciples.

Both vehicles agree on this regulation. If it is claimed that the robes and alms bowl may be discarded by a Buddhist disciple who has left the household life, and that the rules and practices differ between the eastern and western lands, I request that you consult the Tripiṭaka: which Sūtra, which Vinaya, or which Śāstra permits such a thing?
You should know that the words of the Buddha are trustworthy, whereas ordinary speech lacks authority. Those with wisdom should not be defiled by heterodox winds; they must maintain firm faith.

[The text says: "It is so by force. [Commentary] The *Yeshu* (Record of Karma) states: "The reason the robes and bowl must accompany the person is that for those who have left the household life, maintaining an empty mind is fundamental;
they possess no dwelling-attachment. They remain wherever there is benefit; therefore, the rule was established that they must be carried with one. The *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* says: "Provided that..."

One whose nature is that of a śramaṇa defiles the conduct of a śramaṇa; only one whose form is that of a śramaṇa—one who wears the *kāṣāya*—shall attain *nirvāṇa* without remainder at the abodes of Maitreya Buddha and even up to Ruci Buddha. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"If a layperson seeks a piece of a monk’s or nun’s *kāṣāya* that possesses the virtue of the precepts in order to avert calamity..."
[The Buddha] granted [the use of] bedding and a small portion.
Regarding the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat): it belongs to the category of the "one hundred and one" robes; it has the same shape as a felt or mat and is called a "spread."
Complete. Its shape is like that of a quilt or blanket, and it is thus called a "reclining implement" (*śayanāsana*), meaning that one lies down upon what is spread out.
When spread out for sitting, it becomes a "sitting implement. When spread out to cushion the feet, it becomes a "foot-cushion garment. Thus, its name encompasses multiple meanings.
Therefore, it is included among the one hundred and one types of robes.

[End of] Collection. The Sanskrit term is *niṣīdana*; this is translated here as "sitting mat" (*zuòjù*). It is also called the "following-sitting robe" (*suízuò yī*) and the "foot-cushion robe" (*chǔnzú yī*).
Its length is two and a half *vitasti* (spans) of the Buddha’s hand, and its width is two *vitasti*. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The Tathāgata..."
A *zat-shou* (span) is two chi and four cun; this is according to the small measurement. If calculated by the large measurement, it would be approximately two chi.
It must not be used for the three robes (*tricīvara*), nor may it be given as a pure gift (*śuddha-dāna*), nor used for gathering firewood or grass, nor for miscellaneous storage purposes.

It may only be used as a seat-covering. When traveling on a journey, upon reaching a place to sit, one takes it up and sits upon it. The *Śariputra-vinaya* states: "The new [seat] consists of two layers; the old..."

Regarding the four grave offenses (*catur-āpatti*), one should not accept a single-layered sitting mat (*niṣīdana*). The original *Vinaya* establishes the causal basis for this rule for three reasons:

for the sake of the body, for the sake of the robes, and for the sake of the bedding. The *Sìshìchāo* states: "For the sake of the body" means fearing that damage might be sustained by sitting directly on the ground.

Next, "for the sake of the robes" means fearing that the three robes (*tricīvara*) will easily become worn out without a protective layer. "For the sake of the bedding" means fearing that the body may be impure.
Because it defiles the monastic bedding. The Vinaya states: "For a new *niṣīdana*, one should apply borders (*praticchādana*) to the four edges of the old one to blend its color.

When making [a new one], one should likewise install borders. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "Cut it into three parts; the long end should be one part, which is then pasted onto the four corners; if it does not fit, that is sufficient.
In both the *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* and the *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan*, the performance of prostrations [upon such a mat] is not permitted.

It is used for spreading out [the robe]. Its sight or report is rare in the Five Indias of the Western Regions. As for its use for prostration and spreading in this land, it is unknown when the tradition began.
If one follows the sacred regulations, not using it is considered correct. However, if one discusses it as a garment, there is no harm in spreading it for prostration.
This has been explained in detail here; let students act according to their convenience.
The bedding and sitting mat nourish the sprout of the mind’s nature; by unfolding it, one ascends to the ground of the sages and upholds the command of the Tathāgata.
Oṃ damba damba svāhā (three times).
[Note] This verse employs both the exoteric and esoteric teachings in mutual interplay. The first line presents both the Chinese and Sanskrit terms together; this single line may be...
This reveals the function of the whole. The following three phrases reveal the essence of the whole function.
Ultimately, the essence is not separate from the function, and the function is not separate from the essence. "The sprout of the mind" refers to the sprout that grows from the seed of bodhi.
"Spreading out" is like the method of sowing seeds. If one is sitting, it should be changed to say:

"When spreading out the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), it is like a seed obtaining the earth. As for the term "sacred ground" (*āryabhūmi*), it refers to the ground where a thousand sages (*ārya*) travel together;
this is another name for the *niṣīdana* (sitting mat). It is said that no ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) ascends upon this.
The Ground. By what means can one realize the state of a Sage? If all seeds are not sown upon this ground, by what means can the sprouts of the mind be nurtured?

"Tathā" (Thus) refers to the principle of the Dharma-body; "Āgata" (Come) refers to the function of the Response-body. Because the Dharma and its transformation are darkly unified, it is called Tathāgata.
"To uphold" means to follow the regulations of the Buddha and to practice the Dharma that is without grasping or fabrication.
The dharma of non-retention and non-action is precisely the method for cultivating the sprouts of the mind.
The method for cultivating the sprouts of the mind is precisely the upholding of the Tathāgata’s life-force of wisdom.

Long ago, when an arhat bhikṣu was entering meditative absorption in a mountain cave, a macaque took his sitting mat, bared his right shoulder, joined his palms, and circumambulated him three times to the right.
He knelt on the ground in circumambulation. When the bhikṣu emerged from meditative concentration, he sighed and said, "Even an animal possesses Buddha-nature.

The bhikṣu immediately conferred upon him the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts. The macaque, filled with joy, danced and leaped; losing his footing, he fell from the cliff and died, immediately being reborn in the Tuṣita Heaven Palace.
In the *Yiming zhong* (Collection of Names and Meanings), the celestial deity Huangqiong says: "Originally, when the Buddha first converted the five men, [he was] Kā..."
The brothers [Mahākāśyapa and Anuruddha] both wore their *kāṣāya* robes over the left arm, with the sitting mat (*niṣīdana*) placed beneath the robe.
Later, as his disciples gradually increased in number, young bhikṣus of handsome appearance entered the city to beg for food and were frequently pursued by women's affections.
Consequently, the corner of the robe was made to hang from the left shoulder. Later, when it was blown away by the wind, they used the *niṣīdana* to weigh it down.
The *Zenghui ji* (Record of Augmented Radiance) states: The Buddha first permitted the wearing of a *zhenyi* (stabilizing cloth) on the left shoulder.
Later, there was a non-Buddhist practitioner named Dharmatrāta who asked a bhikṣu: "What is the name of that piece of cloth upon your shoulder, and what is its purpose?"
The bhikṣu replied, "It is called the *niṣīdana*; it is a sitting mat. He asked again, "What is the name of the robe you wear?
What are its meritorious qualities? He replied, "It is the 'Robe of Forbearance. It bears the marks of the Triple Gem; above, it restrains the celestial Māras;
below, it subdues the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Dharmatrata said, "Since this robe possesses such noble and meritorious qualities and great majesty..."
"O Venerable One, how could one place the cloth upon which he sat on top of it? If you were doing this yourself, why did your teacher not instruct you?
If your teacher had instructed you, this practice would not be worthy of such honor. The bhikṣu addressed the Buddha.

The Buddha decreed that it should be returned and placed beneath the garment on the left arm, but it must not hang down with pointed corners like an elephant's trunk or the ears of a sheep. Therefore, now...
In accordance with the Buddha’s regulations, he ordered the bhikṣus to place their sitting mats beneath the left arm of their *kāṣāya* robes.

Regarding the phrase "ascending the site of enlightenment" (*dōjō*): "ascending" means to advance upward. When one reaches the state of non-action (*wuwei*) and realizes the ground of truth, it is called a "site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*). Furthermore...
It is said: "The place where the Buddhas of the ten directions attain the Way is the Court of Non-arising (*anutpāda*).
It may be called a *vihāra*, which is the Court of Dharma. It may be called a *saṃghārāma*, which increases merit and gives rise to goodness.
It may be called a 'dwelling of pure abiding,' or a 'dwelling of shared Dharma,' or a 'dwelling transcending the world,' or a 'perfumed chamber' (*prāsāda*), or a 'pure and stainless [abode]'."
The Ultimate Garden. It is also called the Pure Realm of Vajra, or the Site of Quiescent Enlightenment, or the Place Far Removed from Evil, or the Place Closely Approaching the Good;
these names are established according to their respective meanings, each signifying something specific. This is the dwelling place of virtuous people.
A layman of faithful heart thought to himself: "When shall I be able to dwell in such an exalted [place]?"
In a place of dust and defilement, one need not now consider painting, dyeing, or sculpting; wherever a Buddha image is present, that very spot is called a *bodhimaṇḍa*.
Upon seeing it for the first time, one should immediately recite this verse-mantra.
If one should behold the Buddha, one should wish that all sentient beings obtain the unimpeded eye and see all Buddhas.
Oṃ amṛte hūṃ phaṭ (three times). [Commentary:
"If one should behold the Buddha" refers to the earnest intention of the initial mind; it signifies that a Buddha is not easily seen.
This vow is the great resolve for the dual benefit of self and others. It means that having attained the sight of the Buddha, one should give rise to self-congratulation;

yet, since the Buddha-nature is inherently possessed by every person, why is it not easily seen? Precisely because it is inherently possessed, it is not easily seen. This is what is meant by the saying:
"One does not see the true face of Mount Lu simply because one is standing within the mountains. Thus he spoke to the assembly.
That living beings do not easily see the Buddha is solely due to the hindrance of delusive thoughts and attachments.
If delusive thoughts are completely extinguished, fundamental enlightenment and initial enlightenment become one in perfect luminosity and one in purity;

how much less could there be the names of "living being" and "Buddha," or the marks of subject and object, or the discrimination of them? Therefore, upon attaining the unimpeded eye, one immediately sees the Buddha. One attains [this seeing].
"Buddha" refers to the Buddha's vision. This Buddha-vision is the unimpeded eye. To speak of the unimpeded eye means to be endowed with the five eyes in their perfect clarity.
That is to say: the divine eye (divyacakṣus) is penetrating and not obstructed; the fleshly eye (māṃsacakṣus) is obstructed and not penetrating.
The Dharma-eye perceives only the conventional; the Wisdom-eye clearly realizes emptiness. The Buddha-eye is like a thousand suns, illuminating diverse forms as ultimately identical.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Aniruddha sees Jambudvīpa as if looking at an *āmra* fruit in the palm of his hand;
the various Bodhisattvas see hundreds of thousands of worlds; and the Tathāgatas of the ten directions exhaustively perceive even the finest motes of dust. Regarding purity:
The pure land is such that there is nothing it does not behold, much like the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*).

However, it can only see the sentient beings of the six realms as they die here and are born there, perceiving the signs of their suffering and joy, as well as the various forms and colors of the world;
yet, while there is no obstruction, one has not yet attained the ability to see all Buddhas. The "cave-like vision" of sentient beings does not extend beyond a mere fraction of an inch. Now...
That which is called the unimpeded eye is the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; therefore, one is able to see all Buddhas.

[Commentary on the Praise of the Buddha]: The Sanskrit term is *vaśī*; in the Chinese language, it means "to praise. To "praise" (*zan*) is to extol one's virtues. The *Śariputra-bhikṣuṇī-vinaya* states:
"I allow you to perform *bhāṣya* (chanting). *Bhāṣya* refers to the words of speech. The *Fayuan zhulin* states:

"Seeking the origins of *bhāṣya* in the Western Regions, it is like the existence of *zan* (eulogies) in this Eastern land. A *zan* composes chapters based on literary prose; a *bhāṣya* flows as verses through short stanzas.
Comparing their matters and meanings, the names differ, but the intent is truly the same. Regarding the Buddha’s merits, no one can fully praise them."
It is fitting; yet, without praise, there is no way to express one’s reverence. Therefore, whenever one beholds the compassionate countenance [of the Buddha], one should offer hymns of praise.
"Buddha" means the perfection of awakening and conduct. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya-kṣudraka-vastu* states: "Do not remain in a place that is too exposed.

One who violates this incurs an offense against the Dharma. When performing prostrations and paying homage, keep the body upright, the feet together, and with palms joined, recite the following praise:
The Dharma King, the Unsurpassed Honored One, peerless throughout the three realms; the Teacher of gods and humans, the compassionate father of the four modes of birth.
I now take refuge for a moment; he can extinguish the karma of three *kalpas*. To extol or praise him would not reach its end even in billions of eons.

[Commentary] "Dharma" (fa) means "guiding and maintaining. This refers to the fact that every single phenomenon and every single teaching acts as both a guide and a support. "King" (wang) means "to go toward.
This signifies that the Dharma taught by the Buddha is without high or low; it is a teaching of equality through which all sentient beings turn for refuge.
Furthermore, "king" carries the meaning of "sovereignty," signifying that by means of the Dharma, one gathers and protects sentient beings, enabling them to attain peace and security.
Because he delights in the Dharma, he is called the Dharma King (*dharmarāja*). As the Sūtra says: "I am the Dharma King; I possess mastery over the Dharma.

Furthermore, there are two kinds of kings: first, the Wheel-Turning King (*cakravartin*), who rules over the four continents; second, the Dharma King, who governs and encompasses the great trichiliocosm.
Just as in the mundane world the Wheel-Turning King is held most venerable, so in the supramundane the Dharma-King is deemed most weighty;
therefore, he is called the Unsurpassed Honored One (*anuttara*). In the Sanskrit language this is *anuttara*; in the Qin language it means "unsurpassed. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states:
"Just as among all phenomena, Nirvāṇa is unsurpassed, so among all sages, the Buddha is unsurpassed. He has no equal within the three realms."
Regarding these "pairs": according to the *Svāśaya-samādhi Sūtra*, there are first four types in the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*):
first, desire for objects; second, desire for form; third, desire for gain; and fourth, sexual desire. Because desire is predominant and form is slight, it is called the "Desire Realm.

Second, the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*) has two types: first, desire for objects; and second, desire for form. Because form is predominant and desire is slight, it is called the "Form Realm. Third, the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).

There is one kind. Because it is solely characterized by the absence of desire, and because form is cut off and desire is inferior, it is called the Formless Realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). "Lun" means equal; "pi" means to pair.
This refers to those who have realized the realm of the Buddha’s principle and dwell in the Constantly Quiescent Light Land (*nityapraśāntaprabhāsa-kṣetra*). As for the remaining nine dharma-realms:
All are termed "sentient beings. How could they possibly be equated with the Buddha? The Tathāgata is the Great Teacher of the three realms;
he regards all sentient beings as his own infants. Through countless skillful means, he leads them out from the burning house.
Therefore, he is called the Guide of gods and humans and the Compassionate Father of the four modes of birth. I now take refuge in him for a moment; he can extinguish the karma of three *kalpas*.
This refers to practitioners who, with their ordinary conceptual minds, refer to themselves as "I. Those who take temporary refuge do so by means of a single gaze or a single prostration;

through the sincerity of beholding the Buddha’s marks and signs, they cause immeasurable sentient beings to eliminate the defilements of sin from beginningless time and deeply plant the roots of wisdom.
As for the "three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas," in Sanskrit it is fully called *asaṃkhyeya*.
*Kalpa* (劫). In the Chinese language, this means "an incalculable period of time. There are three interpretations of it. First, as stated in the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*:
from the original Śākyamuni up to Śikhin, [the Buddha] encountered seventy-five thousand Buddhas; this is called the first *asaṃkhyeya*.
Next, from Śikhin up to Dīpaṃkara, he encountered seventy-six thousand Buddhas; this is called the second *asaṃkhyeya*. Furthermore, from... [the third *asaṃkhyeya*].
From Dīpaṃkara to Vipaśyin, he encountered seventy-seven thousand Buddhas; this is termed the "three asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
These three asaṃkhyeyas are numbers within the infinite; they are calculated based on the duration of time spent by the Tathāgata practicing the six pāramitās during his causal stage.
Furthermore, the *Commentary on the Awakening of Faith* states: "From the initial generation of the bodhicitta until reaching the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi) is called..."
The first asaṃkhyeya kalpa extends from the second bhūmi to the eighth bhūmi; these are called the two asaṃkhyeyas.
From the ninth bhūmi to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyaksaṃbodhi), these are called the three asaṃkhyeyas.
These constitute the "numberless within the numberless" when discussing the stages of a bodhisattva’s practice. Therefore, it is precisely this present single thought-moment of faith and reverence.
It surpasses the merit of the Tathāgata’s cultivation of the six perfections and ten thousand practices over three great *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;
it can extinguish the sins of birth and death accumulated over those three *kalpas*. How much more so when one extols and praises [the Buddha]?

If one were to discuss the merits of praising the Buddha, even ten million *kalpas* would not suffice to describe them exhaustively. Thus, the *Pratimokṣa-saṃvara-vinaya-vastu* (or *Caryāpraṇidhāna-parivarta*) states: "First, prostrating to all Buddhas; second, praising..."
Praising the Tathāgata, it says, "Each, with an ocean of all voices, universally produces inexhaustible, wondrous words and phrases;
throughout all kalpas of the future, they praise the Buddha’s ocean of profound merits. The *Bodhisattva-mūla-pratipatti-sūtra* states:
Ānanda said to the Buddha, "If there were someone who, by means of a four-line verse, praised the Buddha, the Tathāgata..."
"How much merit does one obtain? The Buddha said: "Suppose there were hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of countless sentient beings, all of whom attained the path of a pratyekabuddha.
If someone were to provide these individuals with offerings of clothing, food and drink, and medicine..."
"Suppose one were to provide bedding and seating for a full hundred years—would the merit thereof be great? Ānanda replied, "It would be very great, World-Honored One.

The Buddha said, "If a person, with a joyful heart, were to praise the Tathāgata with even a single four-line verse, the merit they obtain would exceed the aforementioned blessings by hundreds of thousands of millions of times; it cannot be compared. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If..."
Upon hearing of the merits of the Buddhas, one gives rise to a mind of respect, honoring and praising them with reverence; such a person obtains immeasurable merit.
Because they know that all sentient beings have no one who surpasses [the Buddhas], they are called "Venerable" (zun).

Because their heart of awe and reverence exceeds that felt toward kings, parents, or teachers, they are called "Weighty" (zhong). Because they are humble and wary of difficulties, they are said to be "Reverent" (gong). To deduce this...

Because of their wisdom and virtue, they are called "venerable. To praise their meritorious virtues is to extol them. When such extolling is insufficient, one further proclaims their names to uplift them;
this is to laud them. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The atoms within all lands and the thoughts within every mind may be counted and known;
the waters within the great oceans may be drunk up until they are exhausted; the void may be measured and the wind may be bound; yet no one can fully describe the Buddha’s merits."

**Record on Bowing to the Buddha** "Bowing" (*li*) means "to tread upon" (*li*). It refers to the ritual etiquette wherein there is a measured degree in advancing and retreating, and a distinct demarcation between the honorable and the humble.

The *Ekottarika Āgama* states that there are five kinds of merit in bowing to the Buddha: first, physical excellence, because one gives rise to [joy] upon beholding the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
First, because of the supreme dignity [of the Buddha]. Second, one obtains an excellent voice, because at the time of seeing the Buddha, one proclaims:

"Namo Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha. Third, one becomes abundant in wealth and treasures, because at the time of seeing the Buddha, one makes offerings according to one's means with flowers, incense, and lamps.
Fourth, one is born into a noble and high-ranking family, because at the time of seeing the Buddha...

The mind is free from defilement and attachment. Furthermore, because one kneels with the right knee on the ground, joins the palms in *añjali*, and pays homage, fifthly, one will be reborn in the heavens;
this is due to the natural law (*dharmatā*) of the merit of recollecting the Buddha. The *Avalokiteśvara Xuánjì* states: "The Buddha Tiṣya had two disciples:
first, Śākyamuni, who delighted in practicing altruistic deeds, and thus the beings he was to transform were first to reach maturity; second, Maitreya..."
This person delighted in practicing deeds for his own benefit, and those whom he was to transform would ripen only later. That Buddha thought to himself:
"It is difficult for many people to approach one person, but it is easy for one person to approach many. I wish to cause Śākyamuni to attain enlightenment first."
He then left his two disciples and entered the mountains. At that time, Śākyamuni Bodhisattva followed him into the mountains; searching for his teacher, he could find no trace of him.
As he was walking along, he suddenly saw that Buddha within a jeweled niche, having entered the fire-element meditative concentration (*tejodhātu-samādhi*).

His majestic radiance was so brilliant and magnificent that it was extraordinary compared to ordinary appearances. Walking on, he forgot to set down one foot, remaining there for seven days. Thus it was said:
One verse. Because of this diligence, he surpassed nine kalpas [of practice] and attained Buddhahood before Maitreya. The *Sūtra on Past Deeds* states:
The Buddha told Ānanda, "In the past, there appeared in the world a Tathāgata named Puṣya Buddha.
At that time, that Buddha was in a cave of various jewels; I saw that Buddha, and with a heart of joy, I joined my palms and raised one foot."
For seven days and seven nights, I praised him with these verses. Ānanda, after I had praised that Buddha with these verses, I made this vow:
"Until that Buddha spoke to his attendant, saying, 'This person shall attain Buddhahood ninety-four kalpas hence, under the name Śākyamuni,' at that time, having received my prediction, I—"
Having relinquished worldly diligence and increased my merit, throughout immeasurable lifetimes I served as Brahmā, Lord of the Gods, and as a Wheel-Turning Sage King.
By the power of these causes and conditions of wholesome karma, I have attained four kinds of eloquence;
there is not a single person who can debate with me or defeat me. Having thus attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi, I turn the unsurpassed Dharma wheel.

Wheel. Having understood that the merit of venerating and praising the holy teachings is inconceivable, the practitioner must always maintain this mindfulness and never allow themselves to be indolent, fearing that impermanence might suddenly arrive and leave them with no place for prostration and worship. Whenever one sees a Buddha, [one should act accordingly].
One should offer praise and worship with this mind and these verses:
"Within the heavens above and the earth below, none is equal to the Buddha; throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is likewise no peer.
Having seen all that exists within the world, I find that nothing at all can compare to the Buddha."
The Universal Prostration Mantra: Oṃ Vajra Hūṃ (three praises, three prostrations).
[Note] "In the heavens above and the heavens below, there is none like the Buddha" refers to the three realms (*tridhātu*). This is because, among the nine dharma-realms...
All these are the retributions of sentient beings. The various devas are blinded by their attachment to pleasure and cannot deeply penetrate the Buddha’s principles.

Sentient beings are shrouded by the obstruction of ignorance and cannot awaken to or illuminate the source. The Tathāgata is the God among gods, the Sage among sages, and the most honored in the three realms;
who can equal him? Not only does he transcend vertically through the three periods of time, with none equal to the Buddha, but he likewise pervades horizontally.
Pervading the ten directions, there is likewise nothing with which it can be compared. To summarize:

throughout all of space and across the entire Dharma-realm, there is none who possesses the hundred thousand marks and signs, adorned with myriad virtues, perfected in the three types of awakening, and endowed with the ten titles, as does the World-Honored One.
The first phrase praises his greatness; the second praises his multiplicity; the third praises his excellence; the fourth...
This verse summarizes the praise of the Great and Most Victorious One. Thus, the *Chapter on Vows and Aspirations* (*Pranidhāna-paṭala*) states:
"In all worlds throughout the ten directions, to all the Lions among Men of the three times, I prostrate with my pure body, speech, and mind, everywhere and without exception.
Furthermore, the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The wisdom of the Tathāgata is like space; it perceives all sentient beings coming and going."
His marks are seen and heard throughout all the ten directions. I shall prostrate myself and pay homage to the Dharma King.

If people today, when prostrating to the Buddha and making vows, can praise Śākyamuni as [the Buddha] praised Puṣya, and likewise use these verses to praise Śākyamuni while standing on one foot for seven days and seven nights, that person will certainly see Śākyamuni face-to-face, and he will grant them a prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa).
Furthermore, seeing the thousands of billions of Śākyamunis does not arise apart from one’s own mind. The *Samantabhadra-dhyāna Sūtra* states:

"If there are those who, during the six periods of day and night, pay homage to the Buddhas of the ten directions, recite Mahāyāna sūtras, and contemplate the ultimate truth—the profound dharma of emptiness—for even the duration of a finger-snap, they will eliminate the birth and death of hundreds of thousands of millions of nayutas of Ganges-sands of kalpas."
...of such sins. One who practices this dharma is truly a son of the Buddha. The *Karmavibhaṅga-sūtra* states:
"For every single prostration made to the Buddha, from the knees down to the vajra-ground, for every single mote of dust there is the attainment of the rank of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).
