Ten kinds of merit are obtained: first, one attains a sublime physical form; second, whatever one says is believed by others; third, one is fearless when among the multitude; fourth, all..."

1. The Buddhas will protect and mind them. 2. They will possess great dignified deportment. 3. The multitude will draw near to them with affection. 4. The devas will love and respect them. 5. They will possess great merit and retribution. 6.
At the end of life, they will be reborn in a higher realm. 7. They will swiftly realize nirvana.

In performing the prostrations and praises during the assembly, one must practice with sincere devotion and cultivate meditative visualization. One must not fail to understand that the teachings enumerate seven types of prostration. First is the prostration of pride (*māna-lī*).

This refers to performing the ritual according to the prescribed order without any sense of reverence, while the mind wanders toward external objects; the five points of the body do not touch the ground, and the movement is like that of a pestle going up and down.
Second is the prostration of chanting and responding (*gāthā-pratigāthā-lī*). This refers to a performance where the physical demeanor is merely coarse and correct, while the mind lacks stillness.
1. Prostration with mental visualization: When seeing a person, the body rises quickly to prostrate; when the person departs, the body collapses and the mind grows weary.

This is because the mind is distracted while the mouth chants. 2. Prostration with physical and mental reverence: This means that upon hearing the chanting of the Buddha’s name, one immediately forms the visualization of the Buddha, maintaining physical and mental reverence with diligence free from weariness or indolence.
3. Prostration that gives rise to pure wisdom: This means attaining realization of the Buddha’s realm and accordingly...

5. Prostration by Manifesting the Mind and Penetrating the Dharma Realm: This means that by prostrating to a single Buddha, one prostrates to all Buddhas; by performing a single prostration, one prostrates to the entire dharma realm.
This is because the Buddha’s dharma-body is pervasive and interfused. Regarding this, one contemplates for oneself that the body, mind, and other phenomena are [identical to] the dharma realm.

From the very beginning, one has not been separate from the *dharmadhātu*. Buddhas and the self are equal. Therefore, to now pay homage to a single Buddha is to universally pay homage to all Buddhas throughout the *dharmadhātu*.
Six: Homage through Correct Contemplation. This means paying homage to one's own Buddha and not relying upon other Buddhas. Why is this?
All sentient beings each have a Buddha dwelling within them. This is the seventh [point]: the prostration of equality in the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

In the previous three types of prostration, there was a distinction between the one who prostrates and the object of prostration, as self and other were two different things. Now, in this single prostration, there is neither self nor other;

ordinary beings and sages are of one suchness, for essence and function are non-dual. As Mañjuśrī said: "The nature of the one who prostrates and the object of prostration is empty and quiescent. This refers to the preceding three.
Regarding the matter, there are four subsequent points. In the *Mahāvaipulya Ratnakaraṇḍa Sūtra*, the śrāvaka Jñānapradīpa asked Mañjuśrī:
"How does one pay homage to the Buddha? Mañjuśrī replied: "If one sees the purity of the Dharma, this is called seeing the purity of the Buddha.
Whether body or mind, neither bowing down nor rising up, remaining upright, unmoving and unshaking, with a mind that is tranquil—this is how one acts."
Practicing in tranquility—this is called paying homage to the Buddha. A bhikṣu must not pay homage to the Buddha with both shoulders covered by his *kāṣāya*.

If he does so, upon death he will fall into the Iron Armor Hell (*kavaca-naraka*). Exceptions are when sitting in meditation, receiving food, or when both shoulders are covered; these do not constitute an offense.

A bhikṣu must not wear the meditation robe (*cīvara*) while paying homage to the Buddha, reciting sutras, walking in meditation (*caṅkrama*), paying homage to elders, or proceeding before a stupa or temple. Upon death, he will be transformed into a lump of flesh.
Fish, turtles, tortoises, and their like must not have their heads covered; they must expose their heads. One who violates this incurs an offense, except during times of illness or extreme cold.
All those who have left the household life out of true faith and received the precepts must be most diligent in observing this.
[Commentary] Regarding "prostrating with the five limbs touching the ground": according to the *Vimalaprabhā-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, one should make a vow for each [limb].
First, the general vow says: "I now prostrate to the Buddha with my five limbs touching the ground.

In order to sever the five paths and abandon the five hindrances, I vow that all sentient beings shall always abide in peace, never lose the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*), and be fully endowed with the five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*). May my right knee..."

When my left knee touches the ground, may all sentient beings not give rise to false views regarding the teachings of external paths, but may they all be firmly established upon the path of perfect enlightenment.
When my right hand touches the ground, may it be as when the World-Honored One sat upon the Vajra Seat, his right [hand touching the earth].
He touched the earth with his hand; it shook, manifesting an auspicious omen, as he realized Great Bodhi. I now do likewise:

together with all sentient beings, may we equally realize the path of enlightenment. When my left hand touches the ground, may I cause all sentient beings—those who are difficult to subdue—to leave behind all non-Buddhist paths, and through the four means of attraction (*saṃgrahavastu*), may I gather them in, leading them to enter the True Path. May I...

When the crown of the head touches the ground, it causes all sentient beings to abandon the mind of pride and to give rise to the unsurpassed resolve, whereby they all achieve the mark of the invisible crown of the head (*anavalokitamūrdhatā*). The remaining meanings may be understood accordingly.

**Offering the Purification Vase [Record]** "Offering" (*gōng*) refers to presenting [an item] as an offering. A "vase" (*píng*) is a vessel for drawing water; there are distinctions between those used for purification and those used for contact with defilement.

This is for the purpose of purification, and it is also called the "Vase of Virtue" (*débīng*). This is because it is used for morning and evening ritual practice, thereby generating much merit. The *Xiyùjì* (Records of the Western Regions) states:

The *kuṇḍikā* is the water jar (*kamaṇḍalu*). This is for the purpose of contact. Because the Buddha ordained that a bhikṣu must not perform prostrations or recite scriptures without having washed and rinsed himself, the *śodhanī* jar is used for rinsing the mouth and the *kuṇḍikā* jar for washing the hands. Nowadays, however, this washing and rinsing are no longer practiced;
thus, the two jars have lost their prescribed function. Even if one performs acts of reverence, how can one avoid transgression?

*Ji*. In Sanskrit, it is called *kamaṇḍalu*; here it is translated as "vase. The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states: "There are two types of *kamaṇḍalus*: first, those made of ceramic or earthenware, which are for pure use;
second, those made of copper or iron, which are for [ritual] contact. What is explained here is the pure vase (*śuddha-kamaṇḍalu*).
Every morning at dawn, after a bhikṣu has finished reciting sutras and mantras, he uses the pure vase to fill it with pure water and places it [on an altar].
Before an image of a Buddha or Bodhisattva, when one wishes to fill a flask with water, one should visualize the countenances of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas,
perform prostrations according to the ritual, and upon rising, take up the flask while silently reciting this verse-mantra.

Holding a pure flask in his hand, he should wish: "May all sentient beings be free from defilement within and without, and may they all be made radiant and pure. Oṃ śāntika śānti svāhā (three times). [Note:
"Holding in his hand" means to lift it with the body, thereby manifesting the ritual action. "Free from defilement within and without" means... [all should be made...]
"Radiant purity" means clarifying principle through phenomena. "Internal" refers to body and mind; "external" refers to sensory objects and environments.
This means that when this mind of upholding the precepts is firm and pure, one is not defiled by external dust and toil, nor do internal afflictions arise.
When the inner and outer are as one, the ground of the mind is pure, and the light of wisdom becomes radiant and clear. Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "The faculties and objects..."
It is not so. The remaining physical substance present before you will no longer continue into rebirth; the grasping mind becomes empty and luminous, consisting purely of wisdom.
This nature of wisdom is perfectly bright, illuminating the ten directions—this is precisely what is meant by "intention."
The Mantra for Cleansing the Vase [Record]:
"Dàng" (蕩) means to wash away dust and impurities. Regarding the "mantra," the *Vajradhātu-maṇḍala-sūtra* (Lóugé jīng) states:
"This is the mother of all Buddhas and the seed of Buddhahood; without the mantra, one can never achieve unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment."
However, just as water can wash away the grime from a jar, the Dharma can cleanse the defilements of the mind; this is what is meant by the simultaneous manifestation of both practice and principle.

Having finished prostrating to the Buddha, one rises and takes an empty jar to the place where pure water is kept. With the left hand, one gathers up the robe, and with the right hand, one holds [the jar].
Regarding the flask: first, slowly rinse it with water three times, reciting this mantra seven times for each rinsing.
Do not pour the rinsing water back into clean water; it must be discarded outside.
Oṃ. [Āḥ]. Svāhā (twenty-one times). The Mantra for Pouring Water. [Note]:
"Pouring" means to pour forth.
It signifies that the vessel is purified and ready to receive water, and the mind is clear and capable of receiving the Dharma. The water is poured into...
The ritual vessel is then prepared for the task. When the Dharma is poured into the mind, the principle is realized.
Having thoroughly cleansed the assembly so that it is free from all dust, fill it with pure water and silently recite this mantra.
Oṃ vaśipramani svāhā (three times). [Note] Having performed the consecration, return to your original place.
When walking, do not look to the left or right. If you lose proper decorum or run about distractedly, you must immediately cease all external conditions;
recite the Buddha’s name and hold the mantra with a single mind on the correct path, proceeding with care.

Gather and proceed before the Buddha. Kneel with the right knee on the ground (*huku*). Holding a flask in the left hand, form the Seal of Universal Offering with the right hand and recite the Great Compassion Mantra seven times.
Prostrate and withdraw. At the end of the evening, emerge from the water. Form the seal as before;
first recite the Great Compassion Mantra seven times, followed by the Heart Sutra and the Rebirth Mantra, each seven times. Go outside and sprinkle water.
Purifying the ground. Perform the method of the Amṛta-mudrā with the hands and silently recite the Amṛta-mantra in the mouth.
[Note] "Amṛta" refers to the wondrous medicine of immortality; it is used as a metaphor for the supremacy of the Dharma, which is inconceivable.
For this reason, the mantra is the secret heart-seal (*hṛdaya-mudrā*) of all Buddhas.
Just as ambrosia (*amṛta*) can eliminate the physical ailments of all sentient beings, this mantra can eliminate the mental ailments of all sentient beings.
Furthermore, just as a vase can produce immeasurable precious jewels, this mantra can produce immeasurable merit.
*Namo surūpāya tathāgatāya. Tadyathā. Oṃ suru suru prasu ru prasuru svāhā.* (Recite three times.
When reciting, visualize the flask as a wish-fulfilling vase (*cintāmaṇi-kalaśa*), from which flow forth various kinds of food and drink, first for the devas.

Next, the ghosts and spirits, and finally the hungry ghosts and animals, each obtained their fill. Then, one further visualizes that from the neck of the flask emerge multi-storied pavilions, palaces, precious jewels, necklaces, parasols, incense, flowers, and garments, all provided in full abundance.

Thereafter, one explains the Dharma of the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination and bestows upon them the Three Refuges, causing them to hear the Dharma and receive the Refuges, thereby attaining the three kinds of joy in the Dharma.
[He] prostrated and departed. [Commentary:
As for the "wish-fulfilling vase" (*cintāmaṇi-ghaṭa*), it means that the vase accords with one's wishes; because one merely conceives of an object, it immediately emerges.

It is also called the *maṇi* vase. In the language of China, this means "free from defilement. This vase is luminous and pure, being unstained by dust or grime; therefore, it is named "Free from Defilement."
The *kalaśa* (vase), also known as the *kumbha*, is the vase of the treasure-store (*ratnagarbha-kalaśa*). It is so called because it is able to produce all manner of rare jewels.

As for the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), they are: ignorance (*avidyā*), volitional formations (*saṃskāra*), consciousness (*vijñāna*), name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), contact (*sparśa*), sensation (*vedanā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), grasping (*upādāna*), and becoming (*bhava*).
Birth is old age and death. They function as causes by successively inducing their respective fruits, and they act as conditions through mutual dependence.

There are three periods of time, two periods, and three types within a single moment. Regarding the "three refuges," it means causing them to take refuge in the Triple Gem of Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha so that they may transcend saṃsāra.
Regarding "Dharma-joy," it refers to the joy felt upon hearing the Dharma, because one leaves suffering behind and attains happiness. [In] the Sanskrit language...

Samādhi. This is translated as "concentration that is harmonized and straightened," and is also called "right reception" (samyag-āśraya). Guifeng said: "Not receiving any [further] sensations is called right reception.
(*Vinir-daily-use Essentials: Fragrant Milk Notes*, Vol. 1)

The "Preface to the Phonetic Explanations" (Yinshì xù) refers to the "sequence" (xù). The *Erya* states: "The walls on the east and west are called 'sequences' (xù), for they serve to distinguish the interior from the exterior.
This means that by seeing the walls, one distinguishes the interior and exterior of a residence; by observing the sequence, one knows the interior and exterior of a single record.
The "Wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle": The "One Vehicle" refers to the Buddha-vehicle (*buddhayāna*). "Vehicle" (*yāna*) has the meaning of "transporting.

The Buddha taught the Dharma of the One Vehicle so that sentient beings might rely upon it for practice, thereby escaping the ocean of suffering of birth and death and being transported to the other shore of *nirvāṇa*.
As the *Lotus Sūtra* states: "In all the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the teaching of the One Vehicle. It is wondrous.
This is inconceivable, for it is not something that can be deliberated upon by the minds or discussed by the mouths of ordinary bodhisattvas.
*Yuanjue* (Perfect Enlightenment) refers to the fulfillment of the realization of all phenomena.
*Zi* (鎡) is pronounced as *zi*; it means a hoe. *Nu* (駑) means dull-witted.
“Qianqian tili” (strenuously diligent and alert) means to exert oneself with constant vigilance. The *Yijing* says: “The noble person is strenuously diligent all day long;
at evening, they remain alert as if on guard.
The meaning of “fragrant milk” is derived from the *Sutra of the Avalokiteśvara’s Request*.
The character *fū* (膚) has the phonetic component *fu* (孚). It refers to the skin; here it signifies shallow learning. The *Lunyu* (Analects) speaks of "superficial reception" (*fūshòu*).
When the Buddhist and Daoist teachings declined like the lower reaches of a river, this was used as a metaphor for the downstream flow of a great river.
Regarding the "Hanging Discourse on Mount Sumeru," the *Abhidharmakośa* states: It is called "Wondrous" (*Miao*) because it is composed of four precious substances;

it is called "High" (*Gao*) because it rises above the seven golden mountains. "Mountain" (*Shan*) means "to produce," for it can produce all things. "King" (*Wang*) means "sovereign," as it is the lord of all other mountains.
Because they surround [the Dharma].
Regarding the "Teacher as a Model" (shizimofan): the "Teacher" refers to the one who transmits the Way; "assistance" (*zi*) means to aid, for it aids in the development of one's own karmic practices.
"Model" (*mofan*) refers to a standard or pattern. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Strictly purifying the *vinaya*, he establishes a grand model for the three realms."

Regarding the extinction of all delusions and karma, the *Four-Part Vinaya* verse states: "Having extinguished and removed all fetters and afflictions, this *Saptasatikā-prātimokṣa-sūtra* is preached.
Regarding the generation of various merits and wisdom, the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states: "The nature-precepts fulfill both merit and wisdom."
Regarding the initial cause for its arising, the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The Vinaya is the primary gateway to Nirvāṇa. The *Brahmajāla-sūtra* states:
"All the sarvajñā (omniscience) of the Buddhas emerges from this very source."
The perfection of the Buddha-fruit refers to the accomplishment of the path of awakening.

*Dhāraṇī* is translated here as "total retention" (*zongchi*). This means that it retains all that is wholesome so that it is not lost, and holds back all that is unwholesome so that it does not arise. As the verse says:
"Just as a miraculous elixir transforms iron into precious gold, by reciting and maintaining the *dhāraṇī*, one transforms an ordinary person into a worthy sage."
Furthermore, the teachings of the Tripiṭaka all emerge from dhāraṇī—that is, mantras—which encompass the four *siddhārtha* (purposes).
They eliminate the views of the four marks: self, person, sentient being, and life-span, as well as the view of non-self.
The dharmas are empty and formless: the five aggregates—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness.
Of these dharmas, birth-and-death is the root of defilement, while nirvana is purity.
The Tathāgatagarbha is the nature of True Suchness (tathatā). It is the substratum of the eighth consciousness, replete with all dharmas and encompassing all phenomena;
therefore, it is called a "garbha" (womb/storehouse). The Buddhas realize this mind of the garbha to benefit all sentient beings, its application being inexhaustible.
Sentient beings are deluded regarding this *tathāgatagarbha* mind; constantly obscured by ignorance and entangled by afflictions, they are unable to manifest it.

The Buddha causes sentient beings to practice all wholesome dharmas so that they may sever afflictions and ignorance, thereby manifesting their own *tathāgatagarbha* mind, which is the essence of the pure *dharmakāya*. Thus, *tathatā* (Suchness) is an essence that is not false.

To call that which is false "true" is [the meaning of] *tathā* (thusness). That the nature (*prakṛti*) is without change or alteration is called *tathatā* (suchness); this is the essence of the single reality-mark (*ekasatyalakṣaṇa*).
Because this essence can give rise to all phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane worlds.
Ālaya-vijñāna is the name for the eighth consciousness. It is translated as the "non-perishing consciousness" (amukta-jña), taking non-loss as its meaning.

It is also translated as the "storehouse consciousness" (ālaya-vijñāna) because it is able to contain and store all phenomena. It is also called the "retribution consciousness" (vipāka-vijñāna) and the "seed consciousness" (bīja-vijñāna).

Regarding the distinctions among the eight consciousnesses: the eighth, which is the accumulation [of seeds], is called *citta* (mind); the seventh, which performs reflection, is called *manas* (intellect);

and the sixth, which performs discernment, is called *vijñāna* (consciousness). Alternatively, it is said that the past is called *manas*, the future is called *citta*, and the present is called *vijñāna*.
The critique of teaching refers to the principle of "transmitting mind by means of mind" and not establishing written words.

There are two senses in which one is exhorted to depart from this: first, to cause one to depart from the teaching; second, to cause one to depart from phenomena (*dharma*). Phenomena do not transcend form and mind.
When both mind and form are transcended, one accords with the essence of the mind.
"Dharma" (法) is the general designation for the trichiliocosm; specifically, there are three types: the small chiliocosm, the medium chiliocosm, and the great chiliocosm.

All these are realms transformed by the World-Honored One Śākyamuni. The *Abhidharmakośa* states: "One thousand sets of the four great continents, the sun and moon, Mount Sumeru, the heavens of the desire realm, and the Brahma worlds constitute what is called a small chiliocosm (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*). A thousand times this small chiliocosm is called a medium chiliocosm (*dvisāhasra-madhyama-lokadhātu*).
A thousand times this [medium chiliocosm] is a great trichiliocosm (*trisāhasra-mahāsāhasra-lokadhātu*). All of these undergo formation and destruction simultaneously."
By means of the "place of birth" (the wholesome), one gradually brings to full maturity those wholesome dharmas that have not yet been heard or understood;
by means of the "place of maturation" (the unwholesome), one gradually abandons those unwholesome dharmas that have become habitual through constant practice and causes them to become unfamiliar.

The human title [refers to] the three untainted trainings: precept (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). These three dharmas support one another to bring about the attainment of the Buddha-way. That is to say: precepts deliver one from the three miserable realms;

concentration transcends the six heavens of desire; and wisdom liberates one from the three realms. When afflictions are completely purified, one does not leak or fall back into the cycle of birth and death.
Therefore, learning is like ornamentation. If a vessel is not ornamented, it cannot achieve a beautiful appearance; if a person does not learn, they cannot achieve the fruit of sagehood.
The three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*) are the primary path, while the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are the auxiliaries.
To "break" refers to the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and thoughts (*vitarka-kleśa*). "Views" refers to the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*);

"thoughts" refers to the eighty-one grades [of craving]. These are called "afflictions" (*kleśa*) because they obstruct the true reality (*tattva*). When the afflictions of views and thoughts are exhausted, one reaches the state of non-[arising]...
As for his status:
when he was born as an ordinary person, his mother dreamed that a bright moon entered her embrace.
Upon reading the "Chapter on the Sublime Array of the World-Honored One," he attained awakening to the essence of the Buddha-mind and beheld the wondrous functioning of the Buddha.
The Chan practitioner Dàorén Zhuányú Fǎshī (Master Zhuan-yu) frequently sat in meditation beneath a parasol while reading the scriptures; thus, he took "Under the Parasol" as his title.
Pò'è Mountain was the monastic site of the Fourth Patriarch, and Fēngmào Mountain was the monastic site of the Fifth Patriarch.
When Chong Shouzuo first took up the Ten Branches (of the Vinaya), Meizhu immediately commanded him to ascend the seat and deliver a re-exposition.

An official warrant was issued to protect and support him. In the third year of the Shunzhi era, when government troops entered the mountains to search for local bandits, the Master and the assembly were all taken before the military.
The two Generals, Ba and Ao, were indignant that the Master had concealed [the culprits] and intended to inflict the ultimate punishment upon him.
The monastery’s lands and property were all confiscated by the authorities. Although the Master stood amidst a forest of blades and halberds, his countenance remained unchanging.
He spoke with composure, saying, "How can the great road of Mount Hua prevent people from coming and going?

Consequently, he moved the various officials of Baqiao to offer their sincere respect and submission; they vowed to protect the Dharma and requested that the Master return to the mountain, restoring the fields as well.
The Earth bestowed a decree for eternal illumination:
the model for the growth of plants was found upon the tomb of the Duke of Zhou. Their leaves are green in spring, red in summer, white in autumn, and black in winter.
The *kai* tree grows upon the tomb of Confucius; its branches are sparse yet unbent.
These two trees take uprightness as their defining characteristic, and it is for this reason that the Master serves as a model for future generations.
During the Shunzhi era, a virtuous devotee from Yunnan came to inquire about Kāśyapa’s manifested body. He said, "I, your disciple, went to Mount Jizu to seek an audience with Kāśyapa.
In a dream, I was moved by the deity Vaiśravaṇa, who told me: 'The Venerable One has already arrived at Mount Hua to propagate the Vinaya.'"

Since you wish to behold him in person, you should go to see him; thus I have come to pay homage. Fearing that the multitude might be confused, the Master kept this secret and did not permit its transmission.
Therefore, the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra says: "Without arising from the samādhi of cessation, he manifests all manner of dignified deportment."
The "Three-Life Enmity" at Longmian was resolved at Longmian. This is a place in Tongcheng County where a person of good faith fell critically ill due to the karmic pull of a three-life enmity.
He went up the mountain to seek a resolution; the Master performed a ritual of repentance for him, and his illness was cured and the enmity extinguished.
The dried-up spring at Maling overflowed of its own accord; Maling is located in Xuan County. When the army arrived, the dried-up spring surged forth spontaneously.

The verse states that the six consciousnesses return to their seeds, meaning that during sleep, the six consciousnesses do not function and are subsumed back into the eighth seed-consciousness (*bīja-vijñāna*).
Because they are internal.
The five hindrances (*nīvaraṇa*) are: sensual desire, ill will, sloth and torpor, restlessness and remorse, and doubt.
These five are collectively termed "hindrances" because they cover and envelop the mind so that concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) do not arise.
"Unaffected by the delusion of form" refers to the time when the faculty of the eye has not yet been affected by form as it gives rise to delusion.
*Má* (pronounced like "ma") is the appearance of looking with relaxed eyes. *Mǐ* (pronounced like "mi") means to look askance.
*Nirvāṇa* is here translated as "Great Extinction" (*mahāparinirvāṇa*). It is correlated, respectively, with the *dharmakāya*, liberation (*vimukti*), and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Regarding the "one hundred and eight delusions": being deluded by oneself is "delusion" (*mūḍha*), while deluding others is "ignorance" (*moha*; *sammoha*). These are the afflictions (*kleśa*).
To the ninety-eight underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*), ten entanglements (*paryavasthāna*) are added, resulting in one hundred and eight.
The one hundred and eight samādhis: first, the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, up to the one hundred and eighth, the Samādhi of Non-attachment to Space and Untaintedness.
These are explained in detail in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.
The four noble ones and the six classes of ordinary beings: those without outflows (anāsrava) are called "noble," while those with outflows (sāsrava) are called "ordinary.
These constitute the ten dharma-realms. The "ten stages" (daśabhūmi) refer to the levels realized by Bodhisattvas, for all Buddha-dharmas arise in dependence upon them.

Nevertheless, the stages (bhūmi) differ in their respective degrees of depth; thus, from the initial Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi) to the final Stage of Dharma-Cloud (dharmameghā-bhūmi), they are divided into ten.
The Śrāvakas of the Three Vehicles take the Four Noble Truths as their vehicle; the Pratyekabuddhas take the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination as their vehicle; and the Bodhisattvas...
The Bodhisattva takes the six perfections as his vehicle.
"Six destinies" refers to the six realms; "destinies" means going toward them, signifying that sentient beings proceed toward the six realms according to the karma they have created.

"Entering the stream and losing what is streamed" refers to the dharma-nature. "What is streamed" refers to sounds and sensory objects. This means not following after the dust of sound, suddenly entering the flow of the Dharma, and thereby losing the very thing one has entered.
To realize and enter the nature-body of perfect penetration (*pariccheda*) is called "perfect" (*yuan*); its wondrous function being unimpeded is called "penetration" (*tong*).
This is the original source of the mind inherently possessed by all sentient beings, the sacred realm realized by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Arising from the gateway of the ear, it performs universal illumination; responding to conditions through transformation, it attains sovereign penetration.
"Rightly Awakened" (*samyaksambuddha*) means "right" (*samyañc*) because one is free from error, and "awakened" (*buddha*) because one has turned away from delusion.

Regarding the roots and derivative afflictions (*kleśa*), there are six roots: namely, greed (*lobha*), hatred (*dveṣa*), delusion (*moha*), pride (*māna*), doubt (*vicikitsā*), and views (*dṛṣṭi*). The derivatives number twenty, which are divided into three groups:

the eight major ones are lack of faith (*āśraddhya*), laziness (*kausīdya*), heedlessness (*pramāda*), lethargy (*styāna*), restlessness (*auddhatya*), loss of mindfulness (*muṣitasmṛtitā*), lack of clear comprehension (*asaṃprajanya*), [and non-conscientiousness].

The secondary [afflictions] consist of two: namely, lack of shame (*āhrīkya*) and lack of dread (*anapatrāpya*). The minor [afflictions] consist of ten: namely, anger (*krodha*), resentment (*upanāha*), vexation (*pradāsa*), concealment (*mrakṣa*), deceit (*māyā*), guile (*śāṭhya*), and arrogance (*mada*).
Harmfulness, envy, and stinginess.
Regarding the two final knowledges: fundamental knowledge (*mūla-jñāna*) and subsequently attained knowledge (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*).

*Samādhi*—translated here as "equipoise" (*samā-dhāraṇa*)—is called "equal" (*sama*) because it is free from dullness and agitation; it is called "holding" (*dhāraṇa*) because it causes the mind to abide in a single object.

Attaining two kinds of excellence: above, one accords with the sages, sharing the same power of compassion as all Buddhas; below, one accords with ordinary beings, sharing the same aspiration of pity for all sentient beings.
Because its wondrous function transcends [the mundane], it is called "excellent."
The three obstructions are afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and retribution; these are called the "three" because they obscure and cover the right path.
The three virtues are the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), liberation (*vimukti*), and wisdom (*prajñā*). These constitute the virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity.

The six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā) refer to generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom; by universally practicing these, one is able to cross the stream of birth and death and ascend to the shore of nirvāṇa.
The five objects of desire (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) consist of the five: forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles. "Desire" (*kāma*) refers to that which is sought after.
As stated in the *Zhiguan*: "The five sense-objects are not themselves desire; however, they possess flavors that can give rise to the mind of seeking and desiring in the practitioner."
*Tāla* leaves are translated here as "bank-shaped. They resemble the *tāli* palm trees of this region; they are straight and tall, and their leaves can be used for writing scriptures.
Regarding the term "seeing the path" (*darśanamārga*), it refers to the first fruit (*phala*) because one perceives the principle and thereby destroys delusions.
The Jambū tree is translated as the "Ugly Tree" (Hui-shu). Its color is reddish-yellow with purple luster. When its fruit juice touches an object, it turns it into gold.
As the juice flows into the river, it dyes the stones, turning them into golden sand.

The four evil destinies are hell-beings, hungry ghosts, animals, and asuras; these constitute the four. Because one does not cultivate wholesome dharmas during the causal stage and instead commits evil, one experiences rebirth in a different class of being as a result, which constitutes a destiny (gati).

The "thousand-spoked wheel pattern" refers to the spokes within a chariot wheel. Because the patterns on the soles of the Tathāgata’s feet are like a thousand-spoked wheel, it is pronounced as the sound *zhài* (豸) over the character *chí* (池).
Natural wisdom (svayambhū-jñāna) is not created by Buddhas, devas, or humans; it is inherently possessed from the beginning. It is also called the knowledge of all modes (sarvākārajñatā).
It is teacherless wisdom, not heard from others.
The Heaven of Making Use of Others' Emanations (Paranirmita-vaśavartin) is also called Mahāśvara; it is the zenith of the Desire Realm.
When they require the objects of the five desires, other deities manifest emanations for them, so that they may achieve their own pleasure by making use of what others have produced.
Akaniṣṭha Heaven is the same as the Ultimate Form (Akaniṣṭha) Heaven.
The four formless heavens refer to the Sphere of Infinite Space, the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness, the Sphere of Nothingness, and the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception.
Others say that although the afflictions of views and thought have already been severed, there still remains the physical body currently experienced;
thus it is called "segmented" (*paricchinna*), because the lifespan of sentient beings in the six realms has limitations according to the power of their karma,
and their bodies have distinct physical segments.
"Without remainder" refers to the fact that the two delusions—view-based and thought-based—along with the body composed of the five aggregates they have received, are all extinguished together.
"Transformation" refers to the shifting of causes and the changing of effects.
"Analogy" (*dṛṣṭānta*) refers to using categories for comparison; "illustration" (*upamāna*) refers to opening the way to understanding so that one may awaken.

The *Vairocana-maṇḍala-ādarśa* (the Perfect Mirror of Vairocana) is also called the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*mahā-ādarśa-jñāna*). Because it uses the boundless wisdom of the Buddhas to illuminate the vast mirror of the Buddhas, reaching its very source and bottom.
The three poisons—greed, hatred, and delusion—constitute the "three. They are called "poisons" because they injure the supramundane roots of goodness.
The Ganges is the river *Gaṅgā*; in the language of China, it is called "Coming from Heaven," as it is seen to descend from a high elevation.
There are four reasons why many sutras take this river as a standard of measurement: first, most people recognize it; second, those who enter its waters obtain merit.
Third, it is the largest among the eight great rivers. Fourth, it is the place where the Buddha was born;
its seed is impure, being the physical remains of his parents, composed of the red and white elements. As the Sūtra says: "This body is not a lotus."
Nor does it arise from sandalwood; rather, it is nurtured by excrement and filth and issues only from the urinary tract.
"Self-grasping" refers to the clinging to phenomena such as the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) because of the belief that there is a real, sovereign controller.
Attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) refers to the clinging to phenomena such as the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) as being substantially existent external to the mind.
Śākyamitra is translated here as "Able to Support.

The third fruit is the *anāgāmin* in Sanskrit, which in Chinese means "Non-returner" (*bùlái*). This refers to one who has severed the final three grades of afflictions within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).

His delusions were exhausted; because he would no longer come to take birth in the desire realm, he was known as Master Xianshou (Worthy Head), whose secular name was Fazang and who hailed from the country of Kangju (Sogdiana).
As a layman (*upāsaka*), he delighted in discussing names and terminology, yet he maintained the Way and dwelt in integrity.
The causal practices of the *Avataṃsaka* are like flowers, which adorn the resultant virtues.

Because its fundamental source and intrinsic nature are pure, it is called "Brahma" (*brahma*). Because the life-force of wisdom is transmitted universally throughout all lands and moments, it is called a "net" (*jāla*).
Thus, it is termed the *Brahmajāla*.
To transform others through the Way and instruct them is called "teaching" (jiao). To personally practice it above so that it moves like the wind below is called "transformation" (hua).

The eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*) are calculated as follows: the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) multiply to form one hundred; the ten realms (*dhātu*) multiply to form one thousand;

the seven branches [of action] form seven thousand; the three periods of time form twenty-one thousand; and when the three poisons (*viṣa*) along with the equal portion (*samabhāga*) are added, they constitute the eighty-four thousand.
The eighty-four thousand Dharma gates are said to be those by which the Tathāgata attained enlightenment. There are three hundred and fifty gates of *pāramitā*.
As for *pāramitā*, it means that the practices of both phenomena and principle are fulfilled, thereby crossing the flow of birth and death and ascending to the shore of *nirvāṇa*.

Because these merits are inexhaustible, the verse says: "From the arising of the supreme radiance up to the distribution of the relics, there are three hundred and fifty dharma-gates of the *pāramitās*. Each gate contains the six *pāramitās*, totaling twenty-one.
By multiplying these by the four great elements and the six sense-decays, one reaches twenty-one thousand; adding the three poisons and their equal distribution, this is [the total]."
This makes eighty-four thousand [dharmas].

The "Three Worthies" (sān xián) refer to the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the ten abodes (*daśa-vihāra*), and the ten dedications (*daśa-pariṇāmanā*); these are the thirty minds. The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states:

"The ten stages of setting forth (*daśa-prasthāna*), the ten stages of nurturing (*daśa-poṣaṇa*), and the ten adamantine stages (*daśa-vajra*). They are called "Worthies" because they have not yet entered the stage of the sages (*ārya*).
This refers to the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*), wherein reality is fully exhausted and delusions are completely eliminated.
When one attains the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), the earthworms in the soil retreat four inches; this is the power of the path-concomitant (*mārga-sahagata*) discipline.

A bhikṣu who maintains the precepts vigilantly and without loss is said to "hold them daily. To prevent what is improper and cease evil is called *śīla* (precept). Bhikṣu is a transliteration of... [text truncated]
To eliminate deprivation: sentient beings with meager merit remain in the causal stage; lacking the means to support themselves, they receive retributions that are largely impoverished.
The monastic precepts and conduct are a fertile field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*); they can produce wholesome qualities in beings and thereby eliminate the deprivation of cause and effect.
The power of the Dharma (dharmabala) is so called because it takes the Dharma as its strength.
Regarding the ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*), the *Xiyuji* states: "Of the ninety-five kinds, these are heterodox;
only one is orthodox—namely, that which is affiliated with the Buddha-dharma."

The "fivefold body of the Dharma" (*pañcadharmaskandha*) refers to its divisions, limits, and measures. Precept, concentration, wisdom, liberation, and the knowledge and vision of liberation—these five types constitute the "Dharma.
That which is gathered together without dispersal is called a "body" (*skandha*).
The term *garuḍa* in Sanskrit refers to the "Golden-Winged Bird" (*jīngìniǎo*) in Chinese; it is so called because its wings are golden in color.
The term *dàxiān* (Great Immortal) is a general designation for practitioners who cultivated the Way in ancient times; however, only the Tathāgata is titled the "Great Enlightened Golden Immortal.
As the *Śīla-sūtra* states: "To be able to practice in this manner is the path of the Great Immortals."

The fetters (*saṃyojana*) and the proclivities (*anuśaya*). "Fetters" refers to binding; "proclivities" refers to driving. This means the five dull and five sharp [proclivities] bind the mind and spirit, driving them to transmigrate through the three realms.

In the late autumn of the Buddha-dharma, there are no longer the teachings of the Three Vehicles; thus it is called "the Buddha-dharma. "Late autumn" refers to the final age, when the path of the Dharma has withered and declined.
Regarding the ten kinds of clothing and wealth: first is *koseya* cloth, which means silk cloth; second is *kṣauma* cloth, which means...
1. *Śāṇa* cloth (cotton). 2. *Karpāsa* cloth (cotton). 3. *Kambala* cloth; this is woven from wool, similar in kind to felt or coarse woolen cloth.
4. *Kṣauma* cloth; this is translated as "hemp cloth. 5. *Cīra* cloth; this is translated as "coarse linen cloth. 6. *Śāṇa* cloth; this is the name of a tree.
Its bark is taken and spun into thread for weaving. 7. *Kṣauma* cloth; there are many varieties of hemp, including blue, yellow, and red. 8. [The eighth item is omitted in the source text].
9. Kṣaumalika robes; this is translated as "fine cotton cloth. 10. Kauravika robes; this is translated as "fine felt.
11. Śāṇaka-pāṃsukūla robes; the translation has not yet been seen.
Regarding the "seed of bodhi," it is so called because it can give rise to all the dharmas of the Buddhas. Its essence is twofold:

first, the essential nature itself, which consists of the mind of compassion, the mind of wisdom, and the mind of aspiration; second, the substratum, which is the wondrous mind of intrinsic luminosity.
Liu (Lú) translates this as "loving joy" (*anurāga*).
Joining the palms signifies that the mind is in accord with the Way; it means the Way is in accord with the mind.
First, he converted the five men: Cunda, Kātyāyana, and Daśabala-Kāśyapa—these were from his maternal kin—and Ājñāta-kauṇḍinya, Bhadrika, and Gavāmpati.
The Crown Prince was a member of his father’s kin.
As for the brothers Kāśyapa—namely Uruvilvā-Kāśyapa, Gayā-Kāśyapa, and Nadī-Kāśyapa—they were, during the time of Vipaśyin Buddha, those who together erected the sacrificial pillar.
As a karmic retribution, they became the teachers of King Bimbisāra and had five hundred disciples.

The two younger brothers together had five hundred followers. Relying on their own many skills, they were unwilling to go forth under the Buddha. When the Buddha manifested supernatural transformations, the master and his disciples were moved to submission;
they threw themselves before the Buddha and left the household life.
*Dharmatā* is translated here as "Able to Rescue";
it refers to a monastery where disciples reside to inherit and succeed to the Buddha’s Way.
*Saṃghārāma* is translated here as "Garden of the Assembly"; it is a place for cultivation and growth, serving as the dwelling place for the Buddha’s disciples. Thus, it is able to...
It is for the purpose of producing the sprouts of the Path and the fruits of sagehood, and for bestowing benefit and happiness upon all living beings;
thus, a vihāra is a place where practitioners cultivate pure conduct (brahmacarya) with diligence, rather than being merely a residence of exquisite architecture.
The Vajra Pure Land is the adamantine essence, most firm and sharp; it can shatter all things.

This signifies that by cultivating wholesome dharmas with diligence in this place, one can destroy afflictions and evil karma. In the Western Regions, wherever a śramaṇa attains the Way, a banner is erected to inform the four quarters.

The "tranquil site of enlightenment" (bodhimaṇḍa) is so called because it is the place where one attains the Way by pacifying the afflictions of the five abodes and extinguishing the two kinds of birth-and-death.
Fundamental awakening refers to the essence of the sentient beings' mind; it is numinous, luminous, and vast, equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception.
This is precisely the Tathāgata’s equal *dharmakāya*. Based upon this *dharmakāya*, it is termed "original enlightenment" (*mūlapratibodha*).

"Initial enlightenment" (*ādikṣaṇapratibodha*) refers to the source of the sentient beings' originally enlightened mind; because it is stirred by the permeation of ignorance, enlightenment does not manifest as enlightenment, and for many kalpas one remains in delusion.
Now, for the first time, one awakens to it—this is called initial enlightenment. The non-duality of the initial and the original is termed ultimate enlightenment (*niṣṭhāpratibodha*).
This refers to the attainment of Buddhahood.
Aniruddha (Āniruddha) means "Wish-fulfilling" in this language; he was the Buddha’s maternal cousin.
The āmra fruit is called "Difficult to Distinguish" because it resembles a peach yet is not a peach, and resembles a crabapple yet is not a crabapple.
The Land of Eternal Quiescent Light is the land of the principle-nature (*dharmatā*). "Eternal" refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); "quiescent" refers to Prajñā;
and "light" refers to liberation (*vimukti*). It is called a "land" because it is where the Buddha dwells.
Śikhin is also named Śikhi; this translates as "Fire. Fire has two meanings: first, it illuminates so that various evils do not arise;
second, it burns away afflictions so that they are not produced.
Dīpaṃkara is the Sanskrit name for Ràndēng (然燈). The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that when the Prince was born, the radiance of his body was like a lamp; thus he is called Dīpaṃkara.
Vipaśyin is also called Weiyè (維衛); this translates as "Victorious Vision" (*Jina-darśana*).

The Stage of Joy (Pramuditā-bhūmi) refers to the Bodhisattva’s wisdom being equal to the Buddha’s wisdom, their principle being identical to the Buddha’s principle, and their penetrating vision of the Great Way exhausting the entire realm of the Buddha;
thus, they attain the joy of the Dharma and ascend to the first stage.

When compared to the subsequent state of *samyaksambuddha* (Perfect Enlightenment), the stage of *abhisambuddha* (Sublime Enlightenment) still possesses one further quality; because it transcends all preceding stages, it is designated as "Enlightenment" (*buddha*).
*Tiṣya* is translated here as "Luminous," meaning that its radiance shines everywhere. It is also called "Expounding the Crossing," meaning that he expounds the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.
It is also named *Puṣya*, which means "Flourishing," signifying the clear realization of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
"Bestowal" (*śāsana*) refers to the holy words spoken and given; "prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*) refers to the fruit being granted in accordance with one's mental aspiration.
As the *Ciren* (Compassionate Grace) of the Wheel-Turning Sage King states: "The four kinds of wheel-turning kings who bring all quarters under their majestic authority also have distinctions."

The Iron-Wheel King rules the Southern Continent alone; he establishes order through the exertion of his majesty. The Copper-Wheel King rules the two continents of the East and South; they submit upon the shaking of his majesty.

The Silver-Wheel King rules the three continents of the East, South, and West; they are brought to submission by the dispatching of envoys. The Golden-Wheel Universal Monarch’s virtue resounds throughout the four continents;
they submit to his transformation at the mere sight of his presence. Therefore, he is called a "Holy King" (Cakravartin).
Not relinquishing diligence while remaining untainted by phenomena is called *vīrya* (diligence). The constant, moment-to-moment pursuit [of the goal] is called *pragraha* (exertion).

The four kinds of eloquence (*pratibhāna*) that proceed without obstruction are called *pratibhāna* (eloquence). These four factors—meaning (*artha*), phenomena (*dharma*), phrasing (*nirukti*), and delight in speaking (*pratibhāna*)—constitute *pratibhāna*.
Regarding "Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi": "An" means "non-existent," because it is free from all defilements. "Uttara" means "supreme," because it is peerless within the three realms.
"Bodhi" means "knowledge," because it is the knowledge that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature.
The "turning of the unsurpassed wheel of Dharma" is explained as follows: that which serves as the standard and support for both ordinary beings and sages is called *dharma*.

That which causes others to enter [the path] and brings them to awakening is called "turning. That which crushes and grinds away afflictions and karma is called a "wheel. Because it cannot be fathomed by those on lower stages, it is called "unsurpassed."
Blinded by attachment to pleasure and craving for superior and exquisite desires,
they are obscured by ignorance— that is, their minds are shrouded by afflictions— such that they lack clear comprehension regarding all phenomena.
He is the God among Gods, for all devas take refuge in and look up to him;
he is the Sage among Sages, for those of the Three Vehicles revere him.
Regarding the three periods—past, present, and future—the King Prasenajit said: "When one contemplates the true mark of the body, one contemplates the Buddha in the same way."
Without beginning, without middle, and without end, his body of precepts is adorned with purity;
adorned with concentration and wisdom, he is endowed with all myriad virtues.
Homage, homage! "Shou" (首) means head. With his head touching the ground, he remains prostrate for a short while before rising.

This indicates that because the practitioner offers prayers, they contemplate the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as neither existent nor non-existent. Conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is not non-existent; it is neither existent nor non-existent, which is called the Middle Way, the ultimate truth.
The "Vajra-limit" (*vajrānta*) refers to the boundary. It is called "Vajra" because it possesses the power to firmly sustain the world. As the Sūtra says:
"Beneath the wheels of earth, water, fire, and wind, there is a vajra-wheel; the relics of all past Buddhas are entirely contained therein."
Countless nayutas of koṭis of Buddha-sons,
through true compassion, sustain the lineage of the Buddhas. With their five limbs—
the hands, knees, and forehead— [they prostrate].

The five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) are: the divine eye, the divine ear, knowledge of others' minds, recollection of past lives, and the power of miraculous transformations. Devas, *ṛṣis*, and spirits all possess these.

The five realms (*pañcagati*)—those of devas and humans belong to the wholesome, while those of the three miserable destinies belong to the unwholesome. Because they revolve and circulate through one another, they are called "paths" (*gati*).
Because it can sever that which is difficult to sever, it is called "Vajra" (Diamond). This means that when a Bodhisattva occupies this seat, they sever the fetters and attain Buddhahood.

Furthermore, all Buddhas of the three periods of time sit upon this very seat to achieve the Way; it undergoes not the slightest change or decay, for it is the ground of the mind of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*).
The four means of integration (*saṃgrahavastu*) are: giving, kind speech, beneficial conduct, and cooperation.

The mark of the invisible crown of the head (*anavalokitamūrdhatā*) refers to the fact that no one—whether among gods, humans, those of the two vehicles, or bodhisattvas—is able to see the crown of the Tathāgata’s head.
*Vinaya Daily Essentials: Fragrant Milk Record*, Volume Lower.
Recorded by the Vinaya-transmitting Bhikṣu Shuyu of the Qing Guhang Zhaokeng Wanshou Jietan. Recorded on a jade tablet:
Unfolding the Alms Bowl.

[Commentary] "Unfolding" means opening the cloth to wipe the bowl. This refers to the practice where, fearing that the bowl may have dust upon it, one first opens the cloth and wipes it clean before placing it on a small table to await the arrival of the meal.
The Tathāgata is the vessel of measure; I now obtain to spread forth [this offering]. May I, together with all the assembly, equally realize the emptiness and stillness of the three wheels.
Oṃ smara maṇi svāhā (three times).
[Note] *Tathāgata* in the Sanskrit language is also called *Tatāgata*; this is translated as "Thus Come" (*Rúlái*). It refers to wisdom.
The *Dapilun* (Treatise on the Great Vehicle) states: "The Buddha is called the Tathāgata because he came in the same manner as the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and others.
Having practiced the six pāramitās, they attained the path of Buddhahood; Śākyamuni Buddha likewise came in this same way, and is therefore called the Tathāgata.
Just as the wisdom of the Buddha Dīpaṃkara and others knew the characteristics of all phenomena and came from within suchness (*tathatā*), Śākyamuni Buddha likewise came in this same way."
He is named the Tathāgata, who possesses the three bodies: the Dharma-body, the Reward-body, and the Transformation-body.

As for the Tathāgata of the Dharma-body, he comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. As for the Tathāgata of the Reward-body, he attains perfect enlightenment by means of the self-nature of reality (*dharmatā*).
As for the Tathāgata of the Transformation-body, he comes to deliver sentient beings by riding upon the path of suchness. Now it is said:
Regarding the Tathāgata’s appropriate vessel: this refers to the *saṃbhogakāya* among the three bodies. It is said that this bowl was personally fashioned as a model by the World-Honored One himself.
The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "While the Buddha was traveling through the country of Soma, he saw that the soil there was fine and moist.
Without sparing his hands, which were as soft as *tūla* cotton, he took the earth and fashioned a bowl mold himself, then handed it to a potter."
This bowl was fired until it attained a lustrous, jewel-like color, perfectly round and beautiful. The Buddha permitted its acceptance and possession;
one should know that this bowl is the Dharma-vessel transmitted from one Buddha to the next, the name of which none of the ninety-five kinds of non-Buddhist practitioners (tīrthika) know.
Only our Buddha, the Tathāgata, has revealed this unprecedented Dharma. Thus we know that this bowl is most supreme and most precious.
By what cause and by what good fortune have I been able to spread it out? It is because I have already received the Buddha’s precepts.
This single phrase contains the boundless sense of longing for that which is so difficult to encounter. However, the great purpose of spreading it out is not merely for oneself.

It is merely to benefit one's own mouth and body. First, one should make a vow for the sake of the multitude. Regarding the "emptiness and stillness of the three spheres," the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra Commentary* states:
it means that at the time of giving, one realizes through direct experience that the giver, the recipient, and the object given are all empty.

All are fundamentally empty; thus one can crush and grind away the marks of attachment. This is called the emptiness of the three wheels (*trimaṇḍala-śūnyatā*). First is the emptiness of the giver (*dāyaka-śūnyatā*):
this means that the person who gives realizes that their own body is fundamentally empty. Having known there is no self (*anātman*), they have no mind that hopes for a reward of merit.
This is called the emptiness of the giver. Second is the emptiness of the recipient (*pratigrahaka-śūnyatā*): this means that having realized there is no one who can give...

As for the self, there is likewise no recipient of the gift; this is called the emptiness of the recipient (*pratigrahaka-śūnyatā*). Third is the emptiness of the object of giving (*deya-vastu-śūnyatā*):
regarding objects such as wealth, treasures, and precious goods, once the two marks of "self" and "person" are absent, one realizes that all things are empty.

Furthermore, how could there be anything given that can be obtained? This is called the emptiness of the object. Only by realizing and embodying these principles does one accord with the quiescence of the three spheres (*trimaṇḍala-pariśuddhi*).
To practice giving without abiding in signs is to accord with the profound meaning of Prajñāpāramitā.

Regarding "receiving food": "receiving" (shou) means to accept or take in; it carries the sense of swallowing. "Food" (shi) means substance; it refers to filling the belly with substantial nourishment.
It is the general name for that which can cure all hunger and emptiness, serving as the primary condition for assisting the Path.
Therefore, it is said in the scriptures: "The body dwells in dependence on food; life exists by relying on food.

When this food and drink enter the five viscera, permeate the four limbs, replenish the vital energy, and nourish the muscles, the body and mind become harmonious and joyful, making one capable of advancing upon the Path.
However, one must not be greedily attached.
When a bhikṣu receives food, he sits cross-legged and spreads his cloth for wiping the mouth over his knees, fearing that rice, soup, vegetables, or broth might fall upon his kāṣāya.
When requesting the bowl, he silently recites this verse:
If one sees an empty bowl, one should wish that all sentient beings attain ultimate purity and be empty of afflictions.
[Commentary] "Bowl" (*pātra*) is a half-Sanskrit term; the two characters *tāra* have been omitted. The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states:
"The bowl is the insignia of the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and not a utensil for use in a palace or hall. These are all the repeated exhortations of the Tathāgata.
Instruction on Sincerity: All who receive and uphold [this teaching] should cherish and preserve it.

The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states that the Tathāgata commanded the bhikṣus to receive food with an alms-bowl (*pātra*) in order to distinguish them from the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). The non-Buddhists sew leaves together to make vessels and eat with their hands clasped;
this is not the appearance of a monk, nor the form of a field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*). Therefore, the Buddha established this rule. [In] the Sanskrit language...
"Brahma" (梵摩) here means "purity. "Ultimate" (究竟) carries the sense of thorough investigation and inquiry.
For those of the Two Vehicles, it is only when their Brahma-conduct is established that it is called ultimate. For Bodhisattvas, it is only upon reaching unsurpassed Bodhi that it is called ultimate.
Just as one holds an empty bowl, one should immediately realize the principle of ultimacy within and directly perceive the full extent of the Dharma-realm.
Furthermore, one's own measure is equal to the empty void. Again, seeing that the bowl is empty, the afflictions (*kleśa*) are likewise empty.
Moreover, within emptiness there is that which is not empty; this is the wondrous existence of true emptiness, not a blank, ignorant, or stubborn void.
Within this, one realizes the meaning of the three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*). As the Great Master Zhiyi of Tiantai said: "If one contemplates the mind as empty, then..."
All phenomena are empty; this is the Ultimate Truth (paramārtha-satya). If one contemplates the mind as provisional, then all phenomena are provisional;
this is the Conventional Truth (saṃvṛti-satya). If one contemplates within the mind, then all phenomena are the Middle; this is the Middle Truth (madhyama-satya).
These three contemplations arise entirely from the nature itself and are truly not produced through cultivation. Therefore, within a single mind, there are fully three functions.
This is what is called the threefold contemplation within a single mind. If one penetrates this principle, one enters into the ultimate truth through phenomena.

Thus, by means of the sign of the empty bowl, one realizes the principle of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Since not even the slightest [duality] can be tolerated, how much less could there be any trace of "pure afflictions"?
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "If a person wishes to know the realm of the Buddha, they should purify their mind."

It is like space; therefore, it is said to be "ultimately pure. Since from the beginning it has never been associated with defiled phenomena (*saṃkleśa-dharma*), it is said to be "empty and devoid of afflictions" (*kleśa*). *Piṇḍapātra*:
the Sanskrit term *piṇḍapātra* is translated here as "measured vessel" (*yìngliàng qì*). In the Vinaya, the Buddha did not permit monks to possess [such a vessel].

Alms bowls may be made of various materials such as precious gems, copper, tin, wood, or stone; however, there are essentially two types: first, earthenware, and second, iron. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"The alms bowl is the vessel of those who have left the household life. It is for those of few desires and contentment, and is not suitable for worldly people.
The *Daśabhāṇavāra-vinaya* states: "The alms bowl is the insignia of all Buddhas; it must not be used improperly, nor for washing hands. One should revere it as [one would the Buddha himself]."
[Section on] the Bowl. The *Pañcavargika-vinaya* states: "The Buddha himself fashioned a bowl mold to serve as a model for future generations. Furthermore, the *Fazhen chao* says:
"It is a vessel that accords with the Dharma," meaning that its substance (*tǐ*), color (*sè*), and dimensions (*liàng*) are all in complete conformity with the Dharma.

Regarding the substance, there are two types: clay and iron. As for the color, one uses crushed sesame seeds and apricot kernels to smear the interior and exterior. [The text continues with bamboo...]*
Treatment by fumigation: Fumigate [the bowl] until it takes on the color of a dove's neck or the color of a peacock. What is the purpose of this fumigation?

It prevents stored items from spoiling during the summer and prevents them from becoming stained with grease; because it possesses these functional benefits, one should perform the treatment by fumigation.

As for the measurements, they are divided into superior, middling, and inferior. According to the Chinese *dou*: the superior bowl is one *dou*, the middling bowl is seven and a half *sheng*, and the inferior bowl is five [sheng].
He ascended [to the Dharma-seat], and thus he was named "The Vessel of Response" (Yingqi). Master Daguan said:
[Commentary] His name was Tanying; as a model for all sentient beings and a teacher for humans and devas, he was called "Great Master" (Dashi).
Now, as for the bowl as a vessel: it assists the Three Jewels and is endowed with six virtues. How is its assistance to the Three Jewels made clear?
It is because, were it not for this [bowl], the Sangha would have no means of sustenance. If the Sangha has no means of sustenance, the life-force of wisdom (prajñā-jīvita) would be severed.

If the life-force of wisdom is severed, the lineage of the Buddha (buddha-vamśa) would perish. Regarding its endowment with the six virtues: it is able to be pure, able to be capacious, able to be frugal, able to be expansive, and able to be... [able to be... (text fragmentary).
"Honored One, 'ancient' refers to the six virtues. 'Ancient' is because it was bestowed by a Buddha.

[Commentary] The *Huizheng ji* (Record of Rectifying the Meaning) states: "This is the almsbowl of Kāśyapa Buddha. After that Buddha entered nirvana, the Dragon King invited it to his palace to offer worship, awaiting the attainment of enlightenment by Śākyamuni."
"Venerable One, these were offered by the devas.
[Commentary] The *Huizheng ji* states: After the Buddha had attained enlightenment, the Dragon King brought him to the waters of the sea.

The Four Heavenly Kings all wished to take [the bowl], whereupon it was miraculously transformed into four bowls, allowing each of them to obtain one bowl to offer to the World-Honored One. The world...
Having received [the offerings], he stacked them one upon another in sequence to form a single bowl.
By doing so, he would extensively and universally benefit all beings.

[Commentary] An ancient saying goes: "A single bowl for the rice of a thousand households; a solitary body wandering ten thousand li. Desiring to exhaust the path of birth and death, he begs for alms."
Regarding his life span:
he was frugal, often abstaining from food after midday.

[Commentary] "Abstaining from food after midday" refers to eating according to the Buddhist discipline. This is as the Tathāgata, while dwelling amidst the five [periods of the day], taught the descent [of the mealtime].
He was born in the Middle Kingdom; he left the city at midnight; he attained enlightenment at midnight; he took but one meal at midday; and he taught the Middle Way.
As for his appearance, whether receiving offerings that were coarse or refined, his merit and benefit remained equal.
[Commentary]: For example, during a time of famine, Anuruddha offered a single bowl of millet porridge to a pratyekabuddha;
as a result, for ninety-one kalpas, he experienced every wish-fulfilling joy among gods and humans.
If it is clean, no one in the world would bear to throw pungent food into it.

[Commentary] The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "The alms bowl is the vessel of those who have left the household life. It is for those with few desires and contentment; it is not suitable for worldly people."
For this reason, how could we dare not treasure and revere it? When serving rice, silently recite this verse:
"If one sees a full bowl, one should wish that all sentient beings may be fully endowed with all wholesome dharmas."
[Commentary] Regarding the meaning of the term: A *bhikṣu* is called a "mendicant" (*kṣānti*) for two reasons. First, he begs for food to sustain his physical body;
second, he begs for the Dharma to sustain his life of wisdom. As for "full": it means that which contains and receives things.

Once the bowl of rice is full, one must not give rise to thoughts of mere greed or gluttony. Without cultivating pure conduct (*brahmacarya*), one should contemplate the origin from which the food comes, grain by grain.
All wholesome dharmas obtained from the offerings of the faithful arise entirely from this seed of wisdom;
therefore, the recipient shall be fully endowed with the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and the donor’s fruit of merit shall be abundant and complete, just as a seed brings forth flowers.
The flower further becomes fruit; this signifies the fulfillment of the bodhisattva’s brahmacarya.

The *Xiyu zhuan* (Records of the Western Regions) states that the Buddha’s bowl is in the kingdom of Gandhāra, made of green jade and holding three *dou*. It is treasured by all nations and offered to throughout the day.
If flowers and incense do not fill it, they will spontaneously become full as described. Thus, upon seeing the bowl once filled with food, one should aspire to the virtues one has cultivated.
The Dharma is fully complete and perfectly accomplished; do not let this body be in vain, for it is a vessel for carrying the Way.

When gathering [the offerings] and reciting the text for making offerings, support the rim with the right hand, hold the bowl with the left hand level with the eyebrows, and turn the bowl and spoon outward;
the offering text is as usual.
【Commentary】 Regarding "holding the bowl level with the eyebrows," there are two reasons. First, our current physical forms are composed of the impure karmic consciousness of ignorance;
we fear that the breath from our mouths and nostrils might touch the pure food, making it unfit for offering to the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
Second, out of their habitual perceptions, sentient beings might still harbor discriminations regarding the quality of the food within the bowl, whether it be fine or coarse.

Regarding likes and dislikes: because the three poisons first arise in the mind, one next rests the right palm against the rim of the bowl and so forth; this is called "obstructing the breath of contact. Attached is the Text on Offering (*Gongyang wen*):

"When Confucius attended meals for his ruler, the ruler would perform the sacrifice. Furthermore, when offering vegetables, soup, or melons, he invariably observed the fast (*zhai*). Today, one offers before the meal; this is a great matter of ritual propriety."
[Commentary] The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Food is for the practice of the Path, not for the benefit of the body.

When obtaining food, one should first offer it to the Triple Gem and subsequently bestow it upon the four classes of living beings. The "Chapter on Vows" (*Praṇidhāna-parivarta*) states: "Among all forms of offering, the Dharma-offering is supreme.

Therefore, when a donor brings food for one to receive, one should first straighten the body and maintain right mindfulness, performing a Dharma-offering to the Triple Gem in accordance with the Dharma.

It is a treasure. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "Even if one were to make offerings to immeasurable Buddhas in every moment of thought, if one does not know the true Dharma, it is not called making an offering.
The *Suvikrāntavikramī-paripṛcchā Sūtra* says: "One does not give rise to sinful karma; one does not give rise to meritorious karma."
To not give rise to unconditioned karma is called making an offering to the Buddha. The *Huashou jing* (Kusuma-avataṃsaka-sūtra) states:
"If one makes offerings to the Buddhas with flowers, incense, food, clothing, medicine, and so forth, this is not called true offering.

If one can practice and study the subtle and wondrous Dharma taught by the Tathāgata while seated at the site of enlightenment, this is called true offering. The *Siyi jing* (Arthaviniścaya-sūtra) says: [The same].
Question: Who is able to make offerings to the Buddha? The Buddha replied: "One who can penetrate the limit of non-arising.
In the *Mañjuśrī-prajñā-sūtra*, the Buddha asks Mañjuśrī: "How do you make offerings to the Buddha? Mañjuśrī answers:

"If the mental activities of one who is like an illusionary person are extinguished, then I am making an offering to the Buddha. The Tiantai teachings state: "Making offerings to the Buddha is simply following..."
To follow the Buddha’s words is now to follow the Buddha’s teaching. To cultivate the mind of the three contemplations is itself to make offerings to the Buddha;

to destroy the five stages of dwelling and attain liberation is itself to make offerings to the Dharma; and for the principle of the three truths to be in harmony is itself to make offerings to the Sangha.
I make offerings to the Pure Dharmakāya, Vairocana Buddha.
[Note] *Vairocana* in Sanskrit; in the language of China, it means "Pervading All Places.

This refers to True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is equal and whose nature and characteristics are eternally so, pervading all phenomena because its body is unimpeded. As a sutra says: "The wondrous essence of Vairocana pervades all phenomena."

The *dhātu* (elements) constitute the body. In Sanskrit, *buddha*; in the language of China, "the Awakened One" (*jùézhě*). The *Awakening of Faith* states: "It means that the essence of mind is free from thought.
That which is free from the characteristics of thought is equal to the realm of empty space; it is the Tathāgata’s equal *dharmakāya*. Thus, one names 'non-thought' as the Buddha.
Because the Buddha-body is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it is called pure. As for 'Dharma,' it is that which may be taken as a standard."
Meaning: One rides upon the various vehicles (*yāna*) and thereby attains Buddhahood. Because one takes the Dharma as the body, it is called the *dharmakāya*.
As the Sūtra says: "The *dharmakāya* is precisely the Buddha-body," because the Dharma is able to produce the Buddha. "Body" (*kāya*) has the sense of being that which is relied upon.

Regarding the meaning of "essence" (*tattva*): because the *dharmakāya* serves as the essential basis for the *saṃbhogakāya* and *nirmāṇakāya*, the *dharmakāya* is primary and is therefore placed first.
The *saṃbhogakāya* is the Perfectly Complete Reward Body, the Buddha Vairocana.

[Commentary] The Sanskrit term *Vairocana* is translated here as "Pure and Perfect" (*jingman*). This means that all afflictions have been eliminated without remainder and all virtues are fully possessed;
it also carries the sense of being "perfectly complete. It is also translated as "Universal Radiance of Light," meaning that internally, by means of the light of wisdom...

Illuminating the true *dharmadhātu* is the self-recompense body (*svasaṃbhogakāya*). Illuminating great capacities through external wisdom and clarity is the other-recompense body (*parasaṃbhogakāya*).
Furthermore, it is said: "The suchness of principle and wisdom is called the self-recompense; the inexhaustible marks and signs are called the other-recompense. The *Mahāyāna* states:
"The recompense body possesses supreme and wondrous causes and receives the fruit of ultimate bliss, spontaneously..."

Sovereign, definitively blissful, and far removed from the characteristics of suffering; therefore, it is called "retribution" (*vipāka*). Possessing the three types of awakening in their full perfection, one is named a Buddha.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra Commentary* states: First, self-awakening: because one's own mind is fundamentally without arising or ceasing.

Second, awakening others: because one awakens to all phenomena as being exactly thus. Third, fulfillment of awakening: because the principle of these two awakenings is perfected. This is called [the Buddha].
Because it is complete, the cultivation of causes that elicits a result is termed "retribution" (*vipāka*). Because it accumulates merit and wisdom, it is termed a "body" (*kāya*);
thus, it is called the "Complete Retribution Body" (*pūrṇa-vipāka-kāya*). Since retribution is capable of manifesting transformation, it is placed second.
The thousand billion transformation bodies of Śākyamuni Buddha.
[Commentary: The Sanskrit term *Śākya* means "Capable One" (*Nengren*); *Munī* means "Silent One" (*Jimo*). His mind-nature is boundless.

Because he encompasses all things, he is named Śākyamuni (The Able One). Because his mind-nature is fundamentally quiescent and movement and stillness do not interfere with one another, he is named Tūṣṇīmbhūta (The Silent One).
Furthermore, it is said that "The Able One" represents compassion, which does not abide in nirvana; "The Silent One" represents wisdom, which does not abide in saṃsāra.
He is thus the Lord who preaches the Dharma in this Sahā world. As for his manifestations of a thousand million bodies:
This speaks to the multiplicity of transformations. For now, let us discuss three types. First, the Great Transformation Body (*mahā-nirmāṇakāya*). As stated in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*:
"I, now as Vairocana, am seated upon the lotus pedestal; upon the thousand petals surrounding me, there further appear a thousand Śākyamunis."

1. One flower encompasses ten billion lands; in each land there is one Śākyamuni. This is for the purpose of guiding and drawing in those of the three stages of worthiness (the *tri-śaikṣa*). 2. The minor transformation body (*pariṇāmika-nirmāṇakāya*):

as stated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, "He immediately proceeded to Vārāṇasī and preached to the five bhikṣus. This is for the purpose of guiding and drawing in those of the two vehicles (*dvaya-yāna*).

Third, the manifestation of transformation bodies according to species. This refers to appearing as a monkey among monkeys and as a deer among deer, manifesting in accordance with various forms to guide and receive all beings.
It is like the reflection of the moon dispersing across a thousand rivers, yet in the vast sky only the solitary orb is seen;

or like the sound transmitted through ten thousand mouths, yet in the empty valley there has never been a second echo. The response and transformation are inexhaustible, while the Dharma-body remains unmoving—it is just like this.

That which is non-existent yet suddenly appears is called "transformation" (*nirmāṇa*). By provisionally gathering the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as a body, he has already accepted the offerings of Cunda with his manifested body, and furthermore, he has separately received the offerings of the great assembly; thus, one is the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*) and the other is the transformation-body.

Moreover, when wisdom and principle merge, they accord with the *saṃbhogakāya*, enabling the arousal of great function that universally responds to sentient beings according to their capacities, preaching the Dharma to benefit all living beings. Therefore—

He is named the Transformation Body (*nirmāṇakāya*). His three bodies are unimpeded, and as the most honored among two-legged beings, he is called a Buddha. Because he first manifests through retribution and subsequently through transformation, he occupies the third position.
In the Land of Ultimate Bliss is Amitābha Buddha.

[Commentary] The Sūtra says: "For what reason is that land called 'Ultimate Bliss' (Sukhāvatī)? Because the sentient beings of that country have no manifold sufferings and experience only various joys, it is named 'Ultimate Bliss.
The Sanskrit term is Amitābha, which here means 'Immeasurable Life' (Amitāyus) and also 'Immeasurable Light.
This is because the radiance of that Buddha, as well as his lifespan, are immeasurable. — *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on Wisdom).
It is said: There are two kinds of the immeasurable (*apramāṇa*). First is the truly immeasurable, which cannot be measured even by the noble ones (*ārya*);
such as space, nirvāṇa, and the nature of sentient beings (*sattva-dhātu*), which are immeasurable. Second is that which has measurable phenomena, yet those of inferior capacity cannot measure them;
such as Mount Sumeru, the waters of the great ocean, or the number of weights and drops. [These are known only by] the Buddhas.
