The Bodhisattvas can know this, whereas gods and worldly people cannot. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says:
"Only between Buddha and Buddha is their lifespan immeasurable. Because the ten titles are fully manifested and the three bodies are perfectly revealed, he is called a Buddha.
This is the Teacher of the Western Land who guides and receives sentient beings; by citing one Buddha of the West, the others are illustrated by analogy.
9. Amitābha has already attained Buddhahood; therefore, he is placed fourth.
As for Maitreya, the Honored Buddha who will descend in the future:
[Commentary] In the Sanskrit language, Maitreya means "Kindness" (Maitrī) in the Chinese language; it is his clan name. He was the son of a Brahmin from South India, and his personal name was...
Ajita means "Invincible. In full, it should be called "Compassionate Invincible.
Because he possessed a compassionate heart even while in his mother’s womb, he was given that name as his clan title. Furthermore, in a previous life, he encountered the Tathāgata Mahāmaitreya.
May you likewise receive this title; you shall immediately attain the *maitrīcitta-samādhi*. Furthermore, in the past, when he was a *brāhmaṇa*, his name was Sarvajña (All-Knowing).

For eight thousand years, he cultivated the practice of loving-kindness. The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states that he made a vow to protect sentient beings during the *śastra-yuga* (the age of weapons).
This represents the ultimate height of compassion, wherein loving-kindness flourishes in the present world and pity reaches its zenith in future kalpas.

Maitreya transcends both the ordinary and the small; thus, none can surpass him. One who possesses vast supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) and inexhaustible majestic virtue (*mahā-tejas*) is called a Buddha.
The Verse of the Monk Pūbagha states: "Maitreya is truly Maitreya; he manifests a thousand million transformations.
He dwells in the world at all times, yet the people of the world do not recognize him. The *Mysterious Record of Avalokiteśvara* states: "During the time of Tiṣya Buddha, Maitreya and..."
Śākyamuni Tathāgata and Maitreya both originally resolved to attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.

However, Maitreya frequented the homes of lay families and abandoned his studies and recitations; for this reason, his fruition ripened later, and he shall become the teacher at the Dragon Flower (*Nāgapuṣpa*) assembly.
When the human lifespan reaches eighty thousand years, this Buddha will appear in the world and preach the Dharma in three assemblies. In the first assembly:
In the first assembly, he delivered ninety-six billion people; in the second assembly, ninety-four billion people; and in the third assembly, ninety-two billion people.

All of them realized the fruit of Arhatship. Furthermore, all those who, within the Dharma of Śākyamuni Buddha, maintained the precepts, practiced cultivation, and performed meritorious deeds, shall all receive the prediction of attaining Buddhahood during the Dragon Flower Assembly. Therefore...
In various sūtras, the Buddha addressed Maitreya in verse, saying: "Those in your three assemblies were all previously transformed by me.

Of the nine hundred and sixty million people who received my five precepts, next are the nine hundred and twenty million who took the three refuges, and those who merely once called out 'Namo Buddha'—all shall attain the path of Buddhahood.
This passage cites the one currently in the position of Regent (the Bodhisattva Maitreya) as an illustration for those who have passed away.
"Departure" (gati) encompasses the three periods of time. Because he will descend to be born in the future, he is placed fifth.
Regarding "all Buddhas of the ten directions and three periods":
[Commentary] The "ten directions" refer to east, west, south, north, the four intermediate points, and above and below. The past, present, and future are called the "three."
In this world, every Buddha is honored as "All" (Sarva), for their emanations are immeasurable and pervade the lands of the ten directions; thus they are called "the Buddhas.
If one speaks of the Buddhas currently existing throughout the oceans of kalpas in the past, they are now termed "past";
yet what is currently present is the future of the past, and also the past of the future. This is why [they are so designated].
With each inhalation and exhalation, in a single kṣaṇa, one brings forth the three times. Furthermore, as for the Buddhas:
it is said that throughout the eastern direction, beyond unspeakably unspeakable worlds, unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddhas all appear before me and receive my offerings;
the same applies to the other directions. This is the summary of making offerings to all Buddhas.
[Also. The Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī of Great Wisdom. [Commentary:
"Great Wisdom" distinguishes this from wisdom that relies on external means. This refers to the fact that all Buddhas rely upon Mañjuśrī...

It is because he was distinguished by his initial generation of the mind (*cittotpāda*). Furthermore, when Sudhana first beheld him, he immediately generated the Great Mind (*mahācitta*). Thus, Maitreya said to Sudhana:
"That you were previously able to see the various spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*), hear of the bodhisattva practices, and enter the gates of liberation—all this is through the power of Mañjuśrī.
The *Sūkṣma-rahasya-sūtra* states: "In the language of India, he is called Mañjuśrī; in this [language], it means 'Wondrous Auspiciousness' (*Miaojixiang*)."
It is indeed so. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that in the past, immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Nāga-uttara-rāja (Dragon Seed Supreme King).

The *Aṅgulimālīya Sūtra* states that he is currently the Buddha Ratna-ākara-saṃcaya-maṇi-pramoda-garbha (Jewel Accumulation Joy-Treasury Delight) in the world of Constant Joy (*Sadā-pramuditā*) in the northern direction.
The *Commentary on the Sūtra of Maitreya’s Ascent* cites a scripture stating that he will attain Buddhahood in the future.
The Buddha’s name is Samantamukha (Universally Manifest). The *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* states: "Mañjuśrī is so called because he is approached, honored, and praised by all the world.
Furthermore, Paramārtha says: "Because he benefits enemies and kin equally, without causing them harm or distress.
Moreover, because there were ten kinds of auspicious omens at the time of his birth, his original Sanskrit name is Mañjuśrī; in this [Chinese] language, it means:

“Wondrous Virtue” (Miaode) means wisdom. A sutra states: “The mother of all Buddhas, the teacher of Śākyamuni, uniquely honored for her great wisdom, she is constantly the foremost among all bodhisattvas.
The *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* says: “Clearly seeing the Buddha-nature, just like Wondrous Virtue and others.
In the Sanskrit language, this is called *bodhisattva*; here it is translated as “Awakened Being. Because they have realized the same truth as the Buddha, it is termed “awakening” (*jue*).

When ignorance is not yet exhausted, it is termed "emotion" (qing). This emotion is capable of giving rise to great wisdom (mahājñāna) and great compassion (mahākaruṇā), whereby one awakens to the Buddha-nature inherent within oneself.
Because of wisdom alone, one seeks the fruit of Buddhahood above; because of compassion alone, one transforms sentient beings below.
Only when both compassion and wisdom are present can one benefit living beings. If wisdom is lacking, the path of the Buddha is difficult to accomplish; if compassion is lacking, [sentient beings...]

It is difficult to realize. Because they possess the union of wisdom and compassion, they are called Bodhisattvas; this is the general designation for those who accomplish the dual benefit of self and others.
Mañjuśrī possesses fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). Since faith and understanding (*adhimukti*) are the root of attaining Buddhahood, a sutra states:

"A multitude of Bodhisattvas as numerous as motes of dust attain perfect enlightenment by means of this. Since faith and understanding are the root of attaining Buddhahood, after receiving the food, he himself—
One should cultivate with diligent effort, hoping thereby to give rise to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*).
Regarding the Bodhisattva Samantabhadra of Great Conduct:
[Commentary] "Great Conduct" distinguishes this from the provisional practices of the Lesser Vehicle. Because it is adorned by the myriad practices (*sahasra-caryā*), it is so named.
He acts for the sake of all; because his mind never tires of making offerings to all, he is called "Practice" (*caryā*).

In the Sanskrit language, he is *Vasubhadra*, which here means "Universal Good" (*Samantabhadra*). The *Karunapundarika Sutra* states: "I shall surely excel all bodhisattvas. The Buddha Ratnagarbha said:
"For these reasons, I now change your name and call you Universal Good. His practice is such that there is nowhere it does not pervade. This is called [Universal Good].
“Universal” (Pu). To benefit all above and below is called “worthy” (xian). Because he universally benefits and brings aid to all, he is named Samantabhadra (Puxian).

Furthermore, practice is the foremost of the path of cultivation; without practice, merit and wisdom cannot arise, the mind of giving cannot become universal, the six perfections cannot be cultivated, and sentient beings cannot be delivered.
Therefore, there are no Buddhas or Bodhisattvas who do not proceed through the gateway of practice.

This refers to the emergence from within. However, Mañjuśrī represents the faith and understanding that can give rise [to practice], while Samantabhadra represents the myriad practices that are so given rise to.
Their mutual integration and inclusion symbolize that practice arises based on faith, for practice is able to manifest the underlying principle.
The Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara of Great Compassion.
[Commentary] "Great Compassion" (Mahākaruṇā) means that he employs a mind of pure compassion (*karuṇā-citta*) exclusively for the purpose of transforming and delivering sentient beings.

Because his vows are vast and profound, he is called "Great" (*mahā*); because he seeks out sounds to rescue those from suffering, he is named "Compassionate" (*karuṇā*). In the Sanskrit language, he is called *Avalokiteśvara*. This...
Regarding "Avalokiteśvara": "Avalokita" (觀) refers to the wisdom that contemplates; "Śvara" (音) refers to the object of contemplation. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states:
"The true essence of the teaching in this land resides in the purity of sound and hearing. Without wisdom, one cannot initiate practice; without practice, one cannot give rise to compassion.
By accepting these offerings of food and drink, we vow that wisdom and compassion shall be brought forth together to extensively transform all beings.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī, Samantabhadra, and Avalokiteśvara are established.
As for the various honored Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas [Commentary]:
"The various honored ones" encompasses all Bodhisattvas from every direction, such as Kṣitigarbha, Sthāmaprāpta, and others.
The assembly of noble ones possesses such merit and virtue that it is immeasurable and boundless;
among all sentient beings, there is none who surpasses them, and for this reason they are called "Venerable. In the Sanskrit language, *mahāsattva* means "Great Bodhisattva.

Those whose rank has reached the Ten Stages (*daśabhūmi*) or above the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), who simultaneously exercise both compassion and wisdom to benefit themselves and others—this is the summary of the offering.
The entire Saṃgha. Regarding "Mahāprajñāpāramitā":
[Commentary] The term "Mahā" (Great) refers to profound and vast Prajñā; it distinguishes this from shallow or minor Prajñā. The Sanskrit term for Prajñā...
If this is called "wisdom" (*prajñā*), "pāramitā" is translated here as "reaching the other shore. Birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is the near shore, and nirvāṇa is the far shore.
Prajñā is the foremost among the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) and the myriad practices; pāramitā is the culmination that reaches the far shore of nirvāṇa.
All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas take prajñā as the vehicle and nirvāṇa as that which is to be reached by the vehicle.
By relying on the Dharma of the six perfections, one carries all sentient beings across the ocean of suffering to the other shore of nirvāṇa.
This sentence summarizes the offering to all dharmas. Because the Buddha is the speaker, he is offered to first; because the Saṅgha is the transmitter, they are offered to next;
because the Dharma is that which is spoken and transmitted, it is offered to last. Thus, the Three Jewels are offered as one. [The text concludes with] "the six realms."
Because it brings equal benefit to all, and because it is a comprehensive repayment for the four debts of gratitude, one should first recite the offering before receiving the food.
There are ten benefits to porridge that greatly assist the practitioner; its karmic reward is boundless, leading ultimately to eternal bliss (to be recited at dawn).
[Commentary] The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: When the Buddha was in Śrāvastī, Nanda’s mother prepared food; she first served it to the bhikṣus and then ate herself.
She then prepared rice in a cauldron and, as the rice boiled, she drank the scum that rose to the surface. She realized that the internal wind within her body had been eliminated.
Dormant food is immediately digested. For this reason, one should combine plenty of water with a small amount of rice and boil them together;
furthermore, one may use black pepper and long pepper to season it before offering it to the Buddha. Thus, the Buddha permitted bhikṣus to eat congee for ten kinds of benefits:

first, to nourish the body so that its complexion becomes full and radiant; second, to restore those who are weak and emaciated and to increase their physical strength; third, to nourish the fundamental essence...
1. Vital energy is increased, and the lifespan is extended. 2. It is pure and supple; when eating, one experiences peace and happiness. 3.
It moistens the throat and mouth, allowing for unimpeded discourse. 4. It is harmonious and penetrating, eliminating wind-disorders. 5. It warms the spleen and stomach, digesting undigested food. 6.
The vital energy becomes free from obstruction, and speech is eloquent and refined. 7. It appropriately fills the belly and satisfies the appetite, nourishing the muscles.

[The afflictions] are suddenly eliminated. Tenth: the throat and palate become moistened, and the parching thirst is accordingly dispelled. Thus, the porridge has such benefits that they are inconceivable;
its karmic fruition is likewise inconceivable. Its benefit to the practitioner is the expression of the cause for this aspiration.

The "constant bliss" of the fruition represents the fruit. That is to say, if a donor provides the gruel of the ten benefits as an offering, they will certainly realize the wondrous fruit of *nirvāṇa* and attain the four virtues of permanence, bliss, self, and purity. The *Book of Zhou* states:
"The Yellow Emperor first boiled grains to make gruel. The "Traveling in Hard Cold" (*Kuhan Xing*) by Cao Cao (Wu Di of Wei) says: "As we travel, the days grow ever longer; the people..."
The horse was likewise hungry. Carrying a sack, he went out to gather firewood; he split ice with an axe to prepare a gruel.
With the three virtues and six flavors, he made offerings to the Buddha and the Sangha, universally honoring all sentient beings throughout the Dharma realm.

[Commentary] Regarding the three qualities: First, purity. This means that the food offered to the Buddha and the Sangha must always be kept clean and free from any odor of pungent or impure substances.
Second, softness. This means that the food offered to the Buddha and the Sangha must be tender, sweet, and harmonious, without any coarse or astringent flavors.
Third, accordance with the Dharma. This means that the food offered to the Buddha and the Sangha must be prepared and provided according to the appropriate season.
It is also properly prepared. As for the six flavors, they are: sour, bitter, sweet, pungent, salty, and bland. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states:

"When various upāsakas prepare various food utensils to make offerings to the Buddha and the Saṅgha, they are fully equipped with all kinds of materials, all of which are fuel from sandalwood and aloeswood.
These are matured by water possessing the eight qualities; thus, the food is sweet and delicious."
Therein lies great virtue. "To make offerings to the Buddhas" means to offer to all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
There are two kinds of Sangha: first, the Bodhisattva Sangha; second, the Bhikṣu Sangha. One who makes offerings to the Buddhas cannot fail to make offerings to the Sangha; therefore, it says "and.
As for "universally together," this extends upward to the Buddhas, in the middle to the worthy sages, the devas, nāgas, and Dharma protectors, and downward to even a single [being].
There are no sentient beings whatsoever who are not universally reached; therefore, it is called "universal offering.
When eating, one should wish that all sentient beings take the joy of meditation as their food and be filled with the delight of the Dharma.
[Commentary] "Meditative joy" (*dhyānāhāra*) and "Dharma-joy" (*dharmaprīti*): these are two of the five supramundane foods.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* Commentary states: "Worldly food can only sustain the body within saṃsāra; for a practitioner..."
Regarding worldly delicacies, the mind does not crave them; it constantly maintains right mindfulness and takes the joy of dhyāna and the delight in the Dharma as its food.
Thus, one is able to nurture the roots of goodness, transcend birth and death, and achieve Bodhi. Therefore, there are five kinds of supramundane food:
first, the food of mindfulness, which refers to those who cultivate the Noble Path maintaining constant right mindfulness; second, the food of the joy of the Dharma.
1. The food of delight, which means loving and rejoicing in the Great Dharma, because it nourishes and develops the seeds of the Path. 2.

The food of dhyāna-joy, which arises from attaining the power of concentration (*samādhi*), because it nourishes the life-force of wisdom (*prajñā-jīvita*), brings the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharmas*) to perfect clarity, and causes the mind to be constantly joyful and glad. 3.

The food of aspiration, which means not abandoning the holy life (*brahmacarya*) and nurturing all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), just as worldly food benefits and sustains the physical faculties. 4. The food of liberation... [text continues].
"Transcending food" means being liberated from the bonds of all karma and attaining mastery over the Dharma, thereby nourishing bodhi. These five kinds are the noble foods (*ārya-āhāra*);
the first line of the verse refers to the food of ordinary people (*pṛthagjana-āhāra*). This refers to rice that has been boiled and cooked, called "rice" (*bhojana*).
Furthermore, "rice" carries the sense of being chewed and consumed; it means that at the time of taking food, one makes this vow: "I now receive this solid food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) to sustain..."
I nourish this illusory body and cultivate the supramundane path. I vow that all sentient beings shall not be born from a womb, nor rely upon coarse material food;
instead, may they obtain only the two sustenances of meditative joy and the delight of the Dharma, thereby nurturing their noble faculties and sustaining their life of wisdom.

[Commentary on "Birth"]: Regarding "birth," at that time the World-Honored One [encountered] the Mother of Ghost Children (Hārītī) and others, who were inflicting harm upon the people with incomparable ferocity.
Therefore, he first subdued them with his majestic power and subsequently gathered them in with compassion. He exchanged their food and drink for the food of the Dharma. This is not... [text ends].

It causes life to enter the gate of death; therefore, it is called "birth. However, fearing that the transformation of the Dharma might not be constant and that those of a violent and evil nature might still harm living beings, he commanded his disciples:
"In every place where you practice, when eating, first bestow the Dharma-food so as to fulfill the joy of the Dharma. As the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says: "He who does not bestow food is not my disciple."

Having completed the recitation of the mantra, the food is produced. Using a spoon, take seven grains of rice—no larger than an inch of noodle—and form the *amṛta-mudrā* with the left hand by pressing the thumb against the ring finger. Recite the verse silently as follows:
The power of the Dharma is inconceivable; compassion is without obstruction. Seven grains pervade the ten directions, universally bestowed throughout the realms of sand.
(Ji) Take the rice from the spoon and give it to the attendant to deliver. Hold the spoon facing inward and silently recite the mantra:
Oṃ. Tāraya svāhā (three times; snap the fingers once at each repetition).
[Commentary] "The power of the Dharma" refers to the power of the verses, mantras, and contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
"Inconceivable" means that the power of this contemplative practice cannot be fathomed by the mind nor expressed in words, yet it is able to accomplish the inconceivable.
Compassion (*karuṇā*). By means of loving-kindness (*maitrī*), they satisfy all; by means of compassion, they uproot the suffering of hunger and thirst.
As for the "obstacles," it refers to the three obstacles of the *preta* (hungry ghosts): first, the external obstacle, which means that hungry ghosts constantly suffer from hunger and thirst;
their skin, flesh, blood, and veins are all withered and parched; their hair is disheveled, their faces are dark and sunken, and their lips and mouths are dry and cracked. Constantly...
With their own tongues, they lick their faces; terrified, they run about, seeking food everywhere.

At whatever springs or ponds they reach, they see the water transform into pus and blood, which they themselves do not wish to drink. Such ghosts are hindered from food and drink by external obstacles;

this is called "external obstruction" (bāhyāvaraṇa). Second, internal obstruction (ādhyātmikāvaraṇa) refers to those hungry ghosts with needle-like throats and mouths like flaming torches, whose bellies are vast.

Great! Even if they obtain food and drink, they are unable to eat or drink. Ghosts such as these are called "those with internal obstructions" because their internal conditions obstruct food and drink.
Third, those without obstruction: this refers to hungry ghosts named *Jvalanmālā* (Fierce Flame Garland), who, although they see food and drink...
There is no obstruction; however, whatever food they consume is entirely consumed by flames and turns into glowing embers.

Due to these causes and conditions, they suffer the great agony of hunger and thirst. This is called "unobstructed. Through the power of compassion, they attain freedom from such heavy suffering as described above.
Because they are unobstructed, they are able to transform seven grains of rice into [an immeasurable amount].
They shall become manifold, pervading all sand-grain worlds, causing every ghost and spirit to eliminate their respective obstacles,
partake of the flavor of the Dharma, and attain liberation.
The Great Garuda, the hosts of spirits and ghosts in the wilderness, the Rākṣasas, and the Mother of Ghosts—may all be filled with nectar.
Oṃ. Mudde svāhā. (Recite three times.
[Note] The *Buddhanusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra* states: "The King of the Golden-Winged Birds is named Zhengyin (Correct Sound). Among the various species of winged creatures..."
Living in happiness and sovereignty, he would eat one dragon king and five hundred minor dragons daily in Jambudvīpa;
he would likewise eat the same number each day throughout the four continents, beginning again from the start, for a period of eight thousand years.
When the signs of death appear, the various nāgas spit forth venom so that he cannot obtain food; driven by hunger and filled with terror, he finds no peace.
He goes to the Vajra Mountain and descends straight down from the mountain to the edge of the great waters;

[Note: "To hold" means to support with the hands. The Sanskrit term *pātra* is translated here as "vessel of appropriate measure.

This refers to the three aspects of substance, color, and size being in accord with the Dharma; thus it is called an "appropriate vessel. Although clay or iron are permitted for the substance, the emphasis lies primarily on...
Regarding the bowl: the *Sudarsana-vibhāṣā-vinaya* states that the noble ones of the three vehicles all carry earthenware bowls to beg for food as their livelihood;
because they take the four seas as their home, they are called *bhikṣus*. Regarding the color:

it is permitted only to smoke-tint them to the color of a pigeon’s neck, while blue, yellow, green, white, and variegated painted colors are not allowed. As for the size: although there are three grades—superior, middling, and inferior—[the text continues].

Because the Buddha established the rule that [the bowl] must correspond to the size of one's body, if among these three [sizes] there is anything that does not accord with the Dharma, it is not a proper vessel (*pātra*).
When holding the proper vessel, one must recite dharanis and verses and dedicate the merit to sentient beings; this is the very essence of the Dharma, for it is primordially accomplished.
A single phrase of "accomplishing the Dharma-vessel" encompasses emptiness, the provisional, and the middle. This extends even to the established regulations.

Regarding the methods of the Vinaya, the intent behind the three ladles and five contemplations all originates from the *Yingliang* (The Proper Measure); thus, there are no dharmas that are not fully contained therein.
The *Jieben shoujie jiandu* (Chapter on Receiving Precepts) of the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states: "In the past, at the foot of the Bodhi tree, the World-Honored One..."
When he first attained Buddhahood, there were two merchants who offered honey and parched grain to the Buddha.

The World-Honored One thought to himself, "The Buddhas of the past received food using alms bowls. At that moment, the Four Great Heavenly Kings each quickly presented stone bowls to the World-Honored One.
The Tathāgata further reflected, "If I were to accept [offerings] from only one person, the others would feel resentment."
I now accept all four bowls together; placing them one upon another in sequence within my left palm, I press down with my right hand.
By the Buddha’s supernatural power, they merge into a single bowl. Thus it is said that he has accomplished the vessel of the Dharma and received the offerings of devas and humans.
Therefore, the Vinaya does not permit bhikṣus to possess stone bowls; if one possesses one, it constitutes a sthūlātyaya offense.
If one is unaware of such rules regarding the proper measure [of a bowl], even a single drop of water will be difficult to digest, let alone the offerings of devas and humans.
When receiving food, one must maintain dignified deportment. The *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states: "When a bhikṣu receives food, he should be like an elephant in the Snowy Mountains."
The method for the King’s meal: Once food has entered the mouth, one should use the nose to establish the boundary between the front and back portions.

After the preceding morsel has been swallowed, one should continue to place the subsequent morsel inside; it must be neither too large nor too small, but should be of a size that can be consumed with ease. The Elder (Upādhyāya) should eat slowly.
One must not finish eating too quickly and remain watching, thereby causing junior bhikṣus to eat in distress and fail to be satisfied.
If a ball of roasted flour (maṇḍaka) is large, one should divide it with the hand so that it may fit into the mouth; the same applies to flat cakes (apūpa).
When receiving food, one must not let even a single grain fall to the ground. If eating thin gruel, soup, or drinks, one must not slurp them to make a noise; rather, one should consume them slowly.

[The text continues with: "Swallowing. The *Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinaya* states: One should not eat by flicking the tongue; one should not eat by stuffing the mouth; one should not eat by making gurgling sounds; one should not eat by blowing air [onto the food];
one must not shake the hand while eating. These details are as set forth in the *Vinaya*."
[Commentary on] "Three Scoops with Restraint": "Restraint" (*jie*) means measure. This refers to receiving more than three scoops of rice, or using chopsticks or a spoon to take up soup and eat it.
However, one does not stop at two, nor does one go beyond four; rather, one must take exactly three.
Why is this? It is because it expresses the vow to sever the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion, and manifests the three groups of pure precepts (*tri-śikṣāpada*).
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Food is the foundation for practicing the Way. When receiving food, one must make three vows."
First spoonful: May I sever all evils.
[Commentary] "May I sever all evils" means that there is no evil that is not severed. Tiantai says: There are evils within the realm and beyond the realm;
these refer to the afflictions of view and thought, the dust-and-sand-like delusions, and the ignorance of *avidyā*. When setting down the first spoonful, one should make this vow.
May all the three karmas of body, speech, and mind, as well as all unwholesome dharmas, belonging to this life be completely severed and exhausted.
Second scoop: May I cultivate all wholesome deeds.
[Commentary] "May one cultivate all wholesome qualities" means that there is no wholesome quality that is not cultivated. Next, when lowering the spoon [to eat], one should make this aspiration:

"May all wholesome dharmas possessed in this life be diligently cultivated"—namely, the three trainings of morality (*śīla*), concentration (*samādhi*), and wisdom (*prajñā*) as taught by the Tathāgata, along with the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*) and other such dharmas, up to hundreds of thousands of samādhis and the immeasurable [qualities].
This is the Dharma-gate.
Third, the scoop: the vow to deliver all sentient beings.
[Commentary] "The vow to deliver all sentient beings" means that there is not a single sentient being who is not delivered. It is as when Ānanda made his vow.
Make this vow: "As long as even a single sentient being has not yet attained Buddhahood, I shall never enter *nirvāṇa* here. Next, when placing the spoon [into the food], you should make this vow:
"May the roots of goodness cultivated in this life be dedicated to all sentient beings, so that we may together attain the Way of the Buddha.
The previous two spoonfuls were for one's own benefit; this one is precisely for the benefit of others, which corresponds to the Four Great Vows.

In this way, the practitioner, by virtue of the power of these incantations and vows, surpasses the offering of the seven treasures and food and drink of a hundred flavors— more numerous than the sands of the Ganges—
to all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the assembly of worthy and holy ones.

[Commentary] These three vows are from the *Benqixin lun* (Treatise on the Origin of the Mind of Faith). The text states: "First is the straightforward mind (*ṛju-citta*), which correctly contemplates the dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Second is the profound mind (*gambhīra-citta*), which delights in accumulating all virtuous practices. Third is the compassionate mind (*karuṇā-citta*), which desires to uproot the suffering of sentient beings."
This is also the three skillful means (*upāya*): first, the skillful means of cessation, which stops all unwholesome dharmas;
second, the skillful means of arousal, which gives rise to all roots of goodness; and third, the skillful means of great vows, which vow to deliver all sentient beings.
As the saying goes: "If the three minds are not exhausted, even a drop of water is difficult to digest. Is this not precisely what that refers to?

The Five Contemplations Are Without Contradiction [Record]. "Without contradiction" means the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena. This refers to the fact that within contemplation, one simultaneously engages with phenomena and principle, for through earnest reflection they are harmoniously integrated.
If a practitioner of the Way receives food without maintaining right mindfulness, how does this differ from an ox chewing grass? Therefore...
Chan Master Làn Ān said: "The property of the Sangha of the ten directions is as heavy as a mountain; how easily can it be repaid across ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes?

Though the Golden Mouth speaks of this together with others, people do not yet believe it; in years to come, how can one avoid the gates of the Iron City? He further said: "A human body is difficult to obtain—ponder this well!
Once the horns [of birth] have grown, the years and months are long. It is laughable that for the sake of another’s single grain of rice," and so forth.
In an instant, one loses the provisions for half a year. Viewed from this perspective, if one does not cultivate the Three Learnings, one will fall prey to the devouring [of karma].
How can one not be cautious?
First: calculate the amount of labor expended and measure the distance from whence it came.
[Commentary] "Calculating the amount of labor" means to consider that this single bowl of rice is not something ordinary.
If one traces its origin—from the sowing, planting, harvesting, and reaping; from the farmers' gauging of sunshine and rain, the droughts and floods, and the use of spades, hoes, plows, and harrows;
down to the threshing and cooking—the sweat of all these laborers is gathered together. The food consumed is small, while the sweat shed is vast; such is the magnitude of the labor involved.
It is thus. An ancient saying goes: "When weeding the rice paddies at midday, sweat drips onto the soil beneath the stalks.

Who knows that every grain of food on one's plate is the result of bitter toil? Therefore, the Vinaya states: "A single grain of rice requires a hundred labors. Once it enters the mouth, it becomes impure;
in an instant, it transforms into excrement and urine—so loathsome as to be unworthy of sight. If I were to be greedily attached to it, I would surely fall to the earth.
In hell, one swallows glowing iron balls; upon emerging, one becomes an animal to repay past debts.
Having contemplated this, one should give rise to a sense of weary detachment before being fit to receive food. Regarding the measure of those from whom it comes, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* states:
"All are faithful donors who have reduced their own sustenance for the sake of seeking merit, bestowing it upon us—namely, the fat of the faithful donor (*dānaśraddha*)."
Fat is the blood and sweat of those on the road. Without cultivation, even a single grain of rice is difficult to digest. Thus, the *Mañjuśrīparipṛcchā-sūtra* states:
"If a bodhisattva lacks contemplation, they should not even accept food. Whenever one receives food, one should form this visualization.
2. Reflecting upon one’s own virtuous conduct to determine whether it is complete or deficient regarding the worthiness of receiving offerings.
[Commentary] "Reflecting" (忖) means deliberation. It refers to deliberating upon whether one's own virtuous conduct is complete or deficient.

If one has indeed diligently cultivated the Three Studies and transformed sentient beings, possessing these virtues of the two benefits, it is called "complete. Only then is one fit to receive offerings.
Offerings. If these are not complete, it is termed "deficient," and one should not accept them. Thus, the *Vinayamātṛkā-śāstra* states:

"If one does not recite the sūtras, practice seated meditation, attend to the affairs of the Triple Gem, or maintain the precepts, yet accepts the faithful offerings of others, one will fall because of those offerings.
It further states: "Only when the afflictions of view and thought within the three realms are severed and exhausted, and the fruit of Arhatship is realized, is one [fit to receive such offerings]."
One who is fully worthy of offerings (*arhat*) is so called; those from the first through the third fruits of the path are all termed "deficiently worthy of offerings.

Nevertheless, even if one's virtuous conduct is complete, one must still contemplate the Dharma in order to properly digest the offerings of the faithful. Thus, Tiantai said: "Whether begging for food or partaking of a communal meal, one must always engage in contemplation.
If one does not enter into contemplation, it merely nourishes the cycle of birth and death; this is what is meant by 'the study of the Way being unpenetrated.'"
This is the principle. If this is so when [the food] is complete, how much more so when it is deficient? Whenever receiving food, one should cultivate this contemplation.
Third: Guarding the mind to distance it from transgressions, with the aim of eliminating greed and other afflictions.

[Commentary] "Guarding the mind to depart from faults; taking greed and so forth as the primary tenet" means that the three poisons—greed, hatred, and delusion—are the root of birth and death for all sentient beings and the causal conditions for the creation of karma.
This mind is fully possessed of the faults and afflictions of immeasurable and boundless defilements, and greed, hatred, and delusion are their very foundation;

therefore, they are called the "primary tenet" (*mūla*). As for "tenet": *(Note: The term *mūla* is translated here as "root" or "foundation," while the Chinese character 宗 is rendered as "primary tenet" to reflect its technical usage in Buddhist scholastic contexts.)*
It is the master. Thus, the *Maitreya-paripṛcchā-sūtra* says: "All unwholesome dharmas arise from greed, hatred, and delusion.
We have left home for the sake of the Way; we should be prudent and guard against them. If the root is eliminated, all evils will be kept at a distance."

Therefore, one should not give rise to thoughts of craving toward delicious flavors, nor thoughts of aversion toward coarse food, nor thoughts of delusion toward food that is neither coarse nor delicious.
Whenever receiving food, one should practice this contemplation.
4. Properly employing excellent medicine to treat the withering of the physical form.

[Commentary] "Properly employing excellent medicine to treat the withering of the physical form" means that our bodies, composed of the four great elements, are constantly afflicted by hunger and thirst;
if we do not partake of food and drink, the body will wither and the complexion will fade, leaving no way to advance in the practice of the Path.
Therefore, food and drink are the excellent medicine for sustaining the body and treating illness, and the mechanism for practicing and advancing on the Path.
If one becomes greedily attached to them, they instead become a chronic malady. The *Aśokarāja-sūtra* states that Upagupta said:
He placed a vessel filled with milk-rice and an empty vessel side by side before a gluttonous bhikṣu and said to him, "Wait for it to cool, then drink it little by little.
However, because the bhikṣu’s craving was so intense, he blew upon it to cool it and then ate it all at once. Guptā said, "Though the milk-rice has cooled, your mind remains hot. Again...
"It must be cooled. You should take the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) as water to remove this fever of the mind.
When you see food and drink, regard it as taking medicine. After the bhikṣu had finished eating, he immediately spat it out into an empty vessel.
Guptā said, "You may eat again. The bhikṣu replied, "How can that which is impure be eaten again? Guptā said, "You should contemplate all things [in this way]."
The Dharma is like mucus and spittle. Because he taught the Dharma in this way, the bhikṣu applied himself with diligence, contemplated and investigated it, and attained the fruit of arhatship.
Whenever one receives food, one should maintain this contemplation.
5. One should accept this food for the sake of accomplishing the work of the Path.
[Commentary: "For the sake of accomplishing the work of the Path, one should accept this food" means that those who have left the household life are without conditioned activity and free from desire;

they maintain themselves in purity, partaking of drink and food according to circumstances merely to sustain their physical lives, so as to cultivate the work of the Path of the Three Vehicles. It is not for other purposes.

If one eats [without restraint], the body will become emaciated and the complexion will change, making it difficult to accomplish the work of the Way (*dharma-karman*). Now, because one is about to accomplish the work of the Way, one accepts this food;
were one not practicing the Way, even a single grain of rice would be difficult to digest. Cien said: "It is for the sake of accomplishing the Way that [the donor] brings forth this offering.
If the work of the Way has not yet been accomplished, how can one hope to digest it? Thus, it is evident that food and drink are the primary conditions that assist the Way. Therefore...
Accept it. If you know for yourself that your karmic work regarding the Path has not yet been accomplished, you must most earnestly give rise to a sense of shame and remorse.
Therefore, the *Guhya-pratipatti* (Hugong) says: "When eating, one must give rise to shame and remorse; one should practice the method of contemplation. The *Mātṛkā-vinaya* (Modilejia lun) says:

"When receiving food, one should bring this to mind with every morsel. If one does not apply the mind in this way, it is called 'vainly consuming the offerings of the faithful. In all instances of receiving [alms]...
At the time of eating, one should form this reflection:

"Consider the amount of labor involved. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The production of this food involves much effort—plowing, sowing, harvesting, threshing, grinding, winnowing, boiling, and cooking—and its utility is great.
One should measure its origin from the perspective of the donor; as the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya* says: "The donor..."
One should reduce the portion allotted to one's wife and children and give it away for the sake of seeking merit. Whenever receiving food, one should form this contemplation:

secondly, one should weigh one’s own virtuous conduct to determine whether one is fully or deficiently worthy of offerings. The *Vinayamātṛkā-vinaya* states: "If one does not practice seated meditation or recite the scriptures..."
If one manages affairs for the Three Jewels yet fails to observe the precepts, and accepts the faithful offerings of others only to fall victim to wealth, then it is inappropriate to accept food.
If one’s virtuous conduct is complete, then one may rightfully receive offerings and eat. Whenever accepting food, one should perform this contemplation:

the three ways of guarding the mind to remain free from transgression, with the overcoming of greed and other afflictions as the primary principle. The *Vyākhyāyukti-ṭīkā* states: "A renunciant must first..."
One should guard against three faults of the mind: namely, giving rise to greed for superior flavors, anger toward inferior flavors, and delusion regarding middling flavors.
Because of this, one loses a sense of shame and modesty and falls into the three evil realms. Whenever receiving food, one should cultivate this contemplation.
The four requisites are like excellent medicine for treating the withered body; that is, hunger and thirst are considered the primary ailments, along with the four hundred and four [other] diseases.
Illness is a guest affliction; therefore, one must take food as medicine to sustain the body. Whenever receiving food, one should form this contemplation:
regarding the four hundred and four illnesses, the human body is a provisional formation composed of the four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind.
If even one of these elements becomes unbalanced, then one hundred and one types of illness arise; when all four elements are in discord, they produce the four hundred and four illnesses.

Fifth, for the sake of accomplishing the work of the Path, one should accept this food; for if one does not eat, hunger and thirst will arise as afflictions, and how then can the work of the Path be accomplished?
The *Ekottarika Āgama* states: "Eating too much leads to suffering and illness; eating too little causes the decline of physical strength.
One who eats in moderation is like a scale that has neither high nor low. Whenever one receives food, one should form this contemplation.

[Commentary] These five contemplations of the path are based on the *Śālistamba-sūtra* (The Sutra of the Bequeathed Teaching). The text states: "When receiving various foods and drinks, one should regard them as taking medicine.

This is the meaning of the first contemplation. Next, it says: "Whether toward the good or the bad, do not give rise to increase or decrease. This is the meaning of the second contemplation. Third, it says:
"Obtain only what is necessary to sustain the body in order to eliminate hunger and thirst. This is the meaning of the fifth contemplation. Fourth, it says: "Receiving the offerings of others..."
"Rushing [to eat] removes one's own distress; this is the meaning of the second contemplation. The fifth [contemplation] says: 'Do not seek much, lest it destroy your wholesome mind';
this is the meaning of the first contemplation. An ancient master said: 'If these five contemplations are maintained, even a thousand pieces of gold are easily digested.
For this reason, the Upādhyāya has extensively cited the sūtras and śāstras to elucidate them."

**Washing the Alms Bowl [Commentary]:** "Washing" refers to scouring away grease and food particles. This means that once the meal has been finished, one should cleanse the vessel according to the Dharma.
Regarding the washing methods of the Western Regions (India), it is necessary to use ash, mud, soapberry (*gleditsia sinensis*), *kusha* grass, and so forth, before the bowl can be purified.
"Greasy" means that in those regions, food consists largely of milk products, curds, butter, and oil;
whereas in this region, one merely serves steamed rice, which becomes clean simply by rinsing it with boiling water.
With this water used for washing the bowl, which possesses a flavor like the nectar of the devas, I bestow it upon all the ghosts and spirits, so that they may all obtain full satisfaction.
Oṃ ma-hū-ra-si svāhā (three times).
[Note] The Sanskrit term *sūrpaka* means "water" in Chinese; its metaphorical comparison to nectar (*amṛta*) is because the bhikṣu—
Wash the alms bowl. When cleansing it, recite the dhāraṇī of the empowerment verse. The power and efficacy of this dharma are inconceivable.

By means of this dharma-water, universally save all sentient beings, causing the sprouts of their goodness to grow, washing away the defilements of their sins, freeing them from the feverish afflictions of birth and death, and removing the parching thirst of craving and attachment, so that they may achieve Bodhi and transcend to the shore of enlightenment. This is...

This is illustrated by the analogy of the wondrous medicine of immortality. Worldly people know only that the benefit of giving food is the greatest, yet they do not realize that the merit of this gift of water is even more supreme. For hungry ghosts have throats ablaze with fire;
when they see water, they cannot drink it. Only by drinking this consecrated water can they all attain coolness and liberation from the miserable realms. Therefore:

When washing the alms bowl, through the power of the consecration verses and mantras, one bestows water upon it as if it were celestial nectar (*amṛta*), so that spirits and deities may not suffer from hunger or thirst.
Once the water has been removed, one must again unfold [the bowl-cloth]. If it is not unfolded, the water will not dry;

for internally one fears dampness, and externally one fears the attraction of dust. Therefore, it is necessary to unfold it. As stated in the *Jinglü yìxiàng* (Heterogeneous Phenomena of the Sūtras and Vinaya):
There was an Arhat who frequently entered the dragon palace to receive offerings. Upon returning with his alms, he would have the śrāmaṇera wash his bowl.
Inside the bowl were a few grains of leftover rice; when the śrāmaṇera smelled them, they were exceedingly fragrant, and when he tasted them, they were most delicious.

He then devised a method: he crawled under his teacher’s meditation seat and grasped its legs with both hands. When it was time for the teacher to go, the meditation seat entered the dragon palace along with him.
The Dragon said, "This one has not yet attained the Way; why have you brought him here? It was because the śrāmaṇera had eaten the grains from his alms bowl.
One day, Chan Master Wuzhi Feng entered the Puxian Hall to sit in meditation. Suddenly, a deity knelt before him.

The Master asked, "Who are you? He replied, "I am a deity who protects the precepts. The Master said, "What fault have I committed? The deity said, "Whenever you wash your alms bowl, you always pour away the water;
this is not appropriate. From that time on, the Master drank all of it, whereupon he contracted a spleen ailment.
It was only after ten years that he recovered.

Regarding the term "establishing a *zhāi*" (*jié zhāi*): "establishing" (*jié*) means to gather and return [to the source]. For the sake of generating wholesome roots, the donor (*dānapati*) establishes a *zhāi* feast to make offerings to the assembly of monks. This is the *zhāi*.

Once the offerings have been completed, one recites the Cundī Dhāraṇī first; this is because, through the protective power of the dhāraṇī and the efficacy of the two verses, one binds together these wholesome dharmas so that they are not lost, thereby bringing benefit to both oneself and others, and ensuring that the two kinds of giving are inexhaustible—hence it is called "concluding the meal" (jiezhai). As for the reason for reciting the Cundī Dhāraṇī first: [it is as explained above].
May what you seek be fulfilled according to your wishes.
That which is called giving will surely yield its benefit; if one gives for the sake of happiness, one will certainly attain peace and joy in the future.
[Commentary]: To direct the mind universally is to practice *dāna* (giving); to withhold nothing for oneself while bestowing it upon others is to practice *dāna*.

The *Candrapradīpa-samādhi-sūtra* states: "Generosity is the vanguard that breaks through stinginess and greed; it is the initial gateway for entering the Right Path. The *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* states:
"This was the very first thing the Tathāgata accepted after attaining enlightenment beneath the Bodhi tree: honey from two merchants."
Regarding the dedication verse for roasted flour (piṣṭaka): it is recited at present when concluding a vegetarian feast (*zhāizhai*).
Although the recipient may lack the virtuous conduct of a Tathāgata, by relying on the power of the Buddha’s vows, one will certainly cause the donor to attain peace and happiness. The Vinaya states:
"In whatever offerings a donor provides, there is always a specific aspiration—either seeking rebirth in heaven to enjoy blessings, or seeking liberation from the cycle of birth and death."
[The merit] is dedicated. Whether seeking long life and peace, or seeking the quiescence of nirvana, the recipient should proclaim their aspiration before the Triple Gem.
Therefore, after the Tathāgata has accepted the food, he immediately recites this verse for dedication. That is to say:
"Whatever the intention with which one gives, according to that cause one will experience the fruit; one shall surely obtain therein what is wished for. There is the bestowing of body and mind.

"Benefit" (*li*) refers to the fulfillment of one's sought-after aspirations; "advantage" (*yi*) refers to planting seeds in the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*), for it is not possible without the Sangha.

The first two phrases clarify the cause of invocation (*gan*), while the latter two phrases manifest the response (*ying*). To be far removed from birth and death is called "peace" (*an*); to no longer undergo the various realms of existence is called "bliss" (*le*).
This is what is meant by: "Sitting upright, he receives offerings; the donor attains peace and bliss. Therefore, it is said: "If [one acts] for the sake of bliss..."
Therefore, by giving, one will certainly attain peace and happiness hereafter.
When the meal is finished, one should make this aspiration for all beings: "May all that they have to do be accomplished, and may they be endowed with all the Buddha-dharmas."

[Commentary] "To conclude" means to finish. "To finish" means to exhaust. This refers to the time immediately following the reception of food and the washing of the bowl, which is precisely when the ritual of giving (*dāna*) should be performed.
If one does not generate the aspiration for dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), then the previous three spoonfuls and the five contemplations are all merely superfluous words.
There is a beginning but no end; therefore, one should aspire for all sentient beings to bring all matters to ultimate completion.

Regarding "having accomplished all that was to be done," this is spoken in terms of specific activities: after a bhikṣu in the Buddha’s time has finished receiving food, gathered his robes and bowl, and washed his feet, he spreads out a seat and sits.
He may either practice dhyāna or cultivate contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) in order to increase the three trainings. This is stated briefly.

The practice of contemplation is now complete; the kitchen duties and the distribution of food in the hall have been finished. With no other matters to attend to, one may devote oneself solely to the Buddha-way.
As for entering into the profound discourse on the principle [of reality], how could it be easily explained? The followers of the Two Vehicles merely sever the delusions of views and thought;

the Bodhisattvas are about to exhaust ignorance, yet even they cannot yet be said to have accomplished everything. Only the Buddhas have thoroughly exhausted the five stages of dwelling and forever forgotten the two types of death. This is so.
"Kṛtakṛtya" means "all accomplished. However, after ordinary people have eaten, they either rush about with worldly affairs or increase their sleep;
therefore, [the Buddha] now vows to dedicate [this merit] toward the Buddha-way, hence saying "all that was to be done is accomplished," which means being fully endowed with all Buddha-dharmas.

When the Buddha-dharmas are fully possessed, what is to be done is spontaneously accomplished. When what is to be done is accomplished, there is nothing that is not fully endowed with the Buddha-dharmas.
This is the Dharma.

Regarding the "Receiving of Alms" [Record]: In ancient times, when a *dānapati* provided a meal for the Sangha, they would first spread a cloth mat (*pūta*) beneath the seats. After the midday meal was concluded, they would present the mat as an offering.
Regarding robes: originally, one would personally follow the gift of cloth; later, silver coins were used in place of cloth, so one personally follows the gift of cowrie shells.

This means that merely providing a meal for the Sangha is insufficient to fully express reverence; thus, one adds gifts of material goods to manifest the utmost sincerity and courtesy of the ritual etiquette. At that time, one should perform prayers and recitations.
The two kinds of giving—material wealth and the Dharma—are equal and without distinction;

thus, the *dānapāramitā* is fully perfected. [Commentary] That which is the source for sustaining life is called "wealth" (*dhana*). That which is the realization of the ground of the mind is called the "Dharma" (*dharma*). To "give" (*dāna*) means to bestow or distribute.
The *Vasumitra-śāstra* states: "To perform *dānakṣepa*"; this is translated as "giving of wealth. The commentary explains that the method of giving in recompense is termed "attainment" (*prāpti*).
*Dakṣiṇā*. It guides one toward the field of merit; it is also called *dakṣiṇā*. All characters [for this term] are written with the radical for "mouth.

According to the *Xiyu ji* (Records of the Western Regions), the correct pronunciation is *dakṣiṇa*, which means "right. Alternatively, it is called *dhāraṇī*; because one receives the offerings of others with the right hand, it generates merit for them.
Regarding the statement that the two types of giving—material wealth and the Dharma—are equal and without distinction: this refers to when a donor (*dānapati*) gives material gifts... [comparison].
The Buddha compares the two kinds of merit resulting from giving the Dharma; they are without distinction of superiority or inferiority, and are thus said to be equal and without difference.
*Dāna* is the Chinese term for "giving. *Pāramitā* is translated here as "the perfection of an undertaking. For the sake of sentient beings, the Bodhisattva...
Because all practices have been universally cultivated to perfection, this present giving is fundamentally intended to fulfill the *dānapāramitā*.
This is what is meant by the inexhaustibility of material giving, the inexhaustibility of the giving of Dharma, and the inexhaustibility of merit;
therefore, it is said to be "fully perfected."
"Taking the willow branch" [Commentary]: "Taking" means grasping with the hand. A "willow branch" is a wooden stick used for cleaning the teeth. The Record of Bai Yu-chan states:
"In the void of the Taiwei Palace, the essence of the lunar mansion Jī (the Scorpion) transformed into a willow tree, hanging down and swaying amidst thin clouds."
In the interim, that which was formerly hidden by the willows was likely intended to manifest his gentle and humble resolve.
The *Nanhai Jigui Neifa Zhuan* states: "The Sanskrit term is *daṃṣṭrā-jaṭā*; *daṃṣṭrā* is translated as 'teeth'."
*Kaśeṭha* is precisely that wood. How could one fail to recognize it? To call the *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-stick) by the name "willow branch" (*yángzhī*) is incorrect.
Willow trees are extremely rare in the Western Regions; the translators have arbitrarily transmitted this designation. The Buddha’s *dantakāṣṭha* tree is truly not a willow.
At Nālandā Monastery, I personally witnessed it with my own eyes: its tooth-sticks are as thick as a small finger, and large timber is split for use. Small [branches] are used as well.
[These materials] are cut into strips. Those near mountain villas primarily use *cakravāka* wood and *kṣauma* vines;

those situated on level fields may use mulberry, peach, locust, or willow as they please. These should be collected and prepared in advance so that nothing is lacking. The *Trīṇi-sahasra-vidhi* states:

There are three matters regarding the use of *yángliǔ* (willow) [tooth-sticks]: first, when cutting it, it must be according to the proper measure; second, when splitting it, it must be according to the Dharma;
third, when chewing the tip, one must not exceed one-third [of its length]. Regarding "cutting it according to the proper measure": there are three kinds of tooth-sticks.
The longest is twelve finger-breadths; the shortest is six finger-breadths; those between these two lengths are called medium.
In the Vinaya, these are termed *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-sticks). There are four kinds of willow, all of which may be used for cleaning the teeth: first, the white willow; [the others follow].

1. *Yuan-ye* (Round-leaf): its leaves are round. 2. *Qing-yang* (Green Willow): its leaves are long. 3. *Chi-yang* (Red Willow): its leaves turn red when the frost descends. 4. *Huang-yang* (Yellow Willow):

the wood is hard and compact, making it difficult to grow. Nowadays, willow twigs are universally used as *yang-zhi* (willow branches). Since willow twigs hang downward, they are actually a type of small willow.
If there were no willows, what would one use to clean the teeth? One must know that all types of wood can be used for cleaning the teeth. All...
It is called *dantakāṣṭha* (tooth-stick). One should simply take one that is harmonious in nature and possesses a bitter taste, and chew it; it is not limited to the single species of willow wood.
Holding a *yāśākhā* (willow branch) in hand, one should make this aspiration for all sentient beings: "May they all attain the wondrous Dharma and reach ultimate purity."
Oṃ sarvadhātu-sattva-dharmatā sarvadhātu-ḍhaṃ oṃ laṃ svāhā. (Recite this Mantra of Purifying the Dharmadhātu twenty-one times. [Note]:
Regarding "holding a tooth-stick in hand": this refers to the time after finishing a meal;
it means one should remove impurities in order to investigate the Buddha-dharma.
The Bodhisattva has no thoughts whatsoever; all devas and humans, searching for the place where these arise, cannot find it.
Suddenly, when the faculty and its object meet, one perceives the inexhaustibility of entering into phenomena and entering into principle.

Therefore, as soon as the Bodhisattva raises a willow branch, he makes the vow that all sentient beings—whether through prostration, recitation, contemplation of the mind, or study of the teachings—shall all attain awakening.
One enters the wondrous Dharma. Ultimately, the wondrous Dharma has nothing else; it simply aspires for all sentient beings to be pure.
Taking the purity of upholding the precepts in this life as the cause, one shall attain ultimate purity in the future as the fruit.
For the nature of the *yángzhī* (willow branch) is gentle and its flavor is cool; thus, its meaning is taken as a metaphor. Therefore, the flower...
The *Yan shu* (Commentary by Yan) states: "The five benefits of the *yángzhī* (willow branch) are termed secular methods.

Regarding "chewing the *yángzhī*": [the *Jì* (Record) explains] "chewing" means masticating and biting. This refers to holding a willow branch in the hand and crushing it with the teeth. The *Fayuan* (Garden of the Dharma) says:

The willows hang down with slender branches; their green trunks and fresh shoots are like this. When removing heat, the mouth emits the fragrance of hidden orchids; when cleansing the teeth, the breath contains the scent of *utpala* flowers.
At the time of chewing the *yāshī* (willow twig), one should wish that all sentient beings may have minds that are harmonious and pure, devouring all afflictions.
Oṃ amogha-mīmāle īvākara saṃśodhani padma-kumāra īva-saṃśodhaya dhāraya dhāraya sumi māṃ svāhā.
(Recite this mantra three times.)
[Commentary] Regarding the time for chewing the *yāṣṭika* (teeth-cleansing twig): this means that immediately after receiving food, one should brush the teeth;

one must not delay or procrastinate. The Vinaya states: "If residual saliva remains, the fast is not established [for the following activities]: reciting scriptures, listening to the Dharma, receiving prostrations, or performing prostrations to others."
All of them incur offense because their pure and impure aspects are intermingled. As for the *yāshā* (willow branch), its taste is bitter and astringent;

chewing it is beneficial to both body and mind. The Bodhisattva vows that all sentient beings shall subdue their afflictions (*kleśa*), having no other purpose than to demonstrate the dharma of firm endurance to eliminate those afflictions—just like drinking the bitter taste of the *yāshā*.
It also eliminates feverish affliction. When the mind is harmonized and purified, it devours all afflictions.
This refers to the essence of the *tathatā*-mind, which is inherently pure from the beginning. However, because it is obscured by ignorance, the wondrously pure and luminous mind cannot manifest.
Now, by employing the power of the precepts to subdue it, the pure luminosity is revealed alone; thus, all those afflictions, delusions, and karmic actions [are naturally eliminated].
*Śānti*. It is like a willow twig that has been bitten through; it can never be joined back together again. *Samudaya*.
Whenever chewing a willow twig, one must ensure all saliva is cleared away before rinsing with water. One must not rinse with water while still holding the twig in the mouth as if using a comb.
There are five benefits to chewing the willow twig: first, the mouth does not become bitter; second, the mouth does not [become foul]...
3. It removes wind disorders. 4. It removes heat disorders. 5. It removes phlegm and mucus. If there is any remainder, it should be discarded in a secluded place;
one must not throw it where the assembly walks or sits.

[Recorded Explanation]: Regarding "rinsing the mouth" (*chousou*): to rinse means to wash away the oily residue and slickness within the mouth with water so that it becomes clean. This is done for the sake of preaching the Dharma and performing acts of reverence, ensuring there is no obstruction to either the practice or the principle.

Rinsing the mouth purifies even the heart; sipping water brings the fragrance of a hundred flowers. When the three karmas are constantly pure, one goes to the Western Paradise together with the Buddha. Oṃ. [DAN/HEART]. Oṃ. Haṃ Svāhā (three times). [Commentary]: Regarding "rinsing the mouth purifies even the heart":

this refers to when eating, vegetable fibers or bits of food remain stuck between the teeth; if left for a long time, they cause [illness]. Thus, one must rinse the mouth thoroughly. Furthermore, after rinsing the mouth, one should sip water once more to cleanse the throat and tongue. This is called "sipping water. By doing so, the three karmas—body, speech, and mind—are purified, and one will be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss. Therefore, it is said that one goes to the Western Paradise together with the Buddha. Oṃ. [DAN/HEART]. Oṃ. Haṃ Svāhā. (Recite three times. (Note: The character [噉/心] is a variant or archaic form of *dhan*, representing the seed syllable *dhaṃ*.)

Because of this [residual] air, once the meal is finished and the tooth-stick has been used, one must rinse the mouth to wash away the debris, ensuring it is completely cleared away without remainder.
Inferring from the matter through its principle, this is not merely for the purification of the mouth, but also serves the purification of the mind. *Wen* (吻) means "to contain" or "to hold."

"The fragrance of the hundred flowers" symbolizes that cause and effect are both fully manifested. This means one should hold water in the mouth and spray it outward as the fragrance of the hundred flowers;
this precisely illustrates that when the observance of precepts is firm and true, and the essence of the mind is pure, the fragrance of the precepts will naturally be rich and pervasive.
"The three karmas are constantly pure, and together with the Buddha one goes to the Western Land" refers to the body...
When the karma of speech and mind is thus purified, the precept-essence of both vehicles naturally becomes complete.

With pure precepts as the cause and the Pure Land as the fruit, one is identical to all Buddhas, without duality or distinction. One can transcend to the Western Paradise of Ultimate Bliss in the mere snap of a finger.
One will not fall into the three realms by oneself.

Regarding the phrase "taking out the *khakkhara* staff" [from the *Ji*]: "taking out" means to bring it forth from within for the purpose of carrying it while walking. As for the "staff" (*khakkhara*), its name is manifested through eight meanings; that is to say, it can...

It lightens the afflictions, clarifies the Buddha-dharma, and enables one to emerge from the triple world without turning back. It awakens one to the True Dharma with sudden clarity, severs the pride of self, and thins out the three poisons.
By gathering the jewels of precept, concentration, and wisdom, it brings about the attainment of unsurpassed Bodhi; therefore, it is called a *khakkhara* (staff).
As for the term "staff" (*zhàng*), it means to support or rely upon. This refers to walking and practicing by relying on the staff, which can support one in departing from the three [realms].
Regarding their realms: the four-pronged staff with twelve rings is the staff of Śākyamuni Buddha; the two-pronged staff with twelve rings is the staff of Kāśyapa Buddha.
Furthermore, the applications of the Great and Small Vehicles differ, and their regulations are likewise distinct.
*Ji* (集). In Sanskrit, *khaṭvāṅga*; here translated as "staff with rings" (*sìzhàng*).
This is that which has been held by all Buddhas of the three periods of time to manifest the merit of their wisdom and conduct, and to purify afflictions and karmic obstructions.

Every day, after a bhikṣu has finished his morning meal and used his tooth-stick, he must pay homage to the Buddha and take up his staff. If there are laypeople or śrāmaṇeras present, he should have them hand it to him; if there are none...

Having prostrated three times before the Buddha and arisen, one takes up the staff oneself and carries it out. Facing east, one wipes away the dust and performs the visualization according to the Dharma;

the details of these visualization practices and ritual deportment are explained extensively in the *Śikṣāpada-dhāraṇī* (Staff Scripture). When taking hold of the staff with the hand, one silently recites this verse-mantra:
Holding the *khakkhara* staff, one should make this aspiration:
"May all sentient beings establish great assemblies of giving and reveal the path of suchness. Oṃ kṛṇkṣa kṛṇkṣa kṛṇṭhapate kṛṇḍe nayapane hūṃ phaṭ (recite three times).
[Commentary] "Holding" means to lift with the hand; it has two meanings. First, "grasping," as a ritual for practicing the Way.
Second, "shaking," as one lifts [the staff] for the purpose of begging for food, thereby giving rise to a corresponding vow. The Way of non-reliance is the true Way.
Turning toward the dharma-less state is true *nirvāṇa*. Thus, the Sūtra says: "Such a staff is indeed the Sage..."
It is the banner of humanity, the clear record of the worthy, the upright standard for those pursuing the Dharma, and the resolve for the meaning of mindfulness.

Because it possesses these four meanings, it is named the *khakkhara* (staff). Truly, the Dharma is established upon the mind, and the teaching is expounded in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.
The Dharma of the śramaṇa is to realize emptiness and attain the Way; by wielding the *khakkhara* staff, one awakens all sentient beings in the world.

Therefore, one must first make vows. To establish great assemblies of giving and demonstrate the path of reality (*yathābhūta-mārga*) is to clarify principle through phenomena and to reveal the provisional (*upāya*) based on the real.
Thus, one erects the great banner of the Dharma, opens up the correct path for humans and devas, and closes the gates of [falsehood].
To prevent sentient beings throughout the dharma-realm from entering the paths of delusion at the gates of the various evil realms, he reveals the principle of the single true mark.
By means of the wisdom of suchness, he accords with the principle of suchness; when wisdom and principle are one, they accord with the principle of the Middle Way.
Therefore, it is said that he establishes a great assembly of giving to demonstrate the path of reality as it is.

[Record]: "To spread" means to lay out and adorn. *Dhyāna* in Sanskrit is translated into Chinese as *jinglü* (静虑, meditative concentration). It signifies the non-duality of stillness and illumination;
that is, the inner mind is unstained and the external environment does not entangle it. Having stilled all conditions, one is eternally at peace, perceiving the One.
One realizes the Way through the mind; therefore, it is called *dhyāna*.
When spreading out a seat, one should wish that all sentient beings may cause the wholesome dharmas to blossom forth and perceive the true reality.
[Commentary] To spread out a sitting mat is called *fu* (spreading). That which can support the physical form is called a *chuáng* (bed).
A piece measuring three or five *chi* is a *tà* (bench); one measuring eight *chi* is a *chuáng*. There are rope beds and wooden beds, each having five types:
namely, those with curved legs, straight legs, bent legs, no legs, and those that fit into steps (*ruì-bì*). A *zuò* (seat) is a *tà* (bench). Those who study the Way [sit] upon it.

Sitting cross-legged, with the mind stilled and contemplation settled, this is the place for thoroughly investigating and clarifying the Great Matter. The following two lines reveal the principle through the practice:
this illusory shell has long been sealed and solidified by ignorance; how then could the True Principle be revealed?
It must take the precepts as its foundation. By practicing *dhyāna* and meditative concentration while seated here, the deluded mind is utterly eradicated, and wisdom manifests before one.
This refers to the clouds of delusion dispersing across the vast sky, or a clear pearl being cast into turbid water;

it means opening the net of craving born of ignorance and perceiving the true aspect (*dharmatā*) of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*). It is further said that because the mind and eyes function [to perceive], it is called "opening.

This signifies first shattering ignorance and opening the *tathāgatagarbha* to see the principle of the true aspect, just as darkness is extinguished when the sun rises; therefore, it is called "opening."
To cultivate wholesome dharmas is to perceive the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Now, this true mark is an alternative name for the source of all Buddhas and the ground of the mind (*cittabhūmi*).

Because it is free from all marks, it is identical with all phenomena; it transcends all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), is indestructible, and is neither characterized by marks nor devoid of marks.
For these reasons, it is called the "true mark."
Sitting upright with the body straight, one should wish that all sentient beings sit upon the Bodhi-seat with minds free from attachment.

Oṃ vairocani-pratiniyate svāhā. [Note] "Sitting upright with the body straight" means that the physical form being straight represents correctness; this is the bodily posture, which refers to closing the eyes and clarifying the mind.
The mind: the two hands are interlaced and stacked one upon the other. The countenance is upright and distinguished; the form is like a solitary pine. Hence it is said, "the body is straightened.
When the body is straight, the mind is straight. The *Dhyānapāramitā* fully sets forth the methods for sitting.

If in the half-lotus posture (*ardhaparyaṅka*), press the left leg over the right, drawing it close to the body so that it is level with the left and right thighs. If in the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*), further place the right leg over [the left].

Press the left [leg] like a coiled dragon, encircling and aligning the body. With the hands, press the right over the left and place them upon the right foot, also drawing them close to the body and positioning them at the heart.
All Buddhas of the past and their assemblies of disciples have practiced this method entirely;
it is not a worldly practice, nor is it shared with non-Buddhists. Because it can destroy the armies of Māra and the afflictions, [it is thus].
Internally, one should practice contemplation; further adding recitation is like adding oil to a fire. "Bodhi" is the Chinese term for the Path of Enlightenment.

"Seat" refers to the seat of the Dharma King, which is the realization that one's own nature is originally empty. This seat is inherently possessed by every person; therefore, it is said, "one should aspire [to it].
Because it is like a lotus flower, unstained [by mud], it is called "non-attachment. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "The Bodhicitta..."
This is because it is like a seed, capable of producing all the qualities of a Buddha.

There are one hundred and eighteen kinds of metaphors [in other texts], but there is no way to express this through even a single verse. Furthermore, as for "bodhi," it refers to the external cultivation of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*).
The wisdom of inner illumination is the state where all conditions are simultaneously stilled and the single mind is directed toward the Way.

As for why this is called a "seat," it is because Bodhi is the principle to be realized; thus a sutra says: "When the water of sentient beings' minds is pure, the reflection of Bodhi appears within it.
Furthermore, for the mind to have no attachments is for the sphere of mental activity to cease; because the mind does not cling, all phenomena [are as they are].
It is unarisen, for it is necessarily beyond verbal expression. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "The emptiness of all phenomena is the seat. It also says:
"Transform afflictions into bodhi," meaning that by cultivating various merits, one suddenly transcends all realms of existence.

When the defilements of consciousness and emotion are purified, ignorance is completely severed and ultimate truth manifests of itself. The *Awakening of Faith in the Mahāyāna* says: "Unobstructed, pure wisdom."

All arise from meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Thus we know that to transcend the mundane and enter the sacred, one must rely on pure conditions; to depart while seated or pass away while standing requires reliance on the power of concentration.
If even achieving liberation within a single lifetime is feared to be delayed, how much more so when one procrastinates—how then can one withstand the force of karma?
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "When seeing a painting of one sitting in the full lotus posture, even Māra is struck with awe and fear; how much more so for one who has entered the Way."
The person sits with the body upright and unswaying. Furthermore, one assumes the full-lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) for five reasons conducive to correct observation (*samyag-darśana*):
first, by sitting thus in tranquility, the body and mind are gathered and withdrawn, whereby pliancy (*praśrabdhi*) is swiftly produced; this is the most excellent [reason].
Second, by sitting thus in tranquility, it is possible to remain for a long duration without causing the body and mind to become quickly exhausted. Third, by sitting thus...

1. Seated meditation is an uncommon quality (*āveṇika-dharma*), for it has no counterpart in the paths or doctrines of others. 2. By means of this seated meditation, one’s physical appearance becomes majestic and pure;

when others see it, they develop the utmost reverence and faith. 3. By means of this seated meditation, the Buddhas and their disciples alike hear of it with joy, for it is praised by all the noble ones (*ārya*). 4. By means of this seated meditation, one’s physical form becomes majestic and pure, so that when others see it, they develop the utmost reverence and faith. 5.
By means of this seated meditation, the Buddhas and their disciples alike hear of it with joy, for it is extolled by all the worthy and holy ones (*satpuruṣa* and *ārya*).

Regarding "sleeping" (*supta*), the meaning is as explained previously. At the time of sleep, one should join the palms, face west, and recite the Buddha’s name ten times, or perhaps a hundred or a thousand times;
only after this should one recite the following verse.
